sens: Absence of reason and judgment
Irresponsible or nonsensical behavior
Words or actions devoid of wisdom
Moral or spiritual blindness
H0200.detail:
1. Folly is the absence of sound judgment, the inability or refusal to reason correctly. It is the opposite of wisdom and prudence. The psalmist confesses that his folly has led him to misery (Psalms 38:6).
2. It manifests in irresponsible and hasty acts, such as answering before listening (Proverbs 18:13), which brings confusion and shame. It is acting without weighing the consequences.
3. It appears in foolish words: the folly of the heart is expressed by the mouth (Proverbs 15:14). The simple naturally inherit this folly (Proverbs 14:18).
4. It is also moral blindness: he who commits the iniquity of folly acts against all divine reason (Proverbs 24:9). The fool delights in his foolish thoughts and sinks into them.
H0200.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes dazzling, mental confusion, wandering. It designates the state of one who has lost discernment, who no longer sees straight. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this term is constantly opposed to wisdom (hokma) and prudence (ormah): folly is not mere stupidity, but a deep disorder of the soul that rejects the truth and justice of God.
H0200.emploi: This word appears 24 times in the Hebrew text, concentrated mainly in Proverbs (22 occurrences) and Psalms (2 occurrences). Proverbs uses it to describe the behavior of the simple and the foolish: their folly characterizes them, revealing itself in their hasty words and their refusal of knowledge. The word can also refer to the foolish act itself, the guilty behavior (Proverbs 19:3): "The folly of man perverts his way." In the psalmist, it is linked to suffering and shame, signs of downfall.
H0200.portee: Understanding biblical folly helps the Christian discern the true from the false. The Bible does not tolerate willful blindness: it invites everyone to seek wisdom, to listen before speaking, to think before acting. Recognizing one's own possible folly is the beginning of true wisdom. This category reminds us that rejecting the word of God is the ultimate folly.

sens: Son of Eliphaz and grandson of Esau
Chief of an Edomite tribe during the Patriarchs
H0201.detail: 1. Omar is a figure from the Old Testament, son of Eliphaz and grandson of Esau. He appears in the genealogy of the Edomites, who descend from Esau, the older brother of Jacob. His name means "one who speaks" or "eloquent" in Hebrew. 2. Omar became a chief of tribe among the Edomites, as indicated in the genealogical lists of Genesis 36. He is named chief alongside his brothers Teman, Zepho, Kenaz, and other descendants of Eliphaz, showing his importance in the political and social structure of the Edomite tribes.
H0201.origine: The name Omar (אוֹמָר) comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to speak" or "to say." It carries the sense of "orator" or "eloquent." Omar is an Edomite ancestor, belonging to the lineage of Esau and Eliphaz, placing him at the heart of the origins of the ancient Middle Eastern peoples and the relations between Israel and its neighbors.
H0201.emploi: Omar is mentioned three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in genealogical contexts. Genesis 36:11 presents him as one of the sons of Eliphaz and grandson of Esau. Genesis 36:15 designates him as chief of tribe ("allouph") among the Edomite chiefs descended from Eliphaz. 1 Chronicles 1:36 repeats this genealogy, placing him in the line of descendants of Eliphaz. Omar never appears elsewhere in biblical narratives; his mention remains strictly genealogical, reflecting the Scripture's concern to trace the origins of peoples close to Israel.

sens: Physical strength, power of the body
Vital energy, generative capacity
Wealth, material goods
Violence, brutality
Wickedness, iniquity
Divine power
H0202.detail:
1. Vigor primarily denotes the brute strength of the body, muscular and physical power — that of a young man in full health, or that of a creature like the Behemoth. Reuben, the first son of Jacob, is called "my strength and the firstfruits of my vigor" (Genesis 49:3), an image of vital strength at the moment of youth.
2. More broadly, it is the life energy that animates a person, their capacity to act and to generate. This vital power can be exhausted or decline: he who "faints" receives from the Lord who "increases the vigor" of that one (Isaiah 40:29).
3. The word also designates accumulated wealth and goods, as a form of social and economic strength — what one possesses that makes them powerful.
4. Used in the plural or in certain contexts, it takes on a negative sense: vigor becomes violence, brutality exercised against others. He who accumulates by violence loses "what he has taken by violence" (Job 20:10).
5. With the moral context, the word accompanies the idea of malice: we speak of "wicked men," that is, strength put to the service of evil (Proverbs 11:7).
6. Finally, vigor is an attribute of God, His creative and sovereign power that sustains all things.
H0202.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of energy, generative power. It is a concrete term that first designates the strength of the body and life, before extending to wealth (economic strength) and violence (misdirected strength). The same root is found in other biblical words related to power and action. It is a term from the depths of the Hebrew vocabulary, carrying the primitive image of vital power.
H0202.emploi: The word appears thirteen times in the Old Testament, especially in biblical poetry (Psalms, Proverbs, Job) and in prophetic oracles. In Genesis and Deuteronomy, it evokes physical strength and the vitality of youth (birthright, patriarchal blessing). In Job, it often takes on a negative nuance: strength becomes brutality, violence, or is exhausted in sickness. The Psalms celebrate the divine vigor that sustains creatures. Isaiah uses the word to describe God's eternal power that surpasses all human weakness. Hosea sees it as Jacob's struggle power against the angel. The meaning thus shifts between beneficial strength (that of youth, of God) and malevolent strength (that of the wicked, of the oppressor).
H0202.portee: This word reminds the reader that strength — physical, economic, even moral — lasts only a time and remains under God's control. For the wicked, their vigor becomes violence, a power that will be destroyed. For the believer, it invites seeking strength not in wealth or violence, but in the Lord, whose vigor never exhausts. It is an invitation to humility in the face of a power greater than our own.

sens: Man of the time of Egypt and the desert
Chief of the tribe of Reuben
Rebel against Moses
H0203.detail: 1. On is a man who lived during the time when Israel was in Egypt and in the desert of Sinai. 2. He was an important chief of the tribe of Reuben, son of Peleth. His name means "wealth" or "strength" in Hebrew, which suits his status as chief. 3. On rebelled against Moses and Aaron, alongside Dathan and Abiram, other sons of Reuben, as well as Korah, a Levite. This rebellion is reported in Numbers 16:1, the only place where he is mentioned.
H0203.origine: The name On comes from Hebrew and means "wealth" or "vigor." It evokes power and abundance — an appropriate name for a tribal chief. This man only appears in the account of the rebellion in Numbers, where he embodies pride and contestation of the divine authority established by Moses.
H0203.emploi: On is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in Numbers 16:1, where he is presented as one of the three sons of Reuben who rebel against Moses and Aaron. He is associated with Dathan, Abiram, and Korah in what will be a terrible judgment from God. Unlike Dathan and Abiram, whose story is more developed, On disappears from the narrative after this initial mention: his specific fate is not reported.
H0203.portee: The mention of On reminds us that rebellion against the authority that God has established in His people is serious and leads to judgment. Although powerful and chief of his tribe, no wealth or influence can save one who stands against God's plan. His story invites the Christian to examine their heart in relation to spiritual authority.

sens: City of ancient Egypt, center of sun worship
Residence of the priest Potipherah, father-in-law of Joseph
H0204.detail:
1. On is a city located in Lower Egypt, near the Nile delta, famous in antiquity as a major religious center dedicated to the worship of the sun god. It is here that Pharaoh appointed Potipherah as priest (Genesis 41:45).
2. Potipherah, priest of On, is the father of Asenath, the woman whom Pharaoh gives to Joseph after elevating him to the position of governor. Through this marriage, Joseph integrates into the Egyptian elite and becomes the son-in-law of a high-ranking figure (Genesis 41:45, 41:50).
H0204.origine: The name On means "strength" or "vigor" in Hebrew, an image fitting for a city of religious and political power. On is the Egyptian city of Heliopolis in Greek ("city of the sun"), a major center of study and worship. It represented one of the most prestigious religious cities in Egypt.
H0204.emploi: On appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in connection with Potipherah. It is mentioned during Joseph's marriage to Asenath (Genesis 41:45), during the birth of his sons Manasseh and Ephraim (Genesis 41:50 and 46:20), and once in prophecy (Ezekiel 30:17). These references establish it as a strategic location in ancient Egypt where great religious authority prevailed.

sens: Act or state of wickedness, moral guilt
Suffering or trouble caused by sin
Idolatrous behavior, abandonment of God
Deceitful word or action intended to do harm
H0205G.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes iniquity in a moral sense: the evil committed willingly, the guilt of one who transgresses God's law. In Proverbs 17:4, the wicked man is attentive to the "perverse lip," meaning the word that expresses evil with intent. This is the heart of sin: a rebellious attitude against God.

2. This word also evokes the trouble and suffering that accompany the iniquitous act. When one sows iniquity, one reaps pain: in Job 4:8, "those who plow iniquity" harvest its sorrow. This is the natural effect of sin on the one who commits it.

3. The term includes idolatry, the turning of the heart away from God. In 1 Samuel 15:23, "disobedience" is compared to "divination" and "idolatry," grouped under the same type of guilt: preferring something other than God and His word.

4. Iniquity manifests through deceitful speech and wicked plans. In Isaiah 59:4, men "conceive evil and give birth to crime," showing how malice germinates in the heart before translating into harmful acts.
H0205G.origine: The Hebrew word אָוֶן comes from a root that first evokes emptiness, vanity, then the disorder and ruin brought about by sin. Related terms in Hebrew mean "fragility" and "nothingness." In the ancient Greek Bible, this word is translated by Greek terms denoting injustice and moral evil. Iniquity is essentially the absence of righteousness, the deviation from the just order that God has established.
H0205G.emploi: This word appears 66 times in the Old Testament, particularly in the Psalms and in the book of Job, where it describes the behavior of the wicked and its consequences. In the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel), iniquity is what Israel must abandon to repent. In Job, it is primarily the trouble and suffering caused by evil: he who sows iniquity reaps it. In the Psalms, the believer asks God to deliver him and to judge those who commit iniquity. In Proverbs, it characterizes the wicked man who speaks falsely and acts maliciously. The word can qualify an isolated action (a wicked word, a wicked plan) or the general state of the wicked.
H0205G.portee: Understanding "iniquity" helps the reader see that sin is not an isolated act, but a deviation of the heart towards God, which produces trouble and suffering. This word calls for repentance: in Isaiah 55:7, he who abandons his wicked thoughts to turn to the Lord finds compassion. It is also a reminder that our lives depend on God's justice, and that we need His help to turn away from it.

sens: trouble, distress, moral pain
misfortune, calamity
H0205H.detail:
1. This word primarily denotes an inner trouble, a distress of the soul in the face of sin or suffering. It is the feeling of unease and guilt that accompanies injustice, as when one "sows iniquity" (Proverbs 22:8): one brings forth evil that returns upon oneself. In Numbers 23:21, the seer declares that God "sees no iniquity in Jacob" — He does not see this moral stain that disfigures Israel.
2. More broadly, the word describes the misfortunes and calamities that result: physical suffering, mourning (Deuteronomy 26:14), days filled with "pain and misery" (Psalms 90:10). It is the weight of sin that weighs upon life and history. In Proverbs 12:21, "no misfortune befalls the righteous," while "the wicked are burdened with evils" — the word here expresses the cascade of torments that follows sin.
H0205H.origine: This Hebrew word expresses the idea of a curve that turns away, a deviation from the right path. It thus designates sin as a twisting of the divine order, from which suffering arises. The family of this word in Hebrew includes other terms describing pain and effort. Its primary image is that of a rupture: it breaks peace, it splits life in two — on one side innocence, on the other trouble and punishment.
H0205H.emploi: This word appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Wisdom literature (Job, Psalms, Proverbs) and among the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Hosea, Amos, Habakkuk). It always concentrates on the link between sin and its consequences: it is sown, it is reaped; it is carried in the heart, it becomes mourning and misery. In texts of mourning and lamentation (Deuteronomy 26:14, Psalms 90:10), it takes on a tone of personal sorrow. Among the prophets, it becomes collective iniquity, marking Israel's rupture with its God. The word does not change root: it always retains this alliance of sin and suffering.
H0205H.portee: This word reminds the believer that evil is not an accident of the world, but a moral reality: sin naturally produces misery. It invites one not to seek the innocent guilty: if calamity strikes, it is because an iniquity has preceded it. But it also opens up hope: recognizing one's iniquity is recognizing that only God can wash it away and restore peace.

sens: Region or valley in Syria
Place of idolatrous worship
H0206G.detail:
1. Beth-eden (literally meaning "house of Eden") is a region or valley located in Syria, mentioned by the prophet Amos as an important political and religious center of the kingdom of Aram (Syria) in the 8th century B.C. (Amos 1:5).
2. The prophet uses this name contemptuously to designate a place of idolatry and perverted worship: the word "Eden" is used ironically, for unlike the biblical garden of Eden, which was a place of divine blessing, this valley had become a center of false religions and religious practices that opposed the worship of the true God.
H0206G.origine: The name "Beth-eden" consists of two elements: "Beth" (בֵּית) means "house" and "Eden" (עֵדֶן) refers to the garden of Eden, the primordial paradise of Genesis. However, in Amos 1:5, it designates a real Syrian valley, probably the Bekaa or a nearby region. The prophet chooses this name ironically, as it contrasts the glorious name evoking paradise with the reality of a place given over to idolatry.
H0206G.emploi: Beth-eden appears only once in the Bible, in the prophecy of Amos concerning God's judgment on Damascus and Syria. The prophet announces that the "barriers" (the defenses) of Damascus will be broken and that the inhabitants of the region of Beth-eden will be exterminated, while the one who "holds the scepter" (the king or governor) will be taken captive. Amos uses this place as a concrete example of the power and authority that God is about to destroy among the neighboring nations of Israel.
H0206G.portee: For the Christian reader, Beth-eden illustrates how God judges the nations that turn away from Him and plunge into idolatry. The ironic contrast of the name reminds us that false religion, even if it bears an attractive name, leads to ruin, while only the true worship of the God of Israel brings blessing.

sens: Place of idol worship in Israel
Derogatory nickname given to Bethel
H0206H.detail:
1. Beth-Aven is the name of an Israelite sanctuary where idolatry was practiced, particularly the worship of the golden calf. The prophet Hosea calls it this to denounce Israel's rebellion: "The high places of Beth-Aven, where Israel has sinned, shall be destroyed" (Hosea 10:8). It is a center of false religion that God judges and will destroy.
2. Beth-Aven is a derogatory nickname for Bethel, the great sanctuary of Northern Israel. By calling this place "Beth-Aven" (house of vanity), Hosea expresses divine disdain for Israel's corrupt religious practices. Instead of serving the true God, Israel worships idols, transforming a once-holy place into a symbol of spiritual vanity.
H0206H.origine: The name comes from two Hebrew words: "beth" meaning "house" and "aven" meaning "vanity" or "nothingness." The full name, "Beth-Aven," literally means "house of vanity." It is a critical play on words: the prophet refuses to call this place Bethel ("house of God") and instead calls it Beth-Aven to emphasize that this once-holy place has become nothing but a house of vanity and idol worship.
H0206H.emploi: Beth-Aven appears only once in the Bible, in Hosea 10:8. The prophet Hosea uses it to severely criticize the religious degeneration of Northern Israel. In Hosea's time (8th century BC), the once-important sanctuary of Bethel had become a center of idol worship with golden calves. By calling it Beth-Aven, Hosea denounces this corruption and announces that God will destroy these high places of sin. It is a prophetic act of renaming: to rename the place is to reveal its true nature in the eyes of God.
H0206H.portee: This name reminds us that a corrupt religion, even practiced in an ancient holy place, becomes vain in the eyes of God. It warns us to remain vigilant: it is not enough to have traditions or consecrated places; one must have a heart that sincerely seeks the true God. Hosea calls us to examine our own worship: do we worship God in truth, or have we allowed hollow habits to replace a living relationship with Him?

sens: City of Benjamin in ancient Palestine
Valley near Ono, known for its craftsmen
H0207.detail: 1. Ono is a fortified city located in the land of Benjamin, within the territory of Israel. It was built by Shemer, son of Elpaal (1 Chronicles 8:12), and after the exile, it housed a significant population: its inhabitants are counted among the repatriates (Ezra 2:33 and Nehemiah 7:37). 2. Nearby was a valley of Ono, also called the "valley of workers" or "valley of craftsmen" (Nehemiah 11:35), likely because skilled workers—carpenters, masons, potters—had their workshops there. It was in this region that Sanballat and Geshem attempted to trap Nehemiah by proposing a meeting (Nehemiah 6:2).
H0207.origine: The name literally means "vigorous" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking the strength or fertility of the site. Ono also had another name, Kephirim ("the young lions"), which reinforces this image of power and life.
H0207.emploi: Ono appears five times in the Bible, always as a concrete geographical location. Three mentions are found in the lists of returnees after the Babylonian exile (1 Chronicles 8:12, Ezra 2:33, Nehemiah 7:37), where it is listed among the cities inhabited by the repatriates from Judah. Two other passages situate it historically: Nehemiah 11:35 describes its valley as a center of artisan activity, and Nehemiah 6:2 shows how this retreat location served as the setting for a conspiracy attempt against Nehemiah during the reconstruction of Jerusalem.

sens: Horite chief, grandson of Seir
Son of Jerahmeel, chief of Judah
H0208G.detail: Onam is a character from the Old Testament mentioned twice in the Bible. The first Onam is a Horite chief (a people established in Edom), son of Shobal and grandson of Seir (Genesis 36:23). The second Onam is a chief of Judah, son of Jerahmeel, mentioned in the genealogy of this tribe (1 Chronicles 1:40). These two Onams are ancestors whose names the Bible preserves in genealogical lists, witnesses to the history of the Hebrew people and neighboring peoples.
H0208G.origine: The name Onam means "vigorous" in Hebrew. It appears in the genealogies of Genesis as the name of important ancestors, particularly among the Horites and in the lineage of Judah. This name reflects the values valued in ancient Middle Eastern cultures: strength and vigor.
H0208G.emploi: Onam is mentioned twice in the Bible. The first mention is found in Genesis 36:23, where he is listed among the sons of Shobal, who was a Horite chief and grandson of Seir. The second mention appears in 1 Chronicles 1:40, in a parallel genealogy that also lists the sons of Shobal. These two occurrences are genealogical lists that establish the lineages of the peoples prior to the emergence of Israel.

sens: Chief of the tribe of Judah during the united monarchy
Son of Jerahmeel and Atharah
H0208H.detail: Onam is a man from the clan of Jerahmeel, himself a descendant of Judah. He appears in the genealogy of Judah as the son of Jerahmeel and Atharah (1 Chronicles 2:26). He had two sons, Shammai and Jada, who are also mentioned as family leaders (1 Chronicles 2:28), showing that Onam founded an important branch of the Jerahmeel clan.
H0208H.origine: The name Onam means "vigorous" or "strong" in Hebrew, which evokes power and the ability to found a dynasty. The genealogies in the First Book of Chronicles mention him among the prominent figures of the Jerahmeel clan, an important family of the tribe of Judah.
H0208H.emploi: Onam is mentioned twice in the Bible, both in the First Book of Chronicles. He first appears in 1 Chronicles 2:26 as the son of Jerahmeel and Atharah, and then in 1 Chronicles 2:28 where his two sons, Shammai and Jada, are listed. These mentions are part of a long genealogy of the descendants of Judah, showing the transmission of heritage and family authority within the Jerahmeel clan.

sens: Second son of Judah
Man known for his disobedience to the duty of the brother-in-law
H0209.detail: Onan is the second son of Judah and Bathshua, first mentioned in Genesis 38:4. He is the brother of Er (the eldest) and Shelah. Upon the death of Er, Judah commands him to take his brother's widow to raise up offspring for him, according to the custom of the time (Genesis 38:8). But Onan deliberately refuses to fulfill this duty: he spills his seed on the ground during his relations with the woman, so that the offspring would not be his brother's (Genesis 38:9). This willful disobedience provokes God's anger, and Onan dies in the land of Canaan (Genesis 46:12). His name remains linked to this act of rebellion against the established order and familial duty.
H0209.origine: The name Onan means "strong" or "powerful." He belongs to the lineage of Judah, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. Onan appears in the genealogy of Judah in Genesis 38, a foundational passage that also explains how the messianic lineage passes through Perez, the son that Judah had with Tamar after the death of his two eldest sons.
H0209.emploi: Onan appears six times in the Bible, all in Genesis 38, 46, and 1 Chronicles 2, in the genealogical lists of Judah. In Genesis 38, the narrative details his act of disobedience and his immediate death as punishment. He is then mentioned as deceased in the land of Canaan in the enumerations of Numbers 26:19 and 1 Chronicles 2:3, where he appears alongside his brother Er, also dead. His story illustrates the importance that the Law places on levirate marriage, a sacred duty toward the family of the deceased.
H0209.portee: The story of Onan teaches that God watches over the respect of covenant duties and family solidarity. His swift punishment shows the seriousness of rebellion against the order that God establishes, even concerning succession and the transmission of the name. For the Christian reader, this story highlights how God governs generations and leads His people toward Christ, despite the weakness and disobedience of men.

sens: Region or city renowned for its high-quality gold
H0210.detail: Uphaz is a famous geographical location in antiquity known for the fineness and purity of its gold. The Bible mentions it twice, each time in connection with precious gold: in Jeremiah 10:9, the gold of Uphaz is imported to Tarshish as raw material for idols, and in Daniel 10:5, the gold of Uphaz adorns the belt of a celestial being, highlighting the extreme preciousness of this gold.
H0210.origine: The name Uphaz means "desire for fine gold" or "thirst for gold," emphasizing the wealth of this place. Its Hebrew etymology underscores both the commercial appeal and the mineral reality of this region, which was a prestigious center for the export of precious metals in the ancient world.
H0210.emploi: Uphaz appears twice in the Bible: in Jeremiah 10:9, in a critique of idols that are gilded with the gold of Uphaz imported from Tarshish, showing the luxury and vanity of these human creations; in Daniel 10:5, the gold of Uphaz adorns the belt of a celestial figure, revealing a magnificence worthy of the divine realm. These two usages highlight the exceptional value of the gold from this place, used either for the ornamentation of handmade gods or for that of a divine messenger.
H0210.portee: The contrast between the two uses of Uphaz illuminates the biblical distinction between human wealth and divine glory: the most beautiful earthly gold only serves to adorn vain creations, while the same precious material naturally suits the celestial presence. This invites the reader to reflect on where their gaze and desire truly lie.

sens: son of Joktan in the genealogy of Noah
region in southern Arabia famous for its fine gold
gold of exceptional quality
H0211G.detail:
1. Ophir is a character in the Old Testament: one of the twelve sons of Joktan, mentioned in the genealogy tracing back to Noah (Genesis 10:29). He is an ancestor of the peoples of southeastern Arabia.
2. Very quickly, Ophir also designates a geographical region in southern Arabia, renowned for its wealth in gold: it was a destination on the trade routes during the reign of King Solomon. The name of the character and that of the land become conflated, as often happens in ancient genealogies.
3. By extension, "Ophir" becomes synonymous with pure and precious gold: "gold of Ophir" refers to gold of the highest quality, as the region was famous for its gold mines or gold trade.
4. The name also carries a meaning: it evokes the idea of reducing to ashes, perhaps in reference to the process of refining gold by fire.
H0211G.origine: The Hebrew name אוֹפִיר (Ophir) literally means "to reduce to ashes" or "to burn" — an image that fits the gold purified by fire. Like many proper names in genealogies, it first designates a human ancestor, then becomes the name of a region believed to be the cradle of his descendants. Biblical geography identifies this region in southwestern Arabia, a territory of intense commercial exchanges.
H0211G.emploi: Ophir appears twice in the Bible: in Genesis 10:29 and in 1 Chronicles 1:23, in the same genealogies of the sons of Joktan. It is a personal name in a genealogical context where the eponymous ancestors found nations. The biblical text does not recount anything particular about Ophir as a character; it is his existence in this lineage that gives meaning to the name. Later traditions and historical literature from the time of King Solomon often associate Ophir with distant gold expeditions, but the Bible itself does not elaborate on this narrative in detail.
H0211G.portee: For the Christian reader, Ophir reminds us that Genesis inscribes the history of the known world in a unified genealogy: each people and each region has its place in God's plan. It is also a sign of the extent of trade and prosperity that God allows human kingdoms, especially Israel under Solomon — a reminder that material wealth can be a gift from God when it is not the object of idolatrous desire.

sens: Region or trading port in southern Arabia
Place renowned for the extraction and trade of fine gold
H0211H.detail:
1. Ophir designates a region or port located in southern Arabia, on a major trade route used by merchant ships from the ancient Near East. It was an exchange point where goods were traded for local products (1 Kings 9:28).
2. Ophir became famous in the Bible as the source of gold of exceptional quality, as its reputation was well established. This gold was so prized that the psalmist can refer to "the gold of Ophir" (Psalms 45:10) and Isaiah to the "fine gold of Ophir" (Isaiah 13:12) as symbols of supreme value. Solomon's trading expeditions to Ophir brought back massive quantities of pure gold (1 Kings 10:11; 2 Chronicles 8:18).
H0211H.origine: The Hebrew name אוֹפִיר likely reflects a historical locality in southern Arabia, although its exact geography remains debated among historians. The proposed ancient etymology ("to reduce to ashes") does not correspond to the biblical usages of the word, which never denotes an action but always this specific place. Ophir is mentioned in the annals of ancient Levantine trade voyages.
H0211H.emploi: Ophir appears 11 times in the Bible, primarily in the accounts of the reign of Solomon and his son Jehoshaphat (1 Kings and 2 Chronicles), both of whom sent maritime expeditions to seek gold. Solomon's ships, in partnership with King Hiram of Tyre, sailed to Ophir and brought back enormous quantities of gold (1 Kings 9:28; 2 Chronicles 8:18). An expedition of Jehoshaphat failed before reaching Ophir, as his ships were wrecked (1 Kings 22:49). The word also appears in the poetic books (Job, Psalms, Isaiah), where "the gold of Ophir" or "the fine gold of Ophir" becomes a proverbial expression for the most precious and coveted gold.
H0211H.portee: Ophir reminds the reader of the immense wealth of Solomon's reign and the glory of Jerusalem at the time of its political and commercial splendor. It is also a biblical symbol: the best gold, that which cannot be replaced, evokes what has the greatest value — the most worthy of being sought and kept.

sens: Circular object that turns on an axis and allows a vehicle to roll
Wheel of a war or transport chariot
Mysterious wheel in the prophetic vision of Ezekiel
Wheel carrying the basins of Solomon's temple
H0212.detail:
1. A wheel is a disc or ring that turns around a central axle, allowing a vehicle or object to move. In Exodus 14:25, the Lord removes the wheels from the Egyptian chariots to slow them down at the Red Sea: these are the ordinary wheels of war chariots.
2. Military chariots and transport vehicles had wheels essential to their operation. In 1 Kings 7:33, it is precisely described how the wheels are constructed: they have their axles, rims, spokes, and hubs, all made of cast metal, to support the weight of the chariot.
3. In Ezekiel's vision (1:15-20 and chapter 10), the wheels are mysterious and divine: there are four wheels filled with eyes all around, which move with the cherubim carrying the divine throne. They do not change direction but go where the spirit leads them, embodying divine Providence.
4. In Solomon's temple, King Hiram made bronze wheels to carry the ten basins for the priestly washings (1 Kings 7:30-33). These technical wheels allow the worship furniture to be both stable and mobile.
H0212.origine: The Hebrew word אוֹפָן (ophan) literally means a wheel that turns. It comes from a root expressing rotation and circular movement. The word also appears in biblical compositions and in Talmudic tradition. In Greek, it is translated as τροχός (trokhos, wheel). This notion of a wheel is universal in the Near Eastern antiquity: it represents one of the greatest technical advances, enabling transport and mobility.
H0212.emploi: The word "wheel" appears 21 times, mainly in the historical and prophetic books. In the historical accounts (Exodus, 1 Kings), it describes ordinary wheels of chariots and temple furniture. In Ezekiel, the same word refers to supernatural wheels: the vision shows four complex wheels, full of eyes, linked to the cherubim. This same mysterious wheel reappears in chapter 10, where Ezekiel sees it again near the divine throne during the glory that departs from the temple. The contrast shows that the word retains its material reality (an object that turns), but its use by the prophet elevates it to a spiritual dimension. In Nahum 3:2, we hear the noise of the wheels galloping: the image of the wheel evokes speed and military power.
H0212.portee: The ordinary wheel reminds us that the God of Israel masters material means: He can paralyze enemy chariots and protect His people. The mysterious wheels of Ezekiel's vision teach that divine Providence, though incomprehensible to our eyes, is always vigilant (represented by the eyes) and follows the movement of God's throne without ever erring. It is an invitation to trust in the invisible guidance of the Lord over our lives.

sens: To go quickly, to hasten one's action
To urge someone, to strongly encourage them to act
To be narrow, cramped, lacking space
To act with haste, without reflection
H0213.detail: 1. To hurry means to go quickly or to rush, like the sun that "did not hurry to set" (Joshua 10:13): it is to put speed and urgency into what one does. 2. To insist on someone means to strongly urge them to act: the angels "insisted" with Lot to push him to leave quickly (Genesis 19:15), just as the inspectors "pressed" the slaves to speed up their work (Exodus 5:13). 3. To be narrow or cramped means to not have enough space: the mountain of Ephraim is "too narrow" for the numerous people (Joshua 17:15), it lacks room. 4. To act with haste means to rush without thinking or planning: one who "hurries his steps" falls into sin (Proverbs 19:2), while one who acts with "haste" only ends up in want (Proverbs 21:5).
H0213.origine: The Hebrew verb אוּץ comes from a root that expresses the idea of pressure and narrowness. It has given rise to names that denote discomfort, anguish, and is found in other words of the same family evoking cramped places or pressing situations. The basic image is that of compression, a force that pushes or constricts.
H0213.emploi: This verb appears 10 times in the Old Testament, mainly in Proverbs and historical accounts. In Proverbs (19:2; 21:5; 28:20; 29:20), it carries a moral warning: haste leads to error and failure, while reflection and patience produce abundance. In historical accounts (Genesis 19:15; Exodus 5:13), it describes the action of exerting strong pressure on someone to make them move forward. The word can also describe a physical constraint: a space that has become too narrow (Joshua 17:15). Its meaning thus varies between the urgency to act, the act of pressing others, and the notion of narrowness or discomfort.
H0213.portee: This word reminds us that haste can be a spiritual danger. Proverbs warns against acting without reflection: it is a form of folly. Foolish haste contrasts with patient wisdom. At the same time, the context of Lot showing the angels insisting reminds us that there is a rightful urgency, that of pressing salvation, where delaying would mean perishing. The believer must discern between good urgency and false haste.

sens: Precious wealth: gold, silver, valuable objects
Reserve of food or stored provisions
Place where wealth or provisions are kept
Hidden or mysterious reserve (figuratively)
H0214.detail:
1. A treasure is primarily a concrete, precious, and accumulated wealth: gold, silver, jewels, or objects of great value. When Hezekiah shows the envoys "the silver and gold, the spices and the precious oil" from his treasures (2 Kings 20:13), he displays what he possesses that is most precious. This is what the people bring for the construction of the temple (1 Chronicles 29:8).
2. The treasure can also refer to a reserve of food or provisions—food, water, wine—stored for times of need or scarcity. This concerns the necessary reserves for daily life.
3. The word then designates the very place where these riches or provisions are kept: a room in the palace, a chamber in the temple, a warehouse (1 Chronicles 28:12 mentions the "chambers" for the treasures of the temple). It is a building or a closed room, guarded, intended for secure storage.
4. In a figurative or mysterious sense, the Bible speaks of God's "treasures": the reserves of heaven—rain, snow, hail, wind, seas (Deuteronomy 28:12; Job 38:22)—which God alone controls. These images show that God holds all the forces of creation in His hand and releases them according to His wisdom.
H0214.origine: The Hebrew word אוֹצָר (otsar) comes from a root that literally means "to enclose" or "to keep closed." That is why a treasure is primarily what is enclosed, what is protected, what is set apart from the common. The word thus designates both the precious object (what is enclosed) and the place where it is enclosed (what encloses). This idea of a "kept reserve" is central: one does not leave a treasure lying around, one locks it up.
H0214.emploi: The word appears about 70 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books (Kings, Chronicles) and prophetic writings. It concretely describes the wealth of kings—Hezekiah showing his treasures, kings plundering them in cases of ransom (2 Kings 12:18; 20:13-15), the spoils dedicated to the temple (Joshua 6:19). It is also used for public reserves, donations for worship (Nehemiah 7:70; 12:44). In a figurative sense, especially among the prophets and in the Psalms, it describes God's "treasures": His meteorological reserves (Job 38:22; Psalms 135:7), His arsenals (Jeremiah 50:25), His hidden secrets (Isaiah 45:3). Proverbs uses the word to contrast material treasure with moral treasure: better is little with the fear of God than great treasure with trouble (Proverbs 15:16).
H0214.portee: This word helps the reader understand that all wealth—material, food, natural—is something precious that must be managed with wisdom and responsibility. It also teaches that God fully controls the hidden forces of the world, which He keeps in reserve for the good of His creation. For the believer, this reminds us that true wealth is not the accumulation of earthly goods, but the relationship with God.

sens: To give light, to shine
To become bright, to light up
To make clear and visible what was obscure
To make the face or appearance shine
To symbolically illuminate the mind or heart
H0215.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is to produce or emit physical light: the celestial bodies that illuminate the earth (Genesis 1:15), the lamps of the lampstand that must shine in front (Numbers 8:2), the fire that lights up the night in the desert (Nehemiah 9:19). The verb describes the action of making visible by light.

2. When the word means "to become bright," it speaks of the transition from darkness to light: the day that rises and brightens, or a face that shines. It is the effect produced on what receives the light.

3. In a broader usage, to illuminate means "to bring to light," to make understandable: God's words "illuminate" in the sense that they provide understanding (Psalms 119:130). It is to enlighten the mind.

4. The word can also describe the radiance of a face or appearance: wisdom makes the face of the one who possesses it shine (Ecclesiastes 8:1), or God's face "shines" upon us as a sign of blessing (Psalms 67:2).

5. In a more figurative or theological sense, to illuminate means "to radiate" God's grace or glory upon a person or people, transforming them inwardly and outwardly.
H0215.origine: This verb comes from the Hebrew root אור, which expresses the fundamental idea of light and clarity. The root also exists in neighboring Semitic languages. It gives rise in Hebrew to the noun אוֹר (or), "light," and to several derivatives related to illumination. The verb encompasses all aspects of the luminous process: to shine, to illuminate, to light up, depending on the grammatical form used. It is a very ancient word that dates back to the origins of the Hebrew language.
H0215.emploi: This verb appears 43 times in the Old Testament, notably in Genesis, Psalms, and the poetic books. Its usage is very varied: it first describes the physical light of celestial bodies and fire (Genesis 1, Exodus 13-14), then the illumination of the face as a sign of blessing or happiness (Psalms 67, Ecclesiastes 8:1), and later in Psalms it takes on a figurative meaning when speaking of the light of the Law or the Word that enlightens understanding (Psalms 119:130). The verb also appears in prayers asking God to shine His face upon us (Numbers 6:25, Psalms 67:2), which means granting us His favor. In the accounts of the Exodus, it is the pillar of fire that illuminates the Hebrews in the darkness of the desert (Nehemiah 9:19).
H0215.portee: This word invites the reader to consider how God reveals Himself and guides His people through light — concrete physical light in the Exodus, but also the spiritual light of His Word and His face. To illuminate expresses both divine protection and the inner illumination that wisdom and the Law bring. It is a word that speaks of clarity, truth, and the reassuring presence of God amidst our darkness.

sens: The clarity produced by a light source (sun, moon, stars, lamp, fire)
The day, the time when it is light
The dawn, the daybreak, the rising of the sun
Prosperity, well-being, joy
Instruction, wisdom, knowledge of the truth
The radiant face of a person, their living brightness
H0216.detail:
1. It is primarily the concrete light that illuminates the world. When God says, "Let there be light!", He creates this clarity that makes creation visible (Genesis 1:3). The light can come from the sun, the moon, the stars, or a lamp — anything that illuminates the darkness.

2. The word also refers to the day itself, the time when it is light. It is the time when one can see and act, as opposed to night. When one "walks in the light of the living," one benefits from the life and activity of the day (Psalms 56:14).

3. Light can be the dawn, the moment when the darkness of night gives way to increasing clarity. It is that instant when night ends and a new day begins.

4. The word is also used figuratively for prosperity and joy: someone who receives divine favor "shines," enjoying a happy and secure life. This goes hand in hand with well-being and the absence of misfortune.

5. Light symbolizes instruction and wisdom — the opposite of ignorance. God's Law is called a light because it guides those who follow it and shows them the way of truth (Proverbs 6:23). Only the knowledge of the truth clarifies life.

6. Light can also shine upon the face, expressing the joy, confidence, and kindness of the one who bears witness to it — it is the radiance of authentic life that manifests on the features.
H0216.origine: The Hebrew word אוֹר comes from a simple root expressing the idea of clarity and brightness. It is linked to the primary notion of what makes visible and drives away darkness. This word is found in the Old Testament to translate the divine action of creating and maintaining the clarity of the world. The biblical context imbues this word with a progressive spiritual meaning: from physical light, the word rises to wisdom, well-being, and ultimately to God Himself as the source of all clarity and guidance.
H0216.emploi: This word is among the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible, used about 110 times. It appears as early as the first chapter of Genesis at the heart of the creative act, then is constantly used to describe the day, the dawn, and visibility. Psalms and Proverbs use it extensively in a figurative sense: light becomes the image of divine favor (Psalms 27:1, 36:10), of wisdom (Proverbs 6:23), and of the joy of living. Isaiah uses this word to announce deliverance and restoration — when God makes His light shine, it is a sign of redemption. The contrast between light and darkness structures almost the entire biblical thought: light is always good, guidance, divine presence, while darkness symbolizes evil and absence.
H0216.portee: To understand the word "light" in the Bible is to grasp how God relates to us. Light is never accidental: it is the divine action that drives away darkness, reveals truth, and gives meaning to life. The Christian who meditates on this word understands that living "in the light of God" means walking in the clarity of His word, enjoying His favor, and becoming a reflection of that light in the world. When God is our light, nothing can cause us to lose ourselves in darkness.

sens: Flames and heat that burn a material
Light and heat from the hearth or kitchen
Destruction by fire
Burning environment or center
H0217A.detail:
1. Fire in the literal sense: visible combustion with its flames and heat. In Isaiah 44:16, a man burns wood and says, "I see the flame!" while warming himself — it is the everyday fire that warms and cooks food.
2. Fire as a symbol of divine power or judgment. In Isaiah 31:9, God has "His fire in Zion": it is not just a simple hearth, but the power of the Lord that protects His city and consumes its enemies.
3. Destruction by fire, which consumes everything in its path. In Isaiah 47:14, the fire consumes the stubble (the enemies) without leaving embers to warm oneself — it is total ruin, swift and without remainder.
4. Fire as an element of divine punishment, to which one is delivered. In Isaiah 50:11, those who kindle their own fire will lie "in the midst" of this flaming fire: the expression then designates the heart or center of the blaze, a place of suffering.
H0217A.origine: The Hebrew word אוּר (ur) comes from a root expressing illumination and heat. It belongs to the family of words describing light and energy: similar roots are found in other Semitic languages. The basic image is that of fire that burns, illuminates, and destroys — it is the concrete, visible fire, both of daily life and of divine judgment.
H0217A.emploi: The word אוּר appears 5 times in the provided usages, all in the prophets Isaiah and Ezekiel. It primarily refers to ordinary fire, the one lit for cooking or heating (Isaiah 44:16; 47:14). But very often in these passages, fire takes on a theological dimension: the fire of the Lord (Isaiah 31:9) that consumes enemies, or the fire of judgment to which the rebels are delivered (Isaiah 50:11; Ezekiel 5:2). The prophets thus use this concrete word to express divine anger and its destructive consequences. The usage varies between literal fire, metaphorical fire of judgment, and even fire as a "medium" or center of destruction (Isaiah 50:11).
H0217A.portee: Understanding this word helps grasp how the prophets speak of God's judgment: not by abstraction, but by the powerful and terrifying image of fire that destroys everything. It also shows that the destruction of God's enemies is not a distant theology, but a concrete and inevitable reality. For the believer, the fire of God can be both protective (Isaiah 31:9) and destructive (Isaiah 50:11): it all depends on one's position before the Lord.

sens: Emit light, radiate
Glisten, stand out by its brightness
Be illustrious, famous
H0217B.detail:
1. Shine means properly to emit light, as fire or stars do. In Isaiah 24:15, the prophet calls to glorify the Lord "in the places where light shines," evoking the illuminated regions of the world, particularly the East from which the light of day comes.
2. The word also designates the act of shining, standing out with a particular brightness. It is the image of a light that does not go unnoticed, that catches the eye.
3. Figuratively, to shine can mean to be illustrious or famous, radiating glory or honor — a moral light rather than a physical one.
H0217B.origine: The Hebrew root conveys the idea of flame or luminous region, particularly associated with the East, from which the morning light arises. The word belongs to the family of Hebrew terms that express clarity and brightness. The underlying image is that of fire or light illuminating space.
H0217B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 24:15. The prophet, in a passage that celebrates divine judgment and the restored future, calls the peoples to glorify the Lord "in the places where light shines." The expression "places where light shines" likely refers to the eastern lands, the islands, and the illuminated regions of the known world, that is, the distant nations that must also give glory to God. The use of the verb "shine" reinforces the idea of a divine light that extends to all creation.
H0217B.portee: This passage teaches that God's glory must be recognized wherever light reigns, that is, in all inhabited regions of the world. For the believer, this reminds us that testimony and praise to God know no borders: all peoples, from East to West, are called to acknowledge the Lord. It is an invitation to a universal perspective of divine glory.

sens: Father of Eliphal, one of David's warriors
H0218A.detail: Ur is a man living during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. He is the father of Eliphal, who is among the thirty most valiant warriors of David, listed among the royal heroes (1 Chronicles 11:35). His name means "flame" in Hebrew, but the Bible reports nothing else about his life or exploits.
H0218A.origine: The name Ur comes from the Hebrew root meaning "fire" or "flame." It is a short and simple name, evoking the bright light of a fire. The same word can also refer to an ancient city in Mesopotamia (Ur in French), but here it refers to a man, the father of one of David's heroes.
H0218A.emploi: Ur appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:35, where he is mentioned as the father of Eliphal. This passage lists the thirty-seven elite warriors who served King David, and Ur is simply included to establish Eliphal's genealogy. His absence from the rest of Scripture suggests that he was an ordinary man, whose importance comes solely from his son, who distinguished himself in the service of the king.

sens: City of Chaldea from which Abraham departed
Center of moon worship in ancient Babylonia
Starting point of the divine call to leave his country
H0218B.detail:
1. Ur is a city located in Chaldea (the region of Lower Mesopotamia), from which Abraham and his family left to head towards Canaan. It is the birthplace of Abraham's father, Terach, and it is where Abraham grew up before God's call. The four occurrences of the term all emphasize the importance of this departure: "They went out together from Ur of the Chaldeans to go to the land of Canaan" (Genesis 11:31).
2. Ur was a major religious center of antiquity, dedicated to moon worship — which further highlights God's call to Abraham to detach himself from this idolatrous environment. The name itself means "flame" in Hebrew, which may evoke the sanctuaries and cults of the ancient world.
3. For Abraham, Ur represents the starting point of his obedience: it is by leaving this city that his journey of faith toward the promised land begins. God Himself reminds Abraham: "I am the Lord who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans, to give you this land as a possession" (Genesis 15:7).
H0218B.origine: The Hebrew name אוּר (ur) literally means "flame." It designates the ancient city of Ur in Chaldea (Lower Mesopotamia), one of the largest metropolises of the Akkadian world, currently in Iraq. This historic city was indeed a great urban and religious center in antiquity, famous for its ziggurat (sacred tower) and its lunar cult.
H0218B.emploi: Ur appears four times in the Bible, all in the context of Abraham's call and migration. In Genesis 11:28-31, it is Abraham's cradle and the starting point of his family. In Genesis 15:7 and Nehemiah 9:7, God reminds Abraham that He "brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans" — which emphasizes that the departure from this city is a foundational divine act. The repeated mention of the name "Ur of the Chaldeans" enriches the narrative by clearly situating the city and marking the radical break with Abraham's idolatrous past.
H0218B.portee: Ur symbolizes the breaking point where God calls Abraham to separate from his religious and cultural environment to follow a new vocation. This city embodies the old world that Abraham leaves behind to enter into the divine covenant and become the father of believers. The reminder of the departure from Ur reinforces the greatness of Abraham's faith: obeying God by leaving everything that was familiar.

sens: Physical clarity, radiance that illuminates
Joy, happiness, happy moment
That which revitalizes, gives life and strength back
H0219A.detail: 1. Physical light, that which allows one to see and dispels darkness: in Psalms 139:12, even the deepest darkness becomes "like light" to God, for He sees everything clearly. 2. In a figurative sense, the light of joy and happiness: in Esther 8:16, the Jews experience a moment of "happiness" and rejoicing — a light that shines in their lives after distress. 3. That which revitalizes and restores strength: in Isaiah 26:19, the dew of the Lord is "revitalizing," reminding to life like a light that awakens and transforms.
H0219A.origine: The Hebrew word orah comes from a root that fundamentally designates radiance, clarity. It is close to or, which also means "light." The basic image is that of the day brightening, of light bursting forth. This word always evokes something that illuminates, either physically, spiritually, or morally.
H0219A.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Esther 8:16, it describes the joy of the saved Jews, a moral and emotional light. In Psalms 139:12, it emphasizes God's omniscience: even what is dark for us remains visible to Him, as in broad daylight. In Isaiah 26:19, it takes on a nuance of revitalization, of resurrection — the divine dew that gives life to the dead. The word thus transitions from the concrete (daylight) to the spiritual (joy, new life).
H0219A.portee: This word invites the believer to see divine light not only as intellectual illumination but as a source of authentic joy and renewed life. It reminds that God is the one who sees everything, who knows our inner darkness, and who brings clarity, happiness, and resurrection to those who turn to Him.

sens: Edible herbaceous plant picked in the fields
Vegetable or wild greenery used to prepare broth or soup
H0219B.detail:
1. The word designates the herbs and herbaceous plants found in fields or gardens. These are not the tall grasses of a meadow, but rather the low plants, the green vegetables that can be eaten. In the account of 2 Kings 4:39, the man goes out into the fields to "gather herbs" to eat — a daily gesture to feed the household, in a context of famine where everyone must seek their food.
2. Grass can also be wild greenery, raw or cooked in soup. The example of the wild gourds, picked by mistake and chopped into the pot, shows that there is a distinction between ordinary edible herbs and plants that resemble herbs but can be toxic. It is rustic and accessible food, that of the poor or in difficult times.
H0219B.origine: The Hebrew word אוֹרָה comes from a root meaning that which comes forth or grows from the earth — the grass that springs from the soil. It is a simple word, part of everyday vocabulary, designating the green and tender plants that grow spontaneously or are cultivated for food.
H0219B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in this dramatic passage of 2 Kings 4:39, during a famine. It is a man sent by the prophet Elisha who goes out to gather wild herbs to make a broth and feed the community of prophets. Its use emphasizes the state of precariousness — one must glean in the fields to survive — and the vigilance required, as not all "herbs" are safe: some can be deadly.
H0219B.portee: This passage reminds that divine Providence provides for our needs through creation, but also that our obedience and vigilance are required. The gathered grass is a sign of humility and trust in the face of uncertainty; it invites the believer to remember that God nourishes even in distress, as long as one seeks and discerns.

sens: Facility arranged to house and feed farm animals
Collection of animals raised there
H0220.detail:
1. The stable is the building or enclosure where domestic animals are kept, particularly livestock: cows, oxen, horses. It is the place where they are fed and cared for. In the passage of 2 Chronicles 32:28, King Hezekiah builds stables to shelter his enormous herds — a mark of his wealth and power.
2. By extension, a stable can also refer to the entire livestock housed there: the animals themselves rather than the building. The word thus encompasses both the facility and its contents.
H0220.origine: This Hebrew word belongs to the family of the word urayyah (אֻרְיָה, H0723), with which it shares the same root and meaning. These two forms designate the same biblical reality — the enclosed space reserved for livestock. The word likely comes from a root expressing the idea of "gathering" or "arranging": the stable is the place where animals are gathered.
H0220.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible: in 2 Chronicles 32:28, at the heart of the account of King Hezekiah's extraordinary wealth. After his victories and religious reforms, he accumulates reserves — grain, wine, oil — and builds stables to house his countless herds. It is a concrete example of the divine blessing that filled his granaries and enclosures.
H0220.portee: The stable reminds us that biblical wealth first comes through tangible goods — land, harvests, animals — and that it reflects God's blessing. This word also invites us to see how good management requires not only accumulation but organization: Hezekiah built to arrange and protect his goods, an image of the wisdom and order that faith brings to life.

sens: Father of the master craftsman of the Tabernacle
Head of a family from the tribe of Judah
H0221G.detail: 1. Uri is a man from the tribe of Judah, father of Bezalel, the great artisan and master craftsman chosen by God to build the Tabernacle (Exodus 31:2). He is the grandson of Hur, and he belongs to the genealogy of the leaders of the tribe of Judah. 2. The Bible mentions him as a respected ancestor, father of the son whom God filled with wisdom and talent for the work of the Tabernacle (1 Chronicles 2:20).
H0221G.origine: The name Uri means "fiery" or "brilliant" in Hebrew, evoking the idea of fire or heat. It belongs to the family of names from the tribe of Judah, where names often carried meanings related to power, strength, or distinctive qualities. Uri comes from a prestigious genealogy: son of Hur, father of Bezalel.
H0221G.emploi: Uri is mentioned five times in the Bible, always in relation to his son Bezalel and the work of the Tabernacle. Exodus 31:2 and 35:30 present him as the father of the master craftsman chosen by the Lord. Exodus 38:22 recalls that it is Bezalel, son of Uri, who executed all the works ordered by Moses. In 1 Chronicles 2:20, we see his place in the official genealogy of Judah. The references show that Uri is primarily known through his eminent son and by his role in this lineage of leaders.
H0221G.portee: Uri reminds us that the gifts and talents that God places in a life can be passed on and flourish in subsequent generations. The modest father of Bezalel lives on through the extraordinary work of his son, invited to serve God with excellence. It is an invitation to recognize how God often glorifies Himself through families and spiritual legacies.

sens: Man living during the time of the united monarchy, father of Geber
Officer or father of an officer of Solomon in Gilead
H0221H.detail: 1. Uri is a character mentioned only once in the Hebrew Bible, during the reign of King Solomon. He is the father of Geber, who served as a steward in the region of Gilead, east of the Jordan (1 Kings 4:19). In this administrative role, Geber governed the lands once controlled by Sihon, king of the Amorites, and by Og, king of Bashan — significant territories that God had given to Israel. 2. His name means "fiery" or "burning," evoking energy and strength. Although not detailed in the biblical text, Uri is part of the network of officials that Solomon established to administer and ensure the prosperity of the united kingdom.
H0221H.origine: The name Uri comes from a Hebrew root meaning "fire" or "ardor." The same root appears in names like Uriah ("my fire is God"), which refers to the soldier whose wife David coveted, Bathsheba. This type of theophoric name — formed with the idea of divine fire — was common in Israel to express fervor and power.
H0221H.emploi: Uri appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Kings 4:19, at the heart of the account that lists Solomon's twelve stewards, each responsible for a region of Israel and conquered territories. These officers were to provide for the needs of the king, his court, and his administration. His son Geber, himself a steward, enjoyed a privileged position in Gilead, a fertile and strategic region. This unique mention shows that Uri was a man of rank, integrated into the structures of royal power in the 10th century B.C.

sens: Man of the time of exile and return
Temple porter who married a foreign woman
H0221I.detail: 1. Uri is a man living at the time of the exile of the Judeans to Babylon and their return to the Promised Land. His name means "burning" or "fiery" in Hebrew. 2. More specifically, Uri was a temple porter (gatekeeper) during the time of the prophet Ezra. He appears in the list of men who had married foreign women and had to separate from them to uphold the purity of God's people upon their return from exile (Ezra 10:24).
H0221I.origine: The name Uri comes from the Hebrew "ur" which means "fire" or "light." It expresses the idea of something ardent, burning. In the Old Testament, we also encounter other individuals bearing a name constructed from the same root: Hur (father of the builder Bezalel), and the compound names Urijah or Uriah that incorporate the divine name "Yah."
H0221I.emploi: Uri appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:24. He is mentioned among the temple porters (those who guarded the sanctuary's access) during the great assembly convened by Ezra after the return from exile. Uri is noted for having violated the prohibition by marrying a woman from a foreign nation. Along with other men in the same situation, he had to make the decision to separate from his wife to comply with the purity prescriptions that underpinned the identity of the restored people.
H0221I.portee: The mention of Uri invites the reader to meditate on the importance of separation from the world and the maintenance of spiritual purity within God's community. It also shows that even the servants of the temple, charged with holy functions, could face compromises with neighboring nations. It is a lesson in vigilance: faithfulness to God requires difficult and sometimes costly choices.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Levi living during the time of the divided monarchy
H0222G.detail: Uriel is a descendant of Levi mentioned in the genealogy of the priestly tribe. He is the son of Tahath and the father of Uzziah (also called Zephaniah). According to 1 Chronicles 6:24, he is part of the lineage of the Levites of the house of Kohath, who were responsible for worship and service in the temple during the reign of David and his successors.
H0222G.origine: The name means "God (El) is my light" in Hebrew. It is composed of אוּר (ur), "light," and אֵל (El), the name of God. This theophany (composition with the divine name) is common in Hebrew names, expressing a personal relationship with God.
H0222G.emploi: Uriel is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 6:24, within the genealogy of the Kohath Levites. He appears in the chain of descendants of the Levitical clan responsible for ritual functions in Israel's worship.

sens: Chief Levite during the reign of King David
Maternal grandfather of King Abijah
H0222H.detail: Uriel is a Levite from the family of Kohath who holds an important position at the court of King David. He is mentioned as the chief of his line and is involved in organizing the transport of the Ark of the Covenant, alongside the priests Zadok and Abiathar (1 Chronicles 15:5 and 15:11). He is also the maternal grandfather of King Abijah (also called Abija), who reigned in Judah after his father Rehoboam.
H0222H.origine: The name Uriel means "God (El) is my light." It is composed of two elements: "Ur" (light) and "El" (God). It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God, which was common among the Hebrews to express their faith and relationship to God.
H0222H.emploi: Uriel appears twice in Chronicles, both times in the context of events surrounding the reign of David. He is first presented as the chief principal ("the chief") of the sons of Kohath, one of the major families of Levites (1 Chronicles 15:5). Shortly after, he is seen again summoned by David to participate in a solemn ceremony, where he is listed among other important Levites (1 Chronicles 15:11). These mentions show that he was a trusted and responsible figure in the religious administration of David's kingdom.

sens: Chief Levite of the lineage of Kohath during the reign of King David
Father of Maacah and maternal grandfather of King Abijah
H0222I.detail: 1. Uriel is a chief Levite who lived during the reign of King David, responsible for the priestly lineage of Kohath (one of the three main branches of the Levites). 2. He is best known as the maternal grandfather of King Abijah of Judah: his daughter (or granddaughter according to genealogies) Maacah married King Rehoboam and bore Abijah. In 2 Chronicles 13:2, we learn that the mother of King Abijah was named Maacah and was the daughter of Uriel of Gibeah.
H0222I.origine: The name Uriel means "God is my light" (Uri = my light, El = God). It is a typically Hebrew theophoric name, expressing the personal relationship between the bearer of the name and the Lord. Several biblical characters bear this name, but this passage designates only this chief Levite from the Davidic era.
H0222I.emploi: Uriel appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Chronicles 13:2, where he is presented as the father or grandfather of Maacah, the mother of King Abijah of Judah (reign around 915-912 B.C.). His appearance is situated in the context of royal succession and the genealogy of the kings of the south. Although not detailed, this passage establishes his importance in Israel's religious history as an honorable Levite during the period of the united monarchy.

sens: Hittite military officer in the service of King David
Husband of Bathsheba
Man of great moral and spiritual integrity
H0223A.detail:
1. Uriah is a Hittite soldier (that is, born in Hittite territory, not of Israelite descent) who serves in the army of King David during the time of the united monarchy. He is an experienced and trusted warrior (2 Samuel 11:3).
2. He is married to Bathsheba, a very beautiful woman whom David covets. Despite the king's attempts to get him to sleep with her, Uriah refuses to go home, saying that he cannot enjoy the comfort of his house while the ark of God and the army of Israel are camping in the open fields (2 Samuel 11:11). His refusal shows his dedication to service and his moral conscience.
3. Uriah embodies integrity: seeing his refusal, King David chooses to place him at the forefront of the battle to have him killed (2 Samuel 11:15). His death becomes David's hidden crime, later discovered by the prophet Nathan (2 Samuel 12:9). Uriah's memory remains attached to the king's sin, but also to his personal honor.
H0223A.origine: The name means "the Lord (Yahweh) is my light" or "my flame." It is a theophoric name (which contains the name of God), common in Israel to express trust in God. The use of the name of a Hittite—originating from a foreign region—shows that David had mercenary or foreign warriors integrated into his army, according to a common practice among kings of the time.
H0223A.emploi: Uriah appears 21 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the account of 2 Samuel 11-12, which tells his story with Bathsheba and David. The name also appears in 2 Samuel 23:39 (in the list of David's mighty men), in 1 Samuel 15:5 (an indirect reference to David's sin regarding Uriah), and in 1 Chronicles 11:41 (the same list of warriors). The story of Uriah becomes the major illustration of David's psalm of repentance (Psalm 51) and the divine judgment that follows. The account shows how a secret act of lust leads to murder, and how conscience (expressed by Uriah's faithfulness) accuses the king.
H0223A.portee: The story of Uriah teaches the importance of moral integrity, even for one who is not born in the faith (a Hittite who respects the ark of God better than the king of Israel). It also shows how lust leads to lies and murder, and how God sees hidden crimes. For the believer, Uriah is a call to prefer honor before God over the satisfaction of desires, and a reminder that sincere repentance (that of David after Nathan) is the path to forgiveness.

sens: Prophet of Judah during the Divided Monarchy
Man who announced God's judgment against Jerusalem and Judah
Servant of God persecuted and killed by King Jehoiakim
H0223B.detail:
1. Uriah is a prophet who lived in Judah during the period of the Divided Monarchy, around the 7th century B.C. His name means "the Lord (Yahweh) is my light," which recalls his vocation to bring the illuminating word of God.

2. He pronounced prophecies against Jerusalem and the kingdom of Judah, just like Jeremiah (Jeremiah 26:20): he announced God's judgment on the city and the entire land. His message was unpopular, like that of all true prophets.

3. When Uriah learned that King Jehoiakim, furious to hear these words, sought to have him killed, he became afraid and fled to Egypt for safety (Jeremiah 26:21). But he could not escape for long: the king had him forcibly brought back from Egypt and executed by the sword (Jeremiah 26:23), then abandoned his body without a proper burial. Uriah illustrates the tragic fate of prophets rejected by political power.
H0223B.origine: The name Uriah comes from Hebrew and means "the Lord is my light." It combines the divine name Yah (the Lord) with the word for "light" (or flame), forming a profession of faith: the one who bears this name recognizes the Lord as his light and source of life. Variants of the name existed in Israel; this prophet is distinct from other biblical characters with similar names.
H0223B.emploi: Uriah is mentioned three times in the Bible, exclusively in Jeremiah 26:20-23. He was a prophet in Judah during the reign of King Jehoiakim (early 7th century B.C.). Like Jeremiah, he announced the disaster of Jerusalem and all of Judah (Jeremiah 26:20). When the king heard these words, he sought to kill the prophet; Uriah, warned, fled to Egypt (Jeremiah 26:21). But Jehoiakim found him and forcibly brought him back to execute him by the sword, then throwing his corpse away without honor (Jeremiah 26:23). His story shows the resistance of political power to prophetic word.
H0223B.portee: The example of Uriah reminds us of the cost of faithfulness to God: announcing divine truth, even when it displeases those in power, can lead to persecution and death. His flight to Egypt, followed by his execution, shows that human protection is fragile. Yet, Jeremiah reports his story to affirm that the true prophets of the Lord do not disappear from divine memory, even if they are forgotten by men.

sens: Priest of King Ahaz who built a new altar in the temple of Jerusalem
H0223G.detail: Uriah is a priest who served during the reign of King Ahaz, in the 8th century B.C. The king sent him to Damascus to seek the model of an altar he had seen with the king of Assyria, and Uriah built this altar according to the instructions received (2 Kings 16:10-11). Subsequently, the king ordered him to modify the sacrifices and offerings on this new altar, and Uriah faithfully obeyed all his commands (2 Kings 16:15-16). Uriah also acts as a witness in a prophetic declaration of Isaiah (Isaiah 8:2).
H0223G.origine: The name means "Yahweh is my light" or "Yahweh is my flame": it expresses that the one who bears it recognizes the Lord as his source of light and life. It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the divine name, like many Hebrew names from antiquity.
H0223G.emploi: Uriah appears five times in the Bible, all in the Old Testament texts concerning the reign of Ahaz, king of Judah. He is presented as an obedient priest, who executes the king's orders without hesitation, even when they alter the practices of worship in the temple. The text emphasizes his complacency towards the king rather than his faithfulness to God's Law: he agrees to build a foreign altar and change the order of sacrifices at the king's instructions. He also appears as a respectable witness to the prophet Isaiah (Isaiah 8:2).
H0223G.portee: Uriah illustrates the risk of spiritual compromise when one prioritizes obedience to the powerful of this world over faithfulness to God. Although a priest of the Lord, he modifies worship according to the king's desires, showing how human authority can lead away from true worship. It is a call to ask ourselves whether our choices bring us closer to or further from God, even when it is difficult.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah living during the time of the Exile and Return
Priest responsible for receiving the offerings of the Temple
H0223H.detail:
1. Urie is a man from the house of Hakkots, father of Merémoth. He lived during the time when the Jews were returning from the exile in Babylon, during the time of Ezra and Nehemiah (mid-5th century BC). His name means "the Lord is my light." 
2. He is a priest of the Temple: in Ezra 8:33, he receives the silver, gold, and worship utensils brought back by the returnees, and weighs them in the house of God to entrust them to his son Merémoth and the Levites. His role places him among those who restore the worship of the Lord after the exile.
H0223H.origine: The name Urie comes from Hebrew and means "the Lord is my light" or "the Lord is my flame," composed of the divine name YHWH (God) and a root meaning light. This type of name, where the divine combines with a quality or image, was common among the Israelites. Several biblical figures bear this same name, notably a military officer of King David, but the provided usages refer to this priest living at the time of the return from exile.
H0223H.emploi: Urie is mentioned three times in the Bible, always during the return from the Babylonian exile (Ezra 8 and Nehemiah 3). He first appears in Ezra 8:33, where he is a priest and receives the wealth brought by Ezra for the Temple. His son Merémoth accompanies him in this task. Then, in Nehemiah 3:4 and 3:21, it is his son Merémoth who works on the repairs of the walls of Jerusalem, showing that Urie's family holds a respected position in the restoration of worship and the city.

sens: Man who stood beside Ezra during the public reading of the Law
H0223I.detail: 1. Urie is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 8:4. He stood at the right hand of Ezra the scribe during a solemn assembly where the Law was publicly read to the people. His presence among the notable figures surrounding Ezra suggests that he was a respected and influential figure in the Jewish community at the time of the return from exile.
H0223I.origine: The name Urie means "the Lord is my light" or "the Lord is my flame." It is composed of the divine Hebrew name "Yah" (Yahweh, the Lord) and the word "uri" which evokes light or clarity. This type of theophoric name, where the divine name is incorporated, was common in Israel to express a personal relationship with God.
H0223I.emploi: Urie appears only once in Scripture, in Nehemiah 8:4. He is presented as one of the trustworthy men who stood beside the scribe Ezra during the great assembly where the Law of Moses was read aloud before all the people gathered at the Water Gate, after the return from exile in Babylon. His mention in this official context indicates his status as an important person in the reconstruction of the Jewish community.

sens: The sacred stones of the high priest's breastplate, used to know the will of God
H0224.detail: 1. Urim refers to stones (or objects) kept in a pouch attached to the breastplate (the ornate garment worn by the high priest on his chest). They were used to obtain an answer from God on important questions: yes or no, guilt or innocence, permission or prohibition. When Saul seeks to know if David is guilty, he asks the priest to consult the Urim (1 Samuel 14:41). After the exile, the priests could no longer officiate without being able to use the Urim and Thummim, as no one knew how to interpret them anymore (Ezra 2:63).
H0224.origine: The Hebrew word אוּרִים (Urim) literally means "lights." Its plural suggests multiple stones. They were associated with the Thummim ("perfections" or "integrities"), often mentioned together: "Urim and Thummim." Although the exact mechanism of consultation remained mysterious to the ancients, these objects represented a direct means of seeking divine revelation through the high priest.
H0224.emploi: The Urim appears eight times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the books of the Law and ancient history. During the time of Moses and Joshua, the high priest regularly consulted them to make decisions: during the distribution of the lands (Numbers 27:21), at the time of the blessing of the tribes (Deuteronomy 33:8). In the time of King Saul, it was still a means of discerning the will of God, although Saul did not always receive an answer (1 Samuel 28:6, where God refuses to respond). After the return from exile, the Urim was no longer operational: the priests awaited a prophet to restore this practice (Ezra 2:63 and Nehemiah 7:65).
H0224.portee: The Urim reminds us that in the Old Testament, God provided concrete and regular means for His people to know His will. It is a testimony that seeking divine guidance was a normal and expected practice, not an exception. For today's Christian, this illustrates the importance of actively seeking the will of God, even though the means have changed: we now have the complete Bible and the Holy Spirit.

sens: Accept a proposal, an agreement, a request
Commit to respecting a set condition
Agree together on a decision
H0225.detail:
1. To consent is to say "yes" to what is proposed: to voluntarily accept a request or condition. In the story of Dinah (Genesis 34:15), Jacob's sons say to the Shechemites: "We will not consent to your desire unless you become like us," meaning they will only accept the marriage if their neighbors agree to circumcision. 
2. The word often emphasizes agreement on a specific condition: one consents not simply, but "to" something, "provided that." When the priests agreed not to take the people's money (2 Kings 12:8), they came to an agreement on the terms of an arrangement. 
3. To consent also implies a thoughtful choice: it is not coercion, but a shared will. Both parties must agree for the consent to be valid.
