H0225.origine: The Hebrew verb אוּת comes from a root that evokes the idea of "going together" or "agreeing." The niphal form (passive or pronominal form) that we find here expresses this mutual understanding: "to come to an agreement," "to be in agreement together." The word retains the image of the bond formed between two or more wills.
H0225.emploi: The verb אוּת appears only four times in the Old Testament, always in the sense of "to consent" or "to agree." Three usages concern the negotiation around Dinah (Genesis 34), where delicate agreements are involved: Jacob's sons and the people of Shechem must "consent" to terms before the union can take place. The fourth usage (2 Kings 12:8) shows the priests who "agree" to renounce a financial right. In all cases, it is a voluntary agreement on specific conditions.
H0225.portee: This word teaches us that true consent requires a free will from both parties and clarity on what one is committing to. It is never trivial: when the Bible speaks of consent, it indicates that something important is at stake — a marriage, a covenant, a renunciation.

sens: Distinctive mark, recognizable signal
Banner, standard
Memory, commemoration
Miraculous act, wonder
Omen, warning
H0226G.detail:
1. A distinctive mark that allows one to recognize something or someone. It is a signal agreed upon between two people. For example, in Exodus 3:12, God promises Moses a sign: "When you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall serve God on this mountain" — it is the proof that God has truly sent him.
2. A standard or banner raised to gather a people or mark a territory. The image is that of a flag that can be recognized from afar.
3. An object or event kept in memory to remember something important. It is a visible reminder of the past, helping not to forget.
4. A wondrous act, a miracle that only God can perform, demonstrating His power. In Exodus 8:19, when God separates His people from the Egyptian people through terrible plagues, it is a sign of His sovereignty. Deuteronomy 34:11 speaks of the "signs and wonders" that Moses performed in Egypt: these are the plagues that forced Pharaoh to let go.
5. An omen or warning of what is to come. It is a divine message conveyed through a visible event.
H0226G.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root meaning to mark, distinguish, make visible. It primarily denotes a mark left or worn to be recognized. In the Bible, the word is very ancient and central: it expresses how God manifests Himself and makes Himself known through acts that surpass ordinary nature. The sign is always something that can be seen, pointed out, and that speaks to the observer.
H0226G.emploi: This word appears 46 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the account of the Exodus and the historical books. In Exodus, the signs and wonders are the plagues that force Pharaoh to release Israel: God sends them to prove His power and faithfulness (Exodus 7:3, Psalms 78:43, Psalms 105:27). In other books, the sign can be a personal proof of God's will — thus the shadow that retreats on the sundial is a sign for King Hezekiah (2 Kings 20:9). Sometimes it warns of an impending danger (Jeremiah 10:2) or recalls the covenant (Deuteronomy 6:22). The sign is always concrete, visible, and requires attention and understanding.
H0226G.portee: For the believer, the sign reminds that God is never absent or silent: He manifests Himself through visible acts that need to be recognized and received as proofs of His love and power. Learning to see God's signs in life is learning to trust Him.

sens: Distinctive mark, visible marker that allows recognition of something
Banner, standard raised to gather a group
Memory, something kept to remember an event
Extraordinary act that manifests God's power
Omen, indication of what is to come
H0226H.detail:
1. A sign is primarily a mark or a clearly visible marker: something that allows distinction, identification, or orientation. The luminaries of the sky are signs to mark the seasons and days (Genesis 1:14), just as circumcision is a sign of God's covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17:11).
2. A sign can be a banner or standard raised to gather a community, providing direction, a visible rallying point (Numbers 2:2 where the tribes of Israel are ordered "each by its own standard").
3. A sign can be a concrete memory kept to avoid forgetting: the words of the Law carried on the hand or between the eyes are a mnemonic sign (Deuteronomy 11:18), just as a commemorative stone recalls an event (Joshua 4:6).
4. A sign can be a miraculous act, a visible divine intervention that proves God's power or will: the plagues of Egypt, the blood on the doors on Passover (Exodus 12:13), or the water turning bitter are all signs of God's hand.
5. A sign can finally be an omen, a warning, or an indication of what is to happen: the prophet wears captive's clothing as a sign of the impending disaster (Isaiah 20:3).
H0226H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of making a mark, distinguishing. The basic image is that of something visible, remarkable, that "signals" — that attracts the eye and communicates something. The root is related to the notion of pointing, showing. In Hebrew, this word is used for everything that manifests something else: not only natural markers (stars, colors) but also divine interventions and symbols of the covenant.
H0226H.emploi: This word appears 32 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Torah (Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy), in the Psalms, and among the prophets. It is used for natural signs (stars, rainbow after the flood in Genesis 9), for covenant signs (circumcision, Sabbath), for military standards and banners of the tribes (Numbers 2:2), for memorials (stones of crossings), and especially for the miracles and extraordinary acts of God that attest to His power. Isaiah and Ezekiel particularly use it for prophetic and symbolic signs. The word can denote something with simple marker or reminder value, but also what manifests God's supernatural action.
H0226H.portee: This word reminds us that God communicates with His people through visible signs and concrete acts: the rainbow, the covenant, the miracles. For the Christian, it is an invitation to recognize in creation, in divine promises, and in God's interventions as many signs that should not be ignored. It is also an exhortation not to forget: the signs are there so that we remember what God has done and His commitments to us.

sens: At that moment, at a specific point in the past
At that moment, in a future or hypothetical moment
Before that moment, previously
In that case, therefore, consequently
H0227A.detail:
1. The word designates a moment in the past when something occurred: "Then men began to call on the name of the Lord" (Genesis 4:26). It marks the instant when an event took place.
2. It indicates a future or conditional moment: "Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened" (Isaiah 35:5), announcing what will happen. It is the moment when the consequence of an action or promise will be realized.
3. It refers to an earlier time: "Then" can also mean "previously" or "at that time," placing an event in a distant past.
4. It expresses a logical deduction: "Then I shall be blameless" (Psalms 19:14) means "in that case," "therefore" — one of the logical consequences of the first statement.
H0227A.origine: This Hebrew word is an ancient temporal and logical particle, without a clearly identifiable verbal root. It expresses the link between two moments or two ideas: the tipping point, the threshold. Its initial image is that of the "then-ness" of the present moment becoming past or future. It structures the biblical narrative by marking the stages — when this happened, then that followed.
H0227A.emploi: The word "then" appears 114 times in the Old Testament, in all the historical books (Genesis, Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings, Chronicles), the Psalms, Job, and the Prophets. It is the quintessential marker of the passage of time in the narrative: "Then Horam went up to help Lachish" (Joshua 10:33). In poetic and prophetic passages, it announces future realization: "Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened" (Isaiah 35:5). Logically, it links a condition to its consequence: "If you do this, then…" Its meaning nuances according to context: temporal in history, promissory in prophecy, causal in argumentation.
H0227A.portee: For the Christian reader, "then" reminds us that history is not chaos, but an ordered succession of events where God acts. It is the word that punctuates God's plan: then Abraham received the promise, then Israel came out of Egypt, then the day of the Lord will come. This word invites us to see how each moment connects to the next according to the divine purpose.

sens: The ancient, bygone era
The duration that elapses from a given moment in the past to the present
Since an earlier time, before what is being said
In contrast to the present moment
H0227B.detail:
1. The word designates what belongs to the distant past, the bygone era. It refers to ancient times, the time of beginnings. Proverbs 8:22 speaks of God's "ancient" works, which existed before everything else.
2. It can also refer to the duration that has passed for a long time: the interval that extends from the past to the moment of speaking. Isaiah 44:8 states that God announced what is happening "long ago," meaning that this promise was made many years ago.
3. The word is used to express a break between the past and the present: "since" a given moment in the past until now. Exodus 9:24 specifies that there had never been hail like this "since" Egypt has existed as a nation.
4. Finally, it can mark an opposition between what was true in the past and what is true now. In 2 Samuel 15:34, the servant says, "I was formerly your father's servant, but now I am your servant": the word emphasizes this change between the former state and the new one.
H0227B.origine: The word comes from a root that means "time" or "era." It is composed of a preposition ("of," "since") followed by a word designating the ancient or the distant. This word is found in several biblical contexts where it speaks of what is bygone, of what dates back far in the past.
H0227B.emploi: This word appears about 19 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical books (Samuel) and prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah). It is first used to indicate that something dates back a long time (Isaiah 44:8, 48:3), then to indicate a duration from an ancient date to the present (Exodus 9:24: since the foundation of Egypt), and finally to mark an opposition between yesteryear and now (2 Samuel 15:34). The prophets often use it to remind that God acted or spoke long before the moment when He addresses Israel, which gives weight to His word.
H0227B.portee: This word reminds the reader that God acts over time and that His word is not a novelty: it goes back far. By hearing it, the believer understands that God's plans were established long ago, well before he saw them come to fruition. This strengthens faith by showing that God masters the times and that nothing takes Him by surprise.

sens: To make warm, to raise the temperature of something
To intensify, to increase (in a figurative sense)
H0228.detail:
1. To make warm, to raise the temperature: this is the literal meaning of the word, which designates the action of increasing the temperature of an object. In Daniel 3:19, King Nebuchadnezzar orders the furnace to be heated "seven times more than it was appropriate," which shows the extreme degree of heat he wants to reach to destroy the three young Hebrews.
2. To intensify, to increase: the word is also used in a figurative sense to express a rise in intensity or strength. In Daniel 3:22, it is stated that "the furnace was extraordinarily heated," highlighting not only the temperature reached but also the intensity of the king's anger and the force of his judgment.
H0228.origine: The word comes from an Aramaic root that literally means "to make hot." It belongs to the Aramaic language, spoken in Mesopotamia at the time of Daniel. Its meaning is simple and concrete: to move from a state of cold or lukewarm to that of hot, by applying heat.
H0228.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the same passage of Daniel 3, at the heart of the account of the fiery furnace. In Daniel 3:19, Nebuchadnezzar "ordered to heat the furnace"; in Daniel 3:22, it is described as "extraordinarily heated." These two uses form an echo: first the king's order to raise the temperature, then the terrifying result of that order. The context is one of the king's anger and his desire for vengeance against those who refuse to worship his idol.
H0228.portee: This word reminds us that anger, even that of a powerful king, cannot do anything against true faith. The three young Hebrews remain faithful to God despite the furnace heated to the extreme, which shows the superiority of trust in God over any earthly threat. The account invites the reader not to fear the powers of the world when one remains firm in faith.

sens: Father of the warrior Naaraï, one of David's mighty men
H0229.detail: Ezbaï is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, as the father of Naaraï. This Naaraï is counted among David's mighty men, those renowned warriors who fought alongside him during his reign (1 Chronicles 11:37).
H0229.origine: The name Ezbaï literally means "my humiliations" in Hebrew, formed from the root "zbh" (to humiliate, to lower) with the possessive ending "-aï" (my). It is a rare name in the Bible, illustrating the richness of ancient Hebrew proper names, often constructed from words expressing a spiritual reality or a personal experience.
H0229.emploi: Ezbaï appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:37, in the list of the thirty mighty men who formed David's military elite. He is not described for himself, but only as the father of Naaraï. This brief mention in David's genealogical lists teaches us little about his personal life, but it shows that he descended from a family associated with the defense of the kingdom of Israel under David.

sens: To disappear, to flee, to no longer be present
To be lost from sight, forgotten, no longer accessible
H0230.detail:
1. The word describes the action of disappearing or fleeing: something or someone that is no longer there, that has moved away or has vanished. In Daniel 2:5, King Nebuchadnezzar says that the dream has "escaped" him: he has forgotten his dream, he can no longer find it in his memory, it has slipped from his hands like something that escapes.
2. By extension, the word means to be out of reach, inaccessible: the thing is gone, it is no longer within the power or knowledge of the one who seeks it. In verse 8, the king repeats that the thing has "escaped" him, suggesting that he has lost this knowledge and can no longer recover it by himself.
H0230.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the same root as the Hebrew אָזַל (azal, "to depart, to go away"), which expresses the idea of definitive departure or disappearance. The root describes a movement that moves away and does not return. In Aramaic, the form used here (azda) carries the passive meaning: that which has disappeared, that which has fled.
H0230.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both times in Aramaic in Daniel 2. In these two verses, Nebuchadnezzar uses the same term to express his forgetfulness of the dream: the vision has "escaped" him. It is a total forgetfulness, an irretrievable loss — the king no longer remembers the dream and asks the magicians and sages of Babylon not only to interpret it but to remind him of it by discovering it. The repeated use of the same word in verses 5 and 8 emphasizes the urgency and gravity of the situation.
H0230.portee: This word illustrates the limits of human knowledge, even that of the most powerful of kings. Nebuchadnezzar, master of the world, cannot keep in memory a received vision, while only Daniel, through God's wisdom, will be able to both know the dream and provide its interpretation. It is a lesson on man's dependence on God for true wisdom.

sens: A small herbaceous plant with branched stems and small leaves
Used in the purification rituals of the Old Testament
Symbol of cleansing and the removal of impurities
H0231.detail:
1. Hyssop is a small herbaceous plant, whose branched structure made it practical for sprinkling liquids or blood (Exodus 12:22: "You shall take a bunch of hyssop, and dip it in the blood"). Its modest size and numerous stems made it an effective instrument for ritual sprinkling.

2. It plays a central role in the purification rites prescribed by the Law. To purify a house affected by leprosy, the priest combined cedar wood, scarlet yarn, and hyssop, dipped in the blood of a bird (Leviticus 14:51): this recurring association shows that hyssop was an essential element of the atonement process. It also appears during Passover in Egypt, applied to the doorposts.

3. Beyond its material use, hyssop symbolizes the divine power to purify and erase sin. This is why it recurs as a spiritual metaphor: "Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean" (Psalms 51:9), where the psalmist implores God to cleanse him morally and spiritually, evoking the image of the purification rite.
H0231.origine: The Hebrew word אֵזוֹב (ezov) refers to a small herb known in the ancient Near East, likely the Eastern hyssop (Origanum syriacum or Hysopus officinalis). Its exact etymology remains debated, but the word relates to a plant with well-established properties and uses in Israel. It is a hardy plant, easy to cultivate and abundantly available, hence its frequent use in religious and medicinal rituals.
H0231.emploi: The word appears 10 times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated in the book of Leviticus which describes the purification rituals (6 occurrences for the leprosy rite), once in Exodus (sprinkling of blood at Passover), twice in Numbers (purification related to death), and once in Psalms as a spiritual image. Its use is exclusively cultic and ritual: hyssop never appears in an ordinary or domestic context. It is always associated with blood (animal, thus sacrifice) or water, embodying the process of atonement and restoration of purity according to the Mosaic law. The use in Psalm 51 transposes the image of the external rite to the internal and spiritual realm.
H0231.portee: Hyssop teaches that purity requires an external and concrete means: God does not purify by thought alone, but through visible gestures and rituals. This modest plant reminds us that purification comes through humble acts and simple yet consecrated instruments. For the believer, it evokes how God truly erases the stain of sin when one approaches Him acknowledging their impurity. The contrast between the smallness of the plant and the greatness of the divine work it represents invites trust: even seemingly weak means become powerful when God sanctifies them.

sens: A garment of linen or leather worn around the waist
Mark of belonging, social status, or function
Strength, power, faithfulness of the one who wears it (figurative image)
H0232.detail: 1. It is primarily a strip of fabric (linen) or skin (leather) that is wrapped around the waist and hips: Jeremiah is commanded to buy one and wear it on his hips (Jeremiah 13:1), while Elijah is recognizable by his leather belt (2 Kings 1:8). It holds clothing in place and can carry objects. 2. The belt distinguishes the one who wears it: it marks a state, a dignity. God prepares for battle or work by "girding" His waist, as in Isaiah 11:5 where it symbolizes the justice that envelops His action. 3. It becomes the image of attachment and faithfulness: God says He has bound Israel and Judah to Himself "like a belt is bound around the waist of a man" (Jeremiah 13:11), but this belt becomes spoiled and useless if the people do not listen — a striking image of the broken covenant.
H0232.origine: The Hebrew word אֵזוֹר (ezor) is very ancient and refers to the essential garment that holds other pieces of clothing in place. It is related to the idea of "girding" or "surrounding." In Hebrew, this garment is part of the equipment of a warrior and a servant, and its variants express the idea of limitation, restriction, of what envelops and can also break or wear out.
H0232.emploi: The word appears twelve times in the Old Testament, mainly in prophetic narratives. In 2 Kings 1:8, Elijah's leather belt makes him recognizable. Jeremiah dedicates a long passage (Jeremiah 13:1-11) to a parable of the belt: one buys it, wears it, hides it, it rots — each stage represents the history of the people and their unfaithfulness. In poetic and prophetic passages (Isaiah 5:27; Isaiah 11:5), the belt becomes a metaphor for solidity, divine power, or justice. It is the classic biblical image of the bond, of what attaches and can also detach or tear.
H0232.portee: The belt reminds us that God is faithful and just — He "girds" Himself with these qualities (Isaiah 11:5). But it also shows how unfaithfulness wears down our relationship with God: Jeremiah's rotting belt symbolizes a people who turn away and degrade. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation to remain attached to God through obedience, like a belt that holds firmly.

sens: In that case, in this hypothesis
At that moment, afterwards
In those circumstances, therefore
H0233.detail: 1. The word expresses a logical consequence or a hypothesis: "if this had happened, then that would have followed." In Psalm 124, it introduces what would have happened if the Lord had not been with Israel — "Then the waters would have overwhelmed us" (Psalm 124:4). It is the word of the reasoning chain: "if X, then Y." 2. It also marks the temporal or logical sequence of events: "at that moment, afterwards." The psalmist enumerates the misfortunes that would have followed — first being swallowed by enemies, then (afterwards) being submerged by the floods, then (always) the passing of torrents (Psalms 124:3-5). 3. In these circumstances or therefore: the word summarizes a situation and draws a conclusion. Here, it condenses the idea "in these perilous conditions, if God had not been our help, this is what would have happened to us."
H0233.origine: The word is a conjunction of condition and consequence in ancient Hebrew. It comes from the root that expresses the idea of "case" or "condition." It is closely related to the logic of discourse: it does not just introduce a moment in time, but a link in a chain of reasoning or a series of causally related events.
H0233.emploi: The word appears three times, all in Psalm 124, a psalm of thanksgiving where Israel proclaims that without the Lord, it would have been defeated. Each occurrence reinforces the effect of catastrophic accumulation: first they would have been swallowed, then (v. 4) the waters would have overwhelmed them, then (v. 5) the floods would have gone over their soul. The repeated use of the word creates a crescendo of hypothetical horror that highlights the gravity of the people's danger and God's saving intervention. The word thus functions less as an ordinary temporal adverb than as a logical link: "as a result," "therefore."
H0233.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the logic of faith: "if God were not with us, where would we be?" It teaches that recognizing God is first recognizing our extreme fragility and total dependence. The succession of "then" reveals the reality of danger and the reality of salvation. For the Christian, it is a lesson on grace: without it, we would be overwhelmed.

sens: portion of a burnt offering on the altar as a memorial
that which ascends to God and reminds Him of the offering of the one who prays
H0234.detail:
1. The remembrance is the portion of a grain offering (flour, oil, incense) that the priest takes and burns on the altar: it is an act that consecrates the whole to God and makes it present in worship. In Leviticus 2:2, for example, the priest burns a handful of flour mixed with oil along with all the incense as a remembrance, an offering of pleasing aroma to the Lord.
2. This act signifies that the one offering asks God to remember him, his name, and his prayer. The smoke that rises from the burnt remembrance on the altar is like a voice ascending to God (Leviticus 24:7, where the pure incense on the showbread is a remembrance consumed by fire before the Lord).
H0234.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to recall, mention, evoke." The remembrance is therefore what reminds God of the one who prays and what he offers. The image is that of perfume rising and impressing the one who smells it: the prayer and the offering burnt on the altar ascend as a pleasing aroma to the Lord, who remembers it.
H0234.emploi: The word appears seven times in the Bible, exclusively in the Levitical prescriptions regarding offerings (Leviticus 2, 5, 6, and 24). It always designates the portion taken and burned on the altar. In Leviticus 2:9 and 2:16, it is a part of the grain offering or of ears of grain; in Leviticus 5:12, it is a sin offering. The remembrance is never eaten by the priests: it is entirely consumed by fire, which distinguishes it from other portions. What varies is what the remembrance is taken from (flour, crushed ears), but the function remains the same: to remind God of the offering and the one who brings it.
H0234.portee: For the believer, the remembrance teaches that God never forgets those who approach Him with a sincere offering. It is an act of faith: to recognize that God remembers and that our prayer ascends to Him. Although these Levitical offerings are no longer made, the idea remains: our prayers and acts of consecration rise before God and find in Him an attentive ear.

sens: To go away, disappear
To be consumed, gradually decrease
To be drained of strength, resources
To function hastily or lightly (figurative sense)
H0235.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of an action or a person who goes away, who leaves a place. In daily life, it is the simple movement of departing.

2. Applied to things (water, provisions, strength), the word describes a gradual exhaustion: what was there diminishes and disappears. In Job 14:11, "the waters of the lakes vanish": the reservoir empties, the water flows away and disappears.

3. It is the image of strength being exhausted. In Deuteronomy 32:36, the Lord sees "that their strength is exhausted": the people have no more resources, no more energy. In 1 Samuel 9:7, "there are no more provisions in our sacks": the supplies no longer exist.

4. The word can also describe a hasty or light attitude, as in Proverbs 20:14, where the buyer "in going away" congratulates himself on the deal made, or in Jeremiah 2:36, with the "haste to change your way": a form of hurried flight.
H0235.origine: This Hebrew root first evokes the movement of departure or flight. It refers to the image of what goes away, flows, consumes. The verb describes both the physical gesture (to leave) and the process of exhaustion (a reserve that runs dry, a strength that fades). This evolution of meaning—from outward movement to internal destruction—is characteristic of Hebrew action verbs.
H0235.emploi: This verb appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always to express the idea of disappearance or exhaustion. In Deuteronomy 32:36, it qualifies the strength of the people that declines. In 1 Samuel 9:7, it applies to provisions that no longer exist in the sacks. In Job 14:11, it depicts the evaporation of the waters of the lakes and the drying up of rivers, an image of inevitable destruction. In Proverbs 20:14 and Jeremiah 2:36, the word takes on a nuance of rapid or light action, mixed with a kind of carelessness. In all contexts, it marks absence, consumption, disappearance.
H0235.portee: This word teaches the biblical reader a profound truth: human resources—strength, provisions, water—are never unlimited. They exhaust, dry up, disappear. It is an invitation to recognize our fragility and dependence, especially before God. The Word reminds us that only divine help endures; everything that pertains to the created world passes away and dies. This verb calls us not to place our trust in what exhausts, but in Him who will never falter.

sens: To move from one place to another
To walk towards a specific destination
To leave a place
H0236.detail:
1. To move from one place to another: the verb simply expresses the action of moving, progressing in space. In Ezra 5:8, the royal inspectors "go" into the province of Judah to examine the temple works.
2. To walk towards a specific destination: the movement often has a clear direction and purpose. When Daniel "goes" to his house (Daniel 2:17), he is intentionally heading to that place. Similarly, in Ezra 5:15, the governor orders someone to "go" deposit the utensils at the temple—this is a movement directed towards a goal.
3. To leave a place: the verb can emphasize the departure, the action of leaving a location. In Ezra 4:23, Rehum and his colleagues "go away" hastily to Jerusalem, abandoning their position to move.
H0236.origine: The Aramaic verb azal (אֲזַל) is a simple and common term for designating movement, displacement. It is the key word of action in the narrative: it carries the story from one point to another. Related to the Semitic words for "to go" and "to depart," it is used in the Aramaic passages of the book of Daniel and Ezra, reflecting the spoken language in Babylon and Persia after the exile.
H0236.emploi: This verb appears only in the Aramaic portions of the Hebrew Bible, particularly in the book of Ezra and the book of Daniel. The seven usages provided show that it serves to narrate the movements of characters: the king's messengers rushing to Jerusalem, the inspectors traversing the province, the king retreating to his palace, Daniel seeking his companions. It is a verb of narrative, of historical storytelling, without particular coloring—neither dramatic nor religious—just the action of moving.
H0236.portee: This word reminds the reader that in the biblical story, people move, act, go where they are called. For Daniel or for those who obey the king's orders, "to go" is primarily a concrete act of discipline and intention. It underscores the importance of action, of movement in faith: it is by setting out that one becomes an actor in God's story.

sens: stone or monument located between Ramah and Nob, in the Holy Land
H0237.detail: Ézel is an ancient stone or monument in the Holy Land, situated between the cities of Ramah and Nob. It is here that David and Jonathan said goodbye for the last time, in a scene filled with emotion (1 Samuel 20:19). The name itself means "departure" or "flight," which fits perfectly with the context: David had to leave the court of King Saul in haste to save his life.
H0237.origine: The Hebrew name אֶזֶל (Ézel) is formed from a root that evokes the idea of departure or flight. This place name reflects its role: it is where paths separate, where one says goodbye. The choice of this name for the secret meeting point of David and Jonathan emphasizes that their separation was inevitable and definitive.
H0237.emploi: Ézel appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 20:19. Samuel reports that David was to hide near the stone of Ézel during the new moon, a time when Jonathan and David had planned to meet secretly. This meeting was a test: if King Saul noticed David's absence from his table, it would confirm that Saul sought to kill him. Thus, Ézel represents the place where two faithful friends part in the face of danger, where loyalty prevails over position and safety.
H0237.portee: The stone of Ézel testifies to the intense friendship between David and Jonathan, despite the political obstacles that divided them. For the Christian reader, this place reminds us that true friendships can withstand geographical separation and trials, and that faithfulness may require sacrifice. It is also a symbol of divine protection: despite Saul's threats, God allowed David and Jonathan to say goodbye and to strengthen each other before fleeing.

sens: Perceive by hearing, hear a sound or a voice
Pay attention to someone, give them your ear
Obey an order or follow advice
Grant favor to a prayer or supplication
H0238.detail:
1. Hearing a sound, a voice, a word: this is receiving the message through the physical ear. When Lamech says to his wives, "listen to my voice" (Genesis 4:23), he is asking them to hear and perceive his words.
2. Paying attention, turning towards the one who speaks with the intention of listening: "Give ear to the sound of my words" (Job 34:16) means to deliberately focus on what is being said. It is an active posture, that of someone who makes themselves available.
3. Obeying and following: the verb includes the idea that one who truly listens acts according to what they have heard. When it is said, "they did not heed the warnings" (2 Chronicles 24:19), it means they rejected not only the words but also the warning itself—they did not obey.
4. Being answered, receiving a response: when the psalmist says, "Give ear to my prayer" (Psalms 86:6), he asks God to turn His attention towards him and to grant his request. It is divine listening that changes everything.
H0238.origine: The Hebrew verb אָזַן (azan) comes from a root that evokes the ear, the organ of listening. The ear is the seat of attention and obedience—listening, therefore, is to incline one's ear towards someone. In the Bible, the God who listens is the one who shows grace and love towards His people, while the man who does not listen voluntarily closes himself off to the voice of the Lord.
H0238.emploi: This verb appears 41 times in the Old Testament. It is very frequent in the Psalms, where the believer calls on God to listen to his prayer and supplications (Psalms 54:4, 86:6, 141:1). It is also found in prophetic speeches, notably in Isaiah, where the prophet calls the heavens and the earth to listen to God's message (Isaiah 1:2, 1:10). In the book of Job and Proverbs, the verb denotes attentive listening to wise words. It can also mean obedience: when Israel "did not listen" to the prophets, it means they rejected their call to repentance (2 Chronicles 24:19, Nehemiah 9:30). The context always shows that true listening involves more than hearing: it requires attention and a willingness to respond.
H0238.portee: This verb reminds the Christian reader that listening is not passive: it requires an openness of heart and a willingness to obey. God listens to the prayer of the righteous, but we too are called to truly listen to the voice of God in His Word, not only with our ears but by transforming our lives. True listening leads to obedience, and obedience is the mark of one who loves God.

sens: examine something carefully to judge its value or quality
consider a matter thoroughly before deciding
test or try to verify the solidity or truth of something
H0239.detail:
1. Examining carefully means looking or listening in detail to understand what is truly valuable: it is the act of the weighmaster who puts something on the scale, or the master who assesses the worker—thus, wise words "are like nails firmly fixed" and "given by one shepherd" so that they may be "weighed" and judged (Ecclesiastes 12:11).
2. Considering a matter thoroughly means turning it over in one's mind, weighing it before acting: a judgment that is not made lightly, but after long reflection.
3. Testing or trying means subjecting something to a trial to verify its quality or truth—like testing gold in the fire to see if it is pure.
H0239.origine: The Hebrew verb אָזַן comes from a root that refers to the idea of balance and careful examination. In its Piel form (the one used in the Bible), it means "to weigh" in both a literal and figurative sense: to evaluate, gauge, estimate. This image of the scale—putting one side and the other to compare—illustrates well the work of the mind that examines and judges.
H0239.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ecclesiastes 12:11. There, the Preacher speaks of the words of the wise, described as "nails firmly fixed": they are given by "one shepherd" and are meant to be "weighed"—that is, examined, tested, considered trustworthy by the one who receives them. The context suggests that it is a moral or intellectual trial: the reader must estimate the true value of the teachings received.
H0239.portee: This word invites the believer not to passively accept the words they hear, but to weigh them, to examine them in the light of God's Word. It is a call to discernment and personal responsibility: each one must evaluate what is taught to them, like gold that passes through the fire to be purified.

sens: Tool or utensil used for a specific task
Object carried with oneself in one's luggage or belongings
H0240.detail:
1. The word refers to a concrete tool or utensil intended to accomplish a task. In Deuteronomy 23:13, it refers to an instrument used to dig the ground and cover excrement: a useful and functional object.
2. More broadly, it is something one carries with them, which is part of their luggage or travel gear. It is the utensil one takes along to meet a practical need on the way.
H0240.origine: The Hebrew word אָזֵן comes from a root meaning "to make" or "to prepare." It etymologically designates what has been prepared or shaped, thus a manufactured object, a tool. The word is related to Hebrew terms that express the idea of creation or production of objects.
H0240.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Deuteronomy 23:13. In this context of laws of purity and hygiene for the Israelite camp, it refers to a practical and humble instrument—a kind of shovel or stick—that the soldier or traveler must have with them to fulfill a natural necessity decently. It is a very concrete and utilitarian term.
H0240.portee: This passage teaches that even the most basic physical needs must be treated with order, cleanliness, and respect within the community of God. The instrument mentioned symbolizes how the Law governs daily life in its simplest details, showing that every area of existence—even the most intimate—falls under the will of the Lord.

sens: Physical organ located on each side of the head that allows hearing sounds
Ability to listen, to receive a word or message
Action of paying attention to what is said to us
Receiver of divine revelation or instruction from God
H0241G.detail:
1. The ear is primarily the organ of the body: Moses commands to pierce the ear of the servant (Exodus 21:6), and earrings and rings adorn the ears (Genesis 35:4). In the mute idols of Psalm 115:6, they "have ears but do not hear."
2. To listen means to have an attentive ear: to lend an ear to someone means to truly listen to them. Jeremiah complains that his people "do not lend an ear" (Jeremiah 7:26) — they refuse to listen to God's warning.
3. Learning by hearsay means knowing something not through direct experience, but through what one has heard: the Servant in Isaiah 11:3 "will not judge by hearsay" but by what he truly sees and knows.
4. In particular, the ear is the seat of revelation: God "unlocks the ear" of Samuel (1 Samuel 3:11) to announce His words to him, meaning He calls him to listen. The Psalms continually ask God to lend an ear to our cries (Psalms 17:6, 86:1).
H0241G.origine: The Hebrew word אֹזֶן comes from a root suggesting the idea of "to advance" or "to protrude" — the ear is indeed what protrudes from the skull. In the Old Testament, the ear is often linked to obedience and reception: "to uncover the ear" means to reveal, to make heard. The word belongs to the family of body organs and senses, like the eye or the mouth, and it always carries a spiritual weight: to listen is to obey.
H0241G.emploi: The word "ear" appears 111 times in the Hebrew Bible. From Genesis and Exodus, it refers to the physical organ (earrings, piercing the servant's ear). But very quickly, it becomes metaphorical: "to lend an ear" to God or to wisdom is a common expression in the Psalms, Job, and Proverbs — 43 occurrences just in the Psalms. Proverbs, in particular, invites the young man to "lend an ear" to wisdom (Proverbs 5:1, 22:17). The idea that God listens to our prayers (He lends an ear) intersects with the idea that we must listen to God: the ear becomes the symbol of spiritual obedience. Finally, in a few passages (1 Samuel 3:11, Isaiah 22:14), "to uncover the ear" means to reveal, to make known secretly.
H0241G.portee: The ear reminds us that faith begins with listening: hearing the word of God is the first step of obedience. Proverbs teaches us that wisdom is acquired by lending an ear to instruction. Conversely, refusing to listen is to refuse to submit to God. For the believer, cultivating an attentive ear to the word of God and to wisdom becomes an essential spiritual discipline: "Let him who has ears to hear, hear."

sens: The organ of the body that allows hearing sounds
The action of listening, receiving through hearing
The presence of someone, the fact of being heard by them
The heart, the internal disposition to listen and understand
H0241H.detail:
1. The ear is the physical organ that captures sounds: this is the literal sense of the word. In 2 Kings 18:26, it is requested to speak in Aramaic rather than in Judean "to the ears of the people," meaning in a way that all can hear and understand.

2. To hear means to receive and retain a message: "we have heard this order" (2 Samuel 18:12) means "we have received and memorized the king's command." The ear represents here the ability to grasp a word and to remember it.

3. Being "in the ears" of someone means being in their presence, being heard by them: in Genesis 23:10, Abraham speaks "in the presence of the sons of Heth," literally "to the ears" of the witnesses. This means that the matter is done openly, before witnesses.

4. Metaphorically, the ear represents the heart that listens to the word of God, the disposition to receive His revelation. In Numbers 11:18, the people "cried to the ears of the Lord": this is the image of God who listens, who has His ears open to the prayers of His people.
H0241H.origine: The Hebrew word אֹזֶן (ozen) comes from a root that fundamentally means "to hear" or "to listen." In the Bible, the ear is never a mere passive organ: it is the seat of the active reception of the word, especially that of God. This is why "to uncover the ear" becomes an image of divine revelation — God "opens" the ears of the prophet so that he may receive His message. The word belongs to the fundamental sensory vocabulary of biblical faith: seeing and hearing are the two pillars of the knowledge of God.
H0241H.emploi: The word ear appears 32 times in the provided texts, mainly in the historical books and the prophets. It is used first in the literal sense: it is the organ that receives words and orders (Numbers 11:18, 2 Samuel 18:12). But it quickly shifts to the sense of presence and testimony: to speak "to the ears" of someone (Jeremiah 36:10, Genesis 23:10) means that what is said is done in their presence, officially. Finally, the word is used in the context of religious listening: the people are called to lend an ear to the word of God (Deuteronomy 5:1), and God Himself "lends an ear" to the prayers of His people. This last nuance is fundamental: it shows that the ear, in biblical thought, is the living link between the speaker and the listener.
H0241H.portee: For the Christian, the spiritual ear is crucial. Jesus often says: "He who has ears to hear, let him hear." The ear is the readiness to receive the word of God, to truly listen to it, not just in a distracted manner. Cultivating an "attentive ear" to God is to cultivate a living relationship with Him. It is also to recognize that God listens to us, that He has His ears open to our prayers and cries.

sens: Organ of the human body that allows hearing and balance
The act of hearing, listening to something
The act of reporting information to someone
The act of revealing or manifesting something to someone
H0241I.detail:
1. The ear is the physical organ of the body through which one hears. In Judges 7:3, Gideon is invited to "proclaim" a decision "to the ears of the people": this means speaking literally to the ears of people, so that the words reach them.
2. The ear also refers to the action of listening, of receiving a word. In 1 Samuel 18:23, the words of Saul are "repeated to the ears of David": this means that David receives these words, that they are communicated to him.
3. To be "informed" or "warned" about something means to have received news in one's ear. In Ruth 4:4, Boaz says "I have informed you": he has conveyed to Ohed the information about the right of redemption.
4. Sometimes "to uncover the ear" means to reveal something hidden, as a divine word might come to the inner ear. This is the image of revelation: the one who listens receives what was unknown.
H0241I.origine: The Hebrew word for "ear" comes from an ancient root that designates the opening through which one hears. It is a very concrete word: it primarily depicts the physical organ. But as the ear is the seat of listening and receiving, the Bible broadens its usage: one speaks to someone "to their ears", one reports to their ears, and finally, it is to the ear that God reveals His secrets. Thus, the ear becomes a symbol of receptivity to the divine word.
H0241I.emploi: The word appears about 30 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical narratives (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) and the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel). It is first used in the physical sense: something is made known "to the ears" of an assembly (Deuteronomy 31:28, Judges 7:3, Jeremiah 36:15). It is then used to signify information or warning: one "informs to the ears" of someone, one "warns to the ears" (1 Samuel 22:8, Ruth 4:4). In prophetic speeches, "to uncover the ear" to someone means to reveal a mystery or secret of the Lord (1 Samuel 9:15). The usage varies little from passage to passage, but the meaning enriches: from the bodily organ, it moves to the capacity to receive and be transformed by a word.
H0241I.portee: For the believer, the ear reminds us that faith comes from hearing the word (Romans 10:17). Having an open ear means being willing to receive what God wants to say to us. Many passages invite us to listen to God rather than follow the noise of the world. Recognizing that God reveals His secrets to those He wishes to instruct encourages the Christian to cultivate an attentive and humble listening to His word.

sens: Fortified city built by Scherah, daughter of Ephraim
H0242.detail: Uzzen-Scherah is a city that the daughter of Ephraim, named Scherah, built in the region of Ephraim. Its name literally means "portion of Scherah", indicating that she was its founder or owner. This construction is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 7:24, where Scherah also builds the two cities of Beth-Horon (the lower and the upper), showing that she was a woman of great influence and resources in ancient Israel.
H0242.origine: The Hebrew name is composed of two elements: "Uzzen" (portion or ear, in the sense of "part") and "Scherah" (the proper name of the daughter of Ephraim). This type of place name indicates appropriation or foundation by a person, a common practice in ancient Israel to designate new cities built by important figures.
H0242.emploi: Uzzen-Scherah appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:24. It is listed among the fortified cities built by Scherah in the territory of Ephraim. This isolated mention indicates that the city likely disappeared or lost importance at an earlier time than the other historical books, or that it did not mark Israel's history sufficiently to be mentioned elsewhere.

sens: Pair of hills at the border of the territory of Naphtali
H0243.detail: Aznoth-Tabor refers to two peaks or ridges located on the boundary of the territory assigned to the tribe of Naphtali during the division of the promised land. The Hebrew name literally means "ears of Tabor" or "ridges of Tabor", likely evoking two elevations that resemble the pointed shape of Mount Tabor, a famous mountain in Galilee. This site is mentioned only once in Joshua 19:34 as a geographical landmark used to delineate the territory of Naphtali.
H0243.origine: The name consists of two Hebrew words: az.not ("ears" or "ridges", plural of ozne) and ta.vor (Mount Tabor). The image of "ears" to designate rocky peaks or ridges is natural in geography: pointed shapes that resemble ears. Aznoth-Tabor thus evokes heights associated with Tabor or resembling it.
H0243.emploi: Aznoth-Tabor appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:34, in the context of the division of lands among the tribes of Israel. It is listed among the boundaries of the territory of Naphtali, alongside other geographical landmarks like the Jordan and the Sea of Galilee. It is a border site, used to precisely mark tribal boundaries after the conquest of Canaan.

sens: Son of Gad, ancestor of an Israelite tribe
H0244A.detail: Ozni is a man from the tribe of Gad, living during the time of Egypt and the desert. He is the ancestor of the family of the Oznites, mentioned during the census in Numbers 26:16. His name means "my ear" or "my hearing", which emphasizes the importance of listening in the Hebrew tradition.
H0244A.origine: The name Ozni comes from the Hebrew root "ozen" (אֹזֶן), which means "ear". It is a personal theophoric name, formed by the addition of the possessive pronoun "i" (י), giving the literal meaning "my ear". This type of name often expresses a personal relationship or a request addressed to God.
H0244A.emploi: Ozni is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:16, during the second census of Israel in the desert. He is presented there as the father of the family of the Oznites, one of the families of the tribe of Gad. This is the only biblical use of this name, which appears in the context of the genealogical records of God's people.

sens: Descendant of Ozni, man of the tribe of Gad
H0244B.detail: 1. An Oznite is a person who belongs to the clan of the Oznites, that is, the family group founded by Ozni. Ozni was a son of Gad, and his descendants formed a distinct family within the tribe of Gad. At the time of the census in the desert (Numbers 26:16), the Oznites are counted as a genealogical unit in the organization of the people of Israel.
H0244B.origine: The word "Oznite" derives from the name Ozni, founder of the clan. Ozni literally means "my ear" or "my hearing" in Hebrew, suggesting the idea of hearing or vigilance. Like all names of Israelite clans, "Oznite" is formed by the addition of the suffix indicating belonging to a family lineage.
H0244B.emploi: The word "Oznite" appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:16, during the census of the sons of Israel in the desert of Moab. At that point, the Oznites are listed among the families of the tribe of Gad, alongside the Erites and other Gadite clans. It is an administrative and genealogical term that reflects the social and tribal organization of Israel.

sens: Man of the tribe of Levi mentioned during the time of exile and return
H0245.detail: Azania is a Levite, father of Joshua, who is among the signatories of the renewed covenant under Nehemiah after the return from exile (Nehemiah 10:9). His name appears only once in the Bible, in this list of the leaders of the people who solemnly commit to obey the Law.
H0245.origine: The name Azania means "Yahweh hears" or "God hears": it combines the root "azân" (to hear, to listen) with the divine name Yahweh. It is a theophoric Hebrew name, meaning a name that incorporates the name of God, affirming the faith of the father who bore it.
H0245.emploi: Azania is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:9, where he appears in the list of Levites and leaders of the people who seal the covenant after the return from exile to Jerusalem. He is identified as the father of Joshua (or Jeshua), another important Levite of that time. This appearance contextualizes his role: as a member of the Levitical priestly class, he participates in the religious and civil restoration of the community of Israel returned from Babylonian captivity.

sens: Metal link that immobilizes the hands or feet of a prisoner
Servitude or captivity imposed by force
H0246.detail:
1. A chain is a metal link that restrains the hands or feet of a captive person to prevent escape. It is the material instrument of captivity. Jeremiah is bound with them during his deportation to Babylon: "Jeremiah was bound with chains among all the captives of Jerusalem and Judah who were being carried away to Babylon" (Jeremiah 40:1).
2. By extension, the word also refers to captivity itself, the state of slavery or servitude imposed by force. When Nebuzaradan tells Jeremiah: "I free you today from the chains that are on your hands" (Jeremiah 40:4), he speaks of both the material object and the condition of prisoner of war that this link represents.
H0246.origine: The Hebrew word אֲזֵק (aziq) refers to an object that binds and restrains. It expresses the image of a hindrance, something that immobilizes and makes captive. Its use in the Old Testament is limited: only the book of Jeremiah employs it to describe the captivity of the Judeans during the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C.
H0246.emploi: This word appears twice, exclusively in Jeremiah 40, during the account of Jeremiah's deportation to Babylon by Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guards of King Nebuchadnezzar. In the first usage (Jeremiah 40:1), the chain is the concrete instrument by which Jeremiah is held among the captives. In the second (Jeremiah 40:4), Nebuzaradan offers Jeremiah to free him from these chains or to let him go free. The historical context shows that this captivity is the consequence of God's judgment on unfaithful Jerusalem.
H0246.portee: For the Christian reader, the chain serves as a reminder that sin produces enslavement and that only God can truly liberate. Jeremiah's fate, chained and then freed by grace, foreshadows the plan of salvation: God allows captivity but does not abandon His servant, and His word remains free even when the prophet is bound.

sens: to tighten around the waist with a belt or band
to clothe someone with strength, quality, or power
to prepare for battle, to equip for action
to surround, encircle, hold firmly
H0247.detail: 1. To gird means primarily to tighten around the waist a belt, a strip of cloth or leather. It is a practical gesture: one girds their loins to prepare for work or running (Job 38:3, "Gird up your loins like a man"). 2. By extension, to gird also means to clothe someone with an abstract quality or strength, as one would put on a garment. God "girds" the psalmist with strength (Psalms 18:33, "It is God who girds me with strength"), or fills him with joy (Psalms 30:12, "You have girded me with joy"). 3. To gird also means to prepare for battle, to equip oneself by girding, especially the loins — as the belt held the garments and allowed for free movement in combat. It is an image of military mobilization. 4. The word can also simply mean to surround or encircle something, as one encircles the loins with a leather belt (2 Kings 1:8).
H0247.origine: The Hebrew verb azar has its root in the idea of tightening, binding. It evokes the action of buckling a belt around the body to hold the garments or to prepare for action. The word of the same family, "ezor" (belt), designates the object itself. The image is very concrete: that of the warrior or worker who girds their loins to be free in their movements.
H0247.emploi: This verb appears 15 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the wisdom books (Job, Psalms) and in the prophets. In the Psalms, girding applies to God: He "girds" the righteous with strength or joy to support and protect them. In Job, the expression "gird up your loins" symbolizes preparation to face a trial or divine questioning (Job 38:3). In the prophets like Isaiah and Jeremiah, the verb expresses mobilization, the equipping of forces, or the action of God arming His people or their enemies. The meaning is always linked to the idea of strength, preparation, and the ability to act.
H0247.portee: Girding reminds the reader that strength — whether physical, moral, or spiritual — is never isolated: it is added to us, it clothes us, it envelops us, like a belt. It is a powerful biblical image of divine help: God "girds" the believer with strength so that they can stand in trial and fulfill their mission. It also invites personal preparation: to gird one's loins is to be ready to obey, to fight evil, or to endure suffering with the grace that God provides.

sens: The limb of the body that extends from the shoulder to the hand
Physical strength and power of action
The power and intervention of God
H0248.detail:
1. The arm is the limb of the human body that extends from the shoulder to the hand. Job 31:22 speaks of it literally: "Let my shoulder be pulled from its joint, let my arm fall and be broken!" 
2. The arm represents physical strength and the capacity to act or to fight. It is the instrument by which one exerts their power.
3. In biblical language, the "arm" becomes the image of divine power and God's intervention to save His people. Jeremiah 32:21 states that God brought them out of Egypt "with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm": it is a poetic expression to say that God acted with His sovereign power.
H0248.origine: The Hebrew word אֶזְרוֹעַ (ezroua) literally means "arm." It comes from a root that expresses the idea of strength and power. The arm being the main instrument of action and strength in the body, the word has come to designate power itself. In the Hebrew Bible, this image of God's "arm" is used to speak of His powerful and liberating action.
H0248.emploi: The word appears twice in the French Bible we have, always in the context of power. In Job 31:22, it is in the concrete sense: the arm as a part of the body. In Jeremiah 32:21, it is in the figurative and theological sense: the "outstretched arm" of God symbolizes His liberating power during the exodus from Egypt. This image of the outstretched arm becomes a classic formula to evoke God's powerful and merciful action toward His people.
H0248.portee: The "arm" of God in the Bible invites the believer to contemplate how God acts concretely in history. It is a reminder that God's power is not abstract: it manifests to save, liberate, and protect. Meditating on the outstretched arm of God encourages trust in Him for today's challenges.

sens: Person born and established in the land, a member of the community from the beginning
Indigenous inhabitant of Israel, citizen of the chosen people
One who has equal rights and duties before divine law
H0249.detail: 1. The word designates someone who is "from the soil," born and rooted in the land, in contrast to a foreigner who resides there without being a native. It is the image of a plant that grows naturally in a land: Ezekiel 47:22 speaks of trees "indigenous" to Israel. 2. In the law of Moses, the "indigenous" person is a native Israelite, a member of the covenant people. The laws often address both the indigenous and the foreign resident together to show the equal status of both: "The same law will apply to the indigenous as to the foreigner" (Exodus 12:49). 3. Both the indigenous and the foreigner must observe the same commandments — purity, Passover, respect for festivals, equal punishment in case of blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16). This equality reveals the heart of the law: "You shall treat the foreigner as the indigenous, you shall love him as yourself" (Leviticus 19:34).
H0249.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to sprout, to grow, to arise." The image is of something that is born and rises from the soil, hence "native" or "indigenous." This is why the word also applies to trees: an indigenous tree is one that grows naturally in the region. In Israel, the indigenous person is one who "sprouts" from the promised land, who is its natural fruit.
H0249.emploi: The word appears 16 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Law (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers). It is always used in parallel with "the foreigner" (ger), to define the legal and religious status of each in the community of Israel. Exodus 12:19, 12:49, and Leviticus 17:15 deal with dietary rules and festivals: the indigenous and the foreigner must observe the same law. Leviticus 19:34 goes beyond this legal framework by commanding love towards the foreigner, equal to love towards the indigenous. Leviticus 24:16 shows that the punishment for blasphemy applies equally to the indigenous and the foreigner. Numbers 15:29-30 and Joshua 8:33 maintain this equality. The word is encountered once in the literal sense of tree: Ezekiel 47:22.
H0249.portee: This word reminds us that the law of Israel was not a privilege of those born in Israel alone: God commanded to treat the foreigner with the same justice and love. It is a powerful lesson on welcoming those from elsewhere. It also shows that God's grace is not tied to physical birth, but to covenant and obedience. The Christian discovers that God wants us to defend the weak and the foreigners, and to integrate them into the community without discrimination.

sens: Person belonging to the family of Zerah
Wise man from the time of Solomon
H0250.detail:
1. The Ezrahite is someone who descends from Zerah, an ancestor of a lineage. This name designates belonging to a family, as one might say today "a Martin" or "a Dupont." In the Bible, this family was significant enough that its members were thus qualified.

2. The known Ezrahites were wise men and talented musicians during the reign of King Solomon. Ethan and Heman, both designated as Ezrahites, are presented as renowned sages, more or less compared to Solomon himself (1 Kings 4:31). Heman and Ethan also composed or led psalms, showcasing their artistic and spiritual excellence (Psalms 88:1 and 89:1).
H0250.origine: The word comes from the root that means "to sprout" or "to be born from the soil." The Ezrahite is thus literally "one who is born from the soil" or "one who arises from the earth" — the image of a plant growing from the ground, or a person rooted in a place. This is why this term applies to a descent, an established family. Zerah, the ancestor, is one of the sons of Judah mentioned in Genesis 38:30.
H0250.emploi: The term "Ezrahite" appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always to qualify wise men and musical talent. Ethan and Heman bear this title in 1 Kings 4:31, where King Solomon is compared to these renowned sages — which shows that being an Ezrahite was a sign of distinction. They are also authors or leaders of two psalms (Psalms 88 and 89), confirming their central role in the spiritual life of Israel. The small number of occurrences suggests that it was a particular family, not an entire social class.

sens: A boy or man born of the same parents
A boy or man sharing the same father or mother
A member of the same family, tribe, or close relative
A companion or equal with whom one has a relationship of equality or reciprocity
One who resembles another or shares a common condition
H0251G.detail: 1. The most concrete meaning is that of a male child born of the same father and mother: Cain and Abel are biological brothers, born of the union of Adam and Eve (Genesis 4:2). 2. One also calls "brother" one who shares a single parent, usually the father: thus Esau and Jacob are brothers of the same father (Genesis 27:40 and following). 3. The word extends to all members of an extended family, of the same tribe or people: Laban is called Jacob's brother although he is actually his uncle or more distant relative (Genesis 29:4 and 29:10). 4. In a reciprocal relationship or among equals, "brothers" is used to express camaraderie or alliance: it is a way of saying that one treats each other as equals, with respect and solidarity (Genesis 33:9, where Esau says to Jacob, "Keep what you have," in a reconciled brotherly posture). 5. The word can also denote a resemblance or figurative kinship: what resembles is called "brother," expressing affinity or community of nature.
H0251G.origine: The Hebrew word אָח (ach) comes from a very ancient root, common to several Semitic languages. It simply designates the blood bond in its most obvious manifestation: sharing the same parent, or more broadly, the same household or community. The root carries the idea of bond, proximity, and kinship. Related words include the plural אַחִים (achim, brothers) and the feminine אָחוֹת (achot, sister). In Greek, the New Testament uses ἀδελφός (adelphos) to translate this concept, which also designates a companion or equal in a covenant relationship.
H0251G.emploi: The word appears more than 300 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Genesis where family narratives dominate: Cain and Abel (Genesis 4), Jacob and Esau (Genesis 27-28), Joseph and his brothers (Genesis 37 and following). The meaning varies according to the context: strictly biological when it concerns a true sibling, but also broadened when designating close relatives or members of the same clan. The word can express affectionate relationships (Jacob welcoming Laban, Genesis 29:10) or dramatic tensions (Cain jealous of Abel, Genesis 4:8, or the brothers selling Joseph, Genesis 37). By extension, it also describes the relationship between allied peoples or tribes, or between one who addresses others as their equal in dignity.
H0251G.portee: Understanding the word "brother" in the Bible opens our eyes to the importance of family ties in God's plan: it is never a trivial relationship, but the framework where loyalty, jealousy, betrayal, and reconciliation play out. The word also reminds us that God sees each person as a close one, a relative, worthy of respect and mutual responsibility. In the New Testament, Jesus uses "brothers" to refer to his disciples and all those who follow God, transforming the blood bond into a bond of faith and love.

sens: Boy or man born of the same parents
Child of the same father but a different mother
Member of the same family, clan, or tribe
Person of comparable status or function
Each towards the other, in a reciprocal relationship
One who resembles or is similar (figuratively)
H0251H.detail:
1. A full brother (same father and mother) is the most direct kinship bond after children (Genesis 13:8, where Abram and Lot, though cousins, call each other brothers to express their closeness).
2. A half-brother, sharing the same father but not the same mother, also receives this name; the Bible recognizes this real but distinct blood relationship (Genesis 16:12 refers to the descendants of Ishmael, son of Abraham).
3. The term expands to all members of the clan, tribe, or people: "brothers" designates the Levites among themselves or the priests (1 Chronicles 9:32, where the Kohathites are the "brothers" of the other Levites in temple service).
4. By extension, one who shares the same role, rank, or function is called a "brother": the singers or gatekeepers of the temple are "brothers" in their office (2 Chronicles 35:15).
5. The word also expresses reciprocity, mutual relationship: "his brothers" can mean "those who treat him as such" or "those towards whom he has the same obligations" (Judges 9:1, where Abimelech calls his maternal brothers).
6. Sometimes, the bond of resemblance or common nature replaces the blood bond: two similar or like things can be called "brothers" to each other.
H0251H.origine: The Hebrew word ach comes from a very ancient root expressing proximity and belonging to the same family unit. This root is found in other Semitic languages with the same meaning. In Hebrew, derivatives of the underlying verb denote everything that binds, unites, or brings together; ach is the noun that captures the idea of a natural and permanent bond. The word essentially denotes one who shares with you the same origin, the same home, the same responsibility before the family or clan.
H0251H.emploi: The word "brother" appears 131 times in the Segond. It is used first in the strict sense: Jacob and Esau are brothers (born of the same parents), Joseph and his brothers (sons of Jacob), etc. Very quickly, it expands: Abram and Lot call each other brothers even though they are cousins (Genesis 13:8), showing that the term unites those who live together or share a project. In the religious context of the temple (1 Chronicles 9, 15, 24, 25), "brother" systematically designates the Levites, the priests, or the singers among themselves, emphasizing that they form a community united by the same service. The word can also express a reciprocal relationship or moral reciprocity: "each towards the other" (Judges 9:1-3). Only two usages render "relative" (rather than brother), further broadening the meaning to general kinship.
H0251H.portee: For the Christian reader, this word sheds light on the biblical foundation of brotherhood. It shows that true fraternity does not depend on spontaneous generation: it rests on a common heritage, a shared belonging, a life lived together. Beyond the physical family, the Bible uses this word to express the unity of God's people and the cultic service. This prepares for the New Testament, where Jesus calls his disciples "brothers" and where the Church sees itself as a brotherhood. Understanding "brother" in Hebrew helps grasp that the Christian community is not a voluntary association of convenience, but a bond as deep as that of blood.

sens: son of the same father and mother
son of the same father (but different mother)
member of the same family, clan, or tribe
compatriot, member of the same people
one with whom one has a reciprocal relationship of equality
that which is similar or alike
H0251I.detail:
1. The brother in the strict sense: one who shares the same parents. This is the closest blood relationship after that of children. In Genesis 42:21, Joseph acknowledges: "It is because of our brother that we suffer," referring to the wrong he caused Joseph as a child.
2. The half-brother, son of the same father but a different mother. The law of Israel took this into account for inheritance and family rights.
3. The member of the extended family, the same clan or tribe. Leviticus 25:25 commands: "If your brother becomes poor... you shall come to his aid," designating any Israelite as a potential brother.
4. The compatriot, the Israelite facing another Israelite, or more broadly, one who belongs to the same people. Isaiah 19:2 describes a divided nation: "They will fight brother against brother," meaning Egyptian against Egyptian.
5. The reciprocal relationship of equality or solidarity: two people who treat each other as brothers. Leviticus 19:17 says: "You shall not hate your brother in your heart," calling for respect for one who is your equal.
6. That which is similar or analogous to something else, by figurative extension.
H0251I.origine: The Hebrew word אָח (ach) primarily denotes a blood brother, with the idea of one who shares the same family origin. It is a very ancient word, also attested in Aramaic (אַח) and in other Semitic languages. The root evokes the intimacy of the kinship bond. From this concrete and personal meaning, the word naturally extends to all members of the same family, then to every Israelite as a brother in the covenant, showing how biblical Hebrew progressively generalizes a blood bond into a bond of communal belonging.
H0251I.emploi: The word "brother" appears about 122 times in the Hebrew Bible, making it a central term in Israelite life. It first designates a blood brother (Joseph and his brothers in Genesis 37-42), then expands considerably: every Israelite is the brother of every other Israelite. The Law in Deuteronomy multiplies the ordinances concerning the "brother" — debt forgiveness every seventh year (15:2-3), aid to the poor (15:7-11), commercial regulations (25:3-4). This word creates a legal and moral solidarity: one cannot reduce a brother to perpetual slavery (Leviticus 25:39-46), one must treat him justly. Gradually, in religious or prophetic contexts, it designates one who shares the same covenant with God, which establishes the community of Israel.
H0251I.portee: For today's believer, this word reveals how the Bible creates a radical solidarity within the people of God. Calling someone "brother" is not a sentimentality: it is a legal and moral commitment to treat him justly, to help him in need, not to exploit him. It is also a call to see in every member of the Church not a stranger or a rival, but someone with whom one shares a covenant. Generosity towards the brother is not an option; it is the essence of communal life before God.

sens: a boy or man born of the same parents as another person
a member of one's own family, a close relative
a man of the same people or nation
a believer, a companion in faith
H0252.detail: 1. A brother is primarily a boy or man who comes from the same father and mother: it is the closest familial bond after that of father and mother. 2. More broadly, the word designates any family member, any person linked by blood or covenant. 3. It can also mean a man of the same people, a compatriot with whom one shares history and law. 4. In a religious context, it refers to a believer, someone who shares the same faith and community — as seen in Ezra 7:18, where the Persian king allows Ezra and "his brothers" (the other priests and Levites) to make good use of the royal treasury according to their discernment.
H0252.origine: The Aramaic word אַח (ach) is the direct counterpart of the Hebrew אָח (ach, H0251), which literally means "one who is with" or "the companion." Both forms derive from an ancient Semitic root that expresses the idea of closeness and communion. The Aramaic word appears in the Aramaic passages of the Old Testament, notably in Ezra and Daniel, to designate familial and fraternal bonds as well as bonds of spiritual or communal brotherhood.
H0252.emploi: The Aramaic word אַח (ach) appears very rarely in the Old Testament, as it is only attested once in Ezra 7:18. In this instance, it refers to Ezra's religious companions — the priests and Levites who return with him to Jerusalem. The context shows that the word is not limited to a narrow familial sense: it encompasses all those who share the same function and religious mission. In biblical Aramaic, as in Hebrew, "brother" can thus extend from the bond of blood to any bond of community and solidarity.
H0252.portee: The word "brother" reminds the believer that the Christian faith is never experienced alone, but always in connection with others. Ezra and "his brothers" accomplish their religious mission together: it is the image of a community walking with one heart to serve God. This term invites recognition of every believer as a brother with whom one shares the same belonging to God.

sens: exclamation of pain, desolation, or complaint
expression of a threat or warning
H0253.detail:
1. The word expresses a cry of pain or lament in the face of misfortune, destruction, or injustice. In Ezekiel 6:11, the prophet cries "Alas!" while describing the abominations that will bring the sword, famine, and plague upon Israel — it is the cry of one witnessing an imminent catastrophe and can only lament it.
2. The word can also serve to state a threat or to emphasize a serious warning. In Ezekiel 21:20, "Ah!" introduces the description of the sword that will slaughter — it is less a complaint than an exclamation that reinforces the horror and inevitability of the coming judgment.
H0253.origine: It is an interjection — a word that has no proper meaning but directly expresses an emotion or attitude of the speaker. In Hebrew, אָח is primarily a spontaneous cry in the face of distress, ruin, or danger. The same word appears in other biblical contexts to express dismay or horror.
H0253.emploi: The interjection אָח is rare in the Bible: it appears only three times in the transmitted passages, all in the prophet Ezekiel. It is found in the oracles of judgment — moments when God announces the punishment of Israel for its unfaithfulness. The context is always grave: destruction of Jerusalem, deadly sword, countless victims. It is the exclamation of a prophet confronted with the terrible reality of divine judgment, or the prophetic announcement of a misfortune that cannot be avoided.
H0253.portee: This interjection reminds us that in the face of God's judgment, no "normal" word suffices: only a cry of pain or alert can express the horror of separation from God. It invites the reader to feel, beyond words, the gravity of sin and the reality of judgment.

sens: container holding fire and hot coals, used for heating or cooking
H0254.detail: 1. A brazier is a pot or container filled with hot coals and fire, used to warm a room or cook. It is the image of a portable source of heat. In Jeremiah 36:22, King Josiah is sitting in his winter house with a brazier lit in front of him to keep warm during the cold season — this is exactly the domestic use of the word. Moments later (Jeremiah 36:23), this same brazier becomes the instrument of destruction: the king throws the scroll of the prophet Jeremiah into it, which burns completely. The word designates the same object, but its role shifts from comfort to wrath.
H0254.origine: The Hebrew word אָח (ach) comes from a root that evokes the idea of fire and heat. It is a concrete word, very down-to-earth: it names the object as one sees it, filled with glowing embers. The same image is found in other words in the Hebrew family of fire, all related to combustion and heat. It is an ancient and simple word, part of the everyday vocabulary of Near Eastern homes.
H0254.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the same passage of Jeremiah (36:22-23). This is the only detailed biblical account where this brazier is mentioned. This shows that it was a familiar object in private life — particularly in royal houses and wealthy homes — but that biblical authors do not designate it by this term elsewhere. The absence of this word in other texts suggests that other terms were used to speak of domestic fire. Here, it serves as a backdrop to a dramatic moment: the destruction of a prophetic word by the unbelieving king.
H0254.portee: This passage reminds us that even kings — with all their power and the comfort of their palaces — cannot escape the word of God. The act of the king throwing the scroll into the brazier symbolizes a dismissive rejection. But the biblical story teaches that destroying the message does not destroy the messenger, nor the truth of God. The Christian can see in this an assurance: the Word of God persists beyond any human attempt to erase it.

sens: wild animal that cries at night, jackal or hyena
H0255.detail: 1. The word designates an animal that makes piercing cries, notably the jackal or the hyena — desert creatures known for their mournful howls. In Isaiah 13:21, in the vision of a devastated Babylon, the prophet imagines that "owls will fill its houses": these nocturnal animals will come to inhabit the ruins of a once-powerful city, symbolizing desolation and the silence of death.
H0255.origine: The Hebrew word ʾōaḥ comes from a root that imitates sound — the piercing and sinister cry of this nocturnal animal. In biblical Hebrew, it designates wild creatures that howl in the darkness, those that evoke desolation and abandonment. The biblical context associates it with unclean animals and deserted places.
H0255.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 13:21.
