In this verse, Isaiah describes the future ruin of Babylon: after its fall, the desert will reclaim it, and wild animals — jackals, hyenas, ostriches — will make it their home. It is an image of absolute desolation: a city of power becomes the domain of beasts. The prophet uses this animal to show how God brings human empires back to nothingness.
H0255.portee: This word reminds the reader that human power is fragile and fleeting. The most formidable empires can become ruins inhabited by animals. For the Christian, it is an invitation not to fear the powers of this world and to place trust in God alone, whose kingdom will never fall.

sens: King of Israel in the 9th century B.C., son of Omri and husband of Jezebel
H0256G.detail: 1. Achab is a king of the kingdom of Israel during the period of the divided monarchy. He succeeds his father Omri around 875 B.C. and reigns for about twenty-two years. He is known for marrying the Phoenician princess Jezebel, which marks a religious turning point in the kingdom. His military enterprises, his ivory house, and his urban constructions demonstrate his material wealth and political ambition (1 Kings 22:39).
H0256G.origine: The name Achab literally means "father of a brother" or "brother of the father" in Hebrew. This family name indicates his kinship, following the custom of Hebrew names that expressed a relationship. He belonged to the dynasty of Omri, a prestigious royal house that marked the history of the Northern kingdom.
H0256G.emploi: Achab is mentioned 79 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the historical accounts of 1 Kings 16 to 22 and 2 Kings 1 to 10. His story intertwines with that of the prophet Elijah, particularly during the famous challenge on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18) where the prophets of Baal are defeated. He is also at the center of the drama of Naboth's vineyard, which he covets with the help of Jezebel (1 Kings 21). After his death in battle against the Syrians (1 Kings 22), his sons Joram and Ahaziah succeed him. His name is also associated with divine judgment: the Lord announces the destruction of his house (1 Kings 21:21-24), which will be fulfilled under King Jehu.
H0256G.portee: The reign of Achab illustrates the danger of religious apostasy and alliance with paganism. His marriage to Jezebel and his tolerance towards the worship of Baal lead the kingdom of Israel away from the God of Israel. His story warns believers that political power and material wealth, without faithfulness to God, lead to ruin. It also reminds us that the word of authentic prophets (like Elijah) prevails over false religions and that God remains the sovereign judge of history.

sens: false prophet executed by Nebuchadnezzar at the time of Jeremiah
son of Kolajah
H0256H.detail: Achab is a false prophet, son of Kolajah, who lived among the exiles of Judah in Babylon during the time of the prophet Jeremiah. He prophesied lies while claiming to speak in the name of the Lord (Jeremiah 29:21), thus deceiving the captive people by giving them false hopes. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, executed him by burning him in the fire, which was a terrible punishment (Jeremiah 29:22). His name became a curse among the captives: it was said, "May the Lord treat you like Achab" to curse someone (Jeremiah 29:22), showing how shameful his end was and how hated his memory became.
H0256H.origine: The name Achab means "brother of the father" — it combines the idea of father (ab) and brother (ach). It is the same name as the king of Israel, son of Omri, who was also an ungodly man; here, however, the biblical usages refer solely to the false prophet contemporary with Jeremiah, son of Kolajah.
H0256H.emploi: The name Achab appears only twice in the Bible, both in Jeremiah 29:21-22. It designates a false prophet who lived among the exiles of Judah in Babylon and who deceived the people by prophesying lies in the name of the Lord. God delivered him into the hands of Nebuchadnezzar, who had him killed by burning him in the fire. His death became emblematic of divine condemnation against prophetic lies: his name was invoked to curse someone, so significant was his judgment.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H0257.detail: Achban is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the kingdoms of Israel and Judah were divided. He is the son of Abishur and Abichail, and the brother of Molid (1 Chronicles 2:29).
H0257.origine: The name Achban means "brother of a wise man" or "brother of understanding." It combines two Hebrew elements: "ach" (brother) and "ban" (understanding or wisdom). It is a typical theophoric name from the genealogical tradition of Judah, reflecting values of wisdom and discernment.
H0257.emploi: Achban appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:29, where the genealogist lists the descendants of Abishur and Abichail. He is mentioned alongside his brother Molid in a genealogical list that traces the line of Judah. This mention, although brief, situates him within the context of the royal family of Judah and shows the importance given by the Bible to the complete recording of genealogies.

sens: Concentrate one's forces, fully mobilize
Direct one's attention or energy towards a goal
Sharpen, make sharp (figurative sense)
H0258.detail: 1. The verb primarily means to concentrate or gather one's forces in order to act. In Ezekiel 21:21, the sword must "gather" its forces to strike effectively: this is the image of a weapon that fully mobilizes for its destructive blow. 2. By extension, it designates the action of directing all one's energy, all one's attention towards a single point or direction. 3. The word can also evoke the idea of sharpening or making sharp, as gathering forces also means concentrating effectiveness, honing striking power.
H0258.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of gathering, concentrating, or taking a single direction. The verb in the Hithpael form (reflexive form) emphasizes the action of mobilizing oneself, concentrating one's own forces. This grammatical form reinforces the idea of a voluntary and complete mobilization.
H0258.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible (Ezekiel 21:21), where the prophet describes a sword that gathers its forces to strike. The context is one of judgment: God makes known to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, that his sword must be mobilized against Jerusalem. The military image of gathering forces expresses the certainty and power of divine judgment that is executed.
H0258.portee: This word reminds us that the power of divine judgment cannot be stopped: it gathers and directs itself towards its goal with complete effectiveness. It is an invitation to recognize God's sovereignty, even when it is exercised in judgment. For the believer, this passage also emphasizes the importance of gathering one's spiritual forces in the face of trials.

sens: The number 1, a unit
Each, all elements taken individually
Unique, without equivalent, alone
A certain, something indeterminate
Once, a single occasion
One and the other, forming a pair
H0259.detail:
1. The number 1 in all its meanings: a single unit in a succession. This is the most direct and frequent meaning. Genesis 1:5 speaks of the "first" day of creation — literally "day one".
2. Each element of a set considered individually: it emphasizes the uniqueness of each. Numbers 28:12 asks for an offering "for each bull": each receives the same portion.
3. What is unique, unparalleled, incomparable — often to highlight exception or superiority. 2 Samuel 7:23 proclaims that there is no "only" nation like Israel: no other resembles it.
4. A certain, indeterminate thing, not yet identified: this is the role of the indefinite article. One speaks of a "certain" event whose nature will be specified.
5. Once, a unique occasion, involving totality or definitiveness. The expression can also mean "formerly" or "once for all".
6. Two things or two people forming a pair, often in opposition to each other (one...the other). Exodus 36:15 notes that all the curtains had "the same" shape: they fit perfectly, in a unity of the whole.
H0259.origine: The word אחד comes from a primitive root meaning "to be united, to form a whole." The primary image is that of unity, of what cannot be divided, of what is assembled into a single body. In Hebrew, it is the fundamental cardinal number. This root also appears in the word יחיד ("unique, alone"), which reinforces the idea. The number one establishes the principle of unity from which multiplicity derives: one day, one night, one people.
H0259.emploi: This word is extraordinarily frequent in the Hebrew Bible (740 occurrences in Segond). It is found everywhere: in the creation narrative to number the days (Genesis 1:5), in genealogies and lists of patriarchs, in technical descriptions of the Tabernacle with its precise measurements, in narratives to count people or events. Its meanings vary: it designates the pure number ("there was evening one"), singular identity ("each bull"), absolute uniqueness ("only nation"), or indeterminacy ("a certain"). Some passages use it to express unity and unanimity: "one mouth," "one heart." Others double it to say "one and the other" or "one after the other." It is a key word for structuring the biblical narrative.
H0259.portee: This simple word carries a spiritual depth: the one refers to the unity of God ("Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God is one" — echoed in the New Testament: "one God, one Lord"). It also helps to grasp how God acts with each person individually: each believer, each day, each offering matters. The word one unites what is multiple — creating order in the cosmos, connection in the people, and uniqueness in the relationship with God. It is a word of unity and totality.

sens: Grass and plants that grow in wet or marshy ground
Fertile area along a watercourse where livestock graze
Figuratively, that which nourishes and sustains life
H0260.detail:
1. The word primarily designates reeds, bulrushes, and aquatic plants that grow naturally in marshes and wet areas. Job 8:11 illustrates this by asking: "Does the rush grow without marsh?", showing that these plants are inseparable from the water and moisture that sustain them.
2. It also means the meadow itself, this strip of fertile land along a river where grass abounds. In Pharaoh's dream (Genesis 41:2 and 41:18), the cows "began to graze in the meadow", illustrating a lush and nourishing pasture capable of sustaining livestock.
3. By extension, the word evokes everything that nourishes and supports: a place of life and growth, where the weak can be strengthened.
H0260.origine: The Hebrew word אָחוּ (achu) belongs to the family of words designating water, moisture, and what depends on it. It is related to the image of the marsh, the place where water stagnates and where plant life thrives. Its root refers to the idea of a space soaked with water, fertile and green.
H0260.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. Two occurrences are found in Genesis 41, in the account of Pharaoh's prophetic dream, where the fat and beautiful cows graze in a meadow, an image of abundance and prosperity. The third occurrence, in Job 8:11, uses the word more technically to speak of the reeds and bulrushes that can only grow in moisture. In all cases, the context is that of aquatic and fertile nature, of the dependence between the plant and its moist environment.
H0260.portee: This word reminds the believer that all life, both spiritual and material, needs a nourishing environment: a source of water, a stable place, support. For Israel, the fertile meadow of the Nile symbolized divine abundance; for us, it invites us to seek the living water that alone can nourish the soul.

sens: Judge of Israel from the tribe of Benjamin
Son of Gera
H0261.detail: 1. Ehud is a judge of Israel, a member of the tribe of Benjamin. According to 1 Chronicles 8:6, he is the father of several children and a family leader among the inhabitants of Gibeah. 2. He is the son of Gera, which establishes his genealogy within the tribe of Benjamin, a few generations after the eponymous ancestor.
H0261.origine: The name Ehud means "united" or "joined" in Hebrew, evoking the idea of union or cohesion. This name belongs to the Benjamite lineage and reflects the genealogical importance of this man in the history of Israel.
H0261.emploi: Ehud appears only once in the Segond 1910, in 1 Chronicles 8:6, where he is listed among the descendants of Benjamin with his children: Naaman, Ahijah, Gera, Uzza, and Ahihud. He is presented as an influential family leader among the inhabitants of Gibeah, who are said to have transported inhabitants to Manahath.

sens: To lean in to listen attentively
To pay particular attention to what someone says
To show availability and respect towards the speaker
H0262.detail:
1. The word primarily means the physical action of leaning in to someone to hear well: it is to bend, to turn towards the one speaking to not miss any of their words. Job uses this image when he tells his friends: "Lend an ear to what I am going to say" (Job 13:17) — he invites them to truly listen to him, to focus on his words.
2. The meaning extends to the inner attitude: to lend an ear is not only to hear with the ears but also to welcome with the spirit. It shows that one is attentive, interested, willing to receive what is heard.
3. It also expresses respect and deference: when one asks someone to lend an ear, one acknowledges their authority or right to be listened to, granting them importance.
H0262.origine: The Hebrew word אַחְוָה (aḥvah) belongs to a family of terms expressing the idea of explaining, declaring, making clear. Its Aramaic equivalent אַחֲוָיָה (aḥavayah) literally means "explanation." The root evokes the action of showing, exposing, manifesting something to sight or hearing. The idea of lending an ear naturally follows: it is to turn and open oneself to the declaration, to the explanation of another.
H0262.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 13:17. In this passage, Job urgently asks his three friends to truly listen to him — to really lend attention — while he is going to respond to their accusations. The context shows that it is a pressing request for kindness: Job wants his friends to listen to him, not out of obligation, but recognizing that he has something important to say. It is a call for active and respectful listening.
H0262.portee: This word reminds the reader how true listening is an act of respect and dignity. Lending an ear is not a simple physical action: it is to offer one's attention, to recognize the other in their value. For the Christian, this also speaks to listening to God and His word, and how we should address one another with the concern of truly hearing each other.

sens: the action of clarifying, making clear what was obscure or enigmatic
the result of this action: that which explains, that which makes one understand
H0263.detail:
1. Explanation is the action of making something difficult to understand clear and intelligible. In Daniel 5:12, the king seeks someone capable of "explaining" the enigmas written on the wall of the palace — those mysterious words that no one can decipher. Daniel possesses the gift of revealing the hidden meaning, shedding light on the incomprehensible.
2. It is also the very content of this clarification: the meaning that is discovered, the solution that is provided. When Daniel gives the explanation, he provides the true meaning of the divine message.
H0263.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the same root as the Hebrew achvah (אַחְוָה), which means "declaration" or "statement." The root expresses the idea of saying, of stating clearly. In Aramaic, achavayah reinforces this notion: it is the action of declaring what was hidden, manifesting what was obscure.
H0263.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 5:12, in a dramatic context: King Belshazzar has just seen a hand appear on the wall writing enigmatic words. No one among the wise men of the kingdom can interpret them. The king has Daniel sought out, known for his extraordinary gifts, particularly his ability to provide explanations of dreams and enigmas. It is in this precise sense that it is used: the revelation of the hidden meaning of a divine message.
H0263.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that only divine wisdom can illuminate mysteries. Daniel does not solve the riddle by his own knowledge, but by the Spirit of God who dwells in him. He teaches us that in the face of obscure events, unanswered questions, it is towards the wisdom of God that we must turn.

sens: the bond of kinship between brothers
the relationship of solidarity among members of the same community or people
a feeling of fraternal communion
H0264.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the natural bond that unites brothers, making them members of one family. In Zechariah 11:14, when the prophet breaks his staff to sever the "brotherhood" between Judah and Israel, he evokes this deep kinship that should unite the two kingdoms as brothers of one house.
2. More broadly, the word extends to any bond of solidarity and communion among members of the same community. Brotherhood then becomes the cement that holds together a people or group sharing the same origin, faith, or destiny.
3. On a spiritual level, brotherhood expresses a feeling of emotional and moral kinship — the awareness of a common belonging and mutual responsibility towards other members of the community.
H0264.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "brother." Brotherhood is therefore the state, quality, or relationship proper to brothers. It is primarily a family term that establishes a bond of origin and blood, then broadens to describe any form of communion based on real or spiritual kinship.
H0264.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Zechariah 11:14. The prophet Zechariah, speaking symbolically through the breaking of his staffs, describes how the brotherhood between the northern (Israel) and southern (Judah) kingdoms has been broken — reflecting both their historical political separation and their spiritual inability to remain united despite their original fraternal bond. This passage shows that once brotherhood is broken, it is not easily restored.
H0264.portee: This word reminds God's people of the privileged bond that should unite them as a chosen people, called to live in brotherhood. It highlights the grave sin of division and forgetting fraternal ties, and calls for the restoration of communion among the members of God's body.

sens: A descendant of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible
H0265.detail: Achoach is a man from the tribe of Benjamin, the grandson of Benjamin himself. He is the son of Bela and appears in the genealogy of the sons of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 8:4). His name is passed down through his descendants who are called "Ahohite" to designate the members of his clan.
H0265.origine: The name literally means "brother of rest." It comes from the Hebrew root that speaks of brotherhood and rest. It is a characteristic name in the genealogies of the tribes of Israel, often expressing a quality or familial relationship.
H0265.emploi: Achoach appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:4, in the genealogical list of the descendants of Benjamin. He is named among his brothers Abishua, Naaman, and others. Although his mention is brief, it shows his importance in the Benjaminite genealogy, and his descendants are called the "Ahohites," indicating that he founded a recognizable lineage in the history of Israel.

sens: Descendant of Ahoah, a man of the tribe of Benjamin
Member of the clan of Ahoah
H0266.detail: The Achochites are the members of the clan or descendants of Ahoah, a man from the tribe of Benjamin. Several of David's greatest warriors bear this clan name: Eleazar, son of Dodo (2 Samuel 23:9), and Dodaï (1 Chronicles 27:4) are among the most renowned military leaders of the king.
H0266.origine: The word comes from the proper name Ahoah (אֲחוֹחַ), an ancestor of the tribe of Benjamin. The suffix -ite indicates belonging to a family or tribal group: it is the classic mark to designate a clan or lineage. The meaning of the name Ahoah itself is "brother of rest" or "brother of repose."
H0266.emploi: This term appears five times in biblical texts, always to designate warriors in the service of King David. Two passages from the Second Book of Samuel (23:9 and 23:28) and three from Chronicles (11:12, 11:29, and 27:4) mention Achochites among the most valiant royal soldiers. The name can take the form "Achoach" or "Achochite" depending on the contexts. These mentions group elite warriors who marked David's reign with their military exploits.
H0266.portee: These Achochite warriors remind us that a life faithful to God bears fruit — not only in the personal realm but in the service and courage one can bring to a greater cause. Their presence alongside David shows that the Lord strengthens those who seek Him and places them in positions of honor and responsibility.

sens: A man of the tribe of Judah
Son of Jachath
Grandson of Shobal
H0267.detail: Achumai is a man of the tribe of Judah, mentioned only once in the Bible (1 Chronicles 4:2). He is the son of Jachath and the brother of Lahad. His name appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Shobal, who was himself a son of Judah. He is part of the ancestors of the family of the Tzorathites, a community established in Judean territory.
H0267.origine: The name Achumai literally means "brother of waters" or "reed of water." It comes from Hebrew roots that evoke water and brotherhood, perhaps suggesting a connection with places near springs or waterways. This type of descriptive name was common among the ancient Hebrews, where names often carried a meaning related to nature or the circumstances of birth.
H0267.emploi: Achumai appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:2. He is listed in a genealogical record that enumerates the descendants of Judah. His name is presented simply in a chain of lineage: Shobal begot Reaiah, Reaiah begot Jachath, and Jachath begot Achumai and Lahad. This genealogy served to establish the family and territorial origins of the clans of Judah, particularly the Tzorathites.

sens: The back side, the hindquarters of a creature or object.
To turn backward, to go in the opposite direction.
To be defeated, to be routed.
To move away, to withdraw, to disappear.
What is behind oneself in time; the past or what is bygone.
H0268.detail:
1. The back side, the hindquarters of a creature or object: this simply refers to the part that is behind, as when speaking of the "heel of the horse" that the serpent bites in Genesis 49:17 — it is the back of the animal's body.
2. To turn backward, to go in the opposite direction: the movement of retracing one's steps or turning around, for example when the Jordan "turns back" in Psalms 114:5, as if it were rising toward its source instead of flowing toward the sea.
3. To be defeated, to be routed: a strong image to describe defeat, when enemies are forced to "retreat" or turn their backs in flight, as in Psalms 40:15 where the adversaries "retreat" in shame before the one who cries out to God.
4. To move away, to withdraw, to disappear: the sense of something that moves away or fades, as in Isaiah 59:14 where "deliverance has withdrawn," meaning it has moved away, it is no longer accessible.
5. What is behind oneself in time; the past or what is bygone: used to speak of the past or what belongs to elapsed time, in contrast to what is to come.
H0268.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root that designates the back, the reverse, or the back side. It is a basic, concrete spatial word that is naturally used figuratively to express withdrawal, retreat, or fading. The root is not complex: it simply designates a direction, that of moving backward, in contrast to what is in front of oneself.
H0268.emploi: The word appears 41 times in the Old Testament, particularly in Psalms and Isaiah. It is first used in a concrete spatial sense (the back, the rear of an animal or object). But it often designates the movement of retreat or flight — especially in military accounts (2 Chronicles 13:14: "Joab saw that he had to fight in front and in back"). In the Psalms, the word regularly expresses the defeat or confusion of enemies: they "retreat" or are "turned back" (Psalms 40:15, Psalms 35:4). In Isaiah, it takes on a more spiritual or figurative sense, expressing the distance or fading of deliverance (Isaiah 59:14) or the downfall of the wicked (Isaiah 28:13, Isaiah 42:17). The word is suitable for expressing overturning or rout.
H0268.portee: This word enriches the believer by showing how the Bible expresses victory and defeat: retreating before the enemy or falling backward symbolizes humiliation and powerlessness, while seeing one's adversaries flee and retreat is to experience divine deliverance. The image of retreat or withdrawal also reminds us that certain realities — deliverance, justice — can move away when humanity turns its back on God. It is a metaphor that reinforces the call to faithfulness and trust.

sens: Daughter having the same parents or a common parent
Woman belonging to the same family or clan
Term of affection for a beloved woman
Bond of intimacy or closeness between two things or two peoples
H0269.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a daughter born of the same parents: a "sister" in the strict sense of familial bond. Zillah was the sister of Tubal-Cain, both born of Lamech (Genesis 4:22). The Law of Israel defines the degrees: the full sister was protected, as incest with a sister is forbidden (Leviticus 18:9 and 20:17).

2. The word also designates any female relative or woman of the same clan — a half-sister (of the same father or mother, see Leviticus 18:11), an aunt (Leviticus 18:12-13), or more broadly a close relative. Abraham refers to Sarai as "my sister" (Genesis 20:12), meaning a close relative, not a true sister.

3. "Sister" becomes a term of affection and tenderness. The lover in the Song of Songs calls his wife "my sister": "You have ravished my heart, my sister, my bride" (Song of Songs 4:9-10). The image evokes intimacy, trust, and close union.

4. Between two peoples or two realities, the word expresses intimacy or a relationship of closeness. Jeremiah speaks of Israel and Judah as sisters: Judah has imitated the evil of Israel (Jeremiah 3:7). Among the cords of a tent, the word "other" (sister) means the one that corresponds to it, that is attached to it (Exodus 26:3).
H0269.origine: The word comes from an ancient Semitic root expressing the bond of female kinship. It is the feminine equivalent of the word "brother" (אָח, 'akh). The family of Hebrew kinship words is very ancient and stable: it is found in many Semitic languages. The word implies a relationship of common origin — born of the same mother, the same father, or the same clan — and thus a natural intimacy.
H0269.emploi: The word "sister" appears more than 100 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Genesis, Leviticus, and historical accounts. In Genesis, it first refers to biological sisters (Naamah, sister of Tubal-Cain) or close relatives who were to be protected or respected. The laws of Leviticus (chapters 18 and 20) enumerate the variants — full sister, half-sister, aunt — to delineate marriage prohibitions. The word is also used for the beloved wife (Song of Songs), where it expresses the intimacy of marital love. Finally, the Bible uses it figuratively to speak of the relationship between Israel and Judah (Jeremiah 3:7), or between two parts of a whole (the cords of a tent, Exodus 26:3).
H0269.portee: This word reminds us that a sister is a bond of intimacy woven by birth or closeness. For the believer, it invites recognition of the intimacy created by true kinship, to respect the sister as a person of one's own flesh (Leviticus 18:12), and to understand marital love as a relationship of deep mutual knowledge, as between sister and brother. The sister-brother bond in Israel was a bond of affection and duty: this is also what the Bible expects of believers toward one another.

sens: To take something or someone with the hand, to seize
To hold firmly, to keep in one's power
To establish oneself, to take possession of a place
To be affected, struck (physically or emotionally)
To envelop, surround, retain
H0270.detail:
1. To take something with the hand or to seize it: the most concrete and common meaning. Abraham sees a ram *caught* in a thicket (Genesis 22:13) — the animal is stuck, imprisoned there. It is the simple act of *seizing* something.
2. To hold firmly, to keep in one's power, to possess: when one seizes, one does not let go. The children of Israel had *settled* in Gilead according to the Lord's command (Joshua 22:9) — they held firmly there, they had taken root.
3. To establish oneself or take possession of a place, to settle there: this derives from the previous meaning. When one seizes a land, one possesses it, becomes its master, and remains there.
4. To be affected or struck, especially in the affections of the soul or body: the days of suffering have *seized* him (Job 30:16) — suffering holds him, grips him like an invisible hand.
5. To envelop, surround, or retain something: a variant of the literal meaning, rarer. In the constructions (1 Kings 6:6), the beams *seize* and enclose the framework.
H0270.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that depicts the action of taking, seizing, grasping. The basic image is that of a hand closing around an object. The root is connected to the idea of firmness, solidity: what one seizes, one holds. It conjugates in several forms: simple (Qal), passive (Niphal), intensive (Piel), or complete (Hophal), each nuance the action of seizing according to the context.
H0270.emploi: The verb *seize* appears 63 times in the Old Testament, mainly in narratives (Genesis, Joshua, Judges), the Psalms, and the wisdom books. In historical narratives, it often describes a concrete and military action: *seizing* an enemy (2 Samuel 2:21), *seizing* a city or spoils (2 Chronicles 25:5). In the Psalms and Job, the meaning becomes more spiritual and emotional: affections, fear, suffering *seize* the heart of the psalmist (Psalms 56:1, Job 30:16). Isaiah uses it to describe how the Lord *seizes* His people or how fire *seizes* the enemies. The central idea remains that of a grip, a firm hold.
H0270.portee: This word reminds the reader that nothing escapes the hand of God: when the Bible says that God *seizes* His people, it affirms that His protection is real and infallible, not theoretical. Conversely, when suffering or sin *seizes* us, it shows the inevitable and concrete nature of judgment or distress. It is also a call to be vigilant: to keep a hold on what belongs to us in God, not to let go in faith.

sens: King of Judah, son of Jotham and father of Hezekiah
Benjamite, son of Micah and great-grandson of Jonathan
H0271G.detail:
1. Ahaz is a king of Judah who reigned during the period of the divided monarchy, succeeding his father Jotham (2 Kings 15:38). He is known primarily for his troubled political alliances and religious unfaithfulness: he went to Damascus to meet Tiglath-Pileser, king of Assyria (2 Kings 16:10), and shut the doors of the temple of the Lord by rejecting the worship of God (2 Chronicles 28:24). His son Hezekiah succeeded him on the throne (2 Kings 16:20).
2. A Benjamite bearing the same name, son of Micah and descendant of the lineage of Jonathan, appears in genealogies, but he occupies a minor place in sacred history.
H0271G.origine: The name Ahaz literally means "he has seized" or "he has grasped," formed from the Hebrew root חזק (khaza) which evokes the action of taking or seizing with force. This name reflects an intention of authority or power, although the historical king Ahaz did not always act with the moral strength expected of a king of Judah.
H0271G.emploi: Ahaz appears 36 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in 2 Kings 16, 2 Chronicles 28-29, and in the prophecies of Isaiah. The biblical account presents him as a spiritually weak king: he received a message from the prophet Isaiah inviting him to ask for a sign from God, but he refused (Isaiah 7:10-12). He is also mentioned in the titles of the prophecies of Isaiah, Hosea, and Micah, indicating that he lived in a time of great political turmoil. The New Testament cites him in the Greek form Ahaz in the genealogy of Christ in Matthew.
H0271G.portee: Ahaz illustrates the danger of turning one's heart away from God to seek human alliances and earthly solutions. His reign reminds the Christian reader that true security and true power reside not in political treaties or military strength, but in trust in God. The contrast with his son Hezekiah, who restored the worship of the temple, shows that even an unfaithful king cannot prevent God's redemptive plan from being fulfilled.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin, living during the time of the united monarchy
Son of Micah and brother of Pithon, Melech, and Thaeréa
Father of Jehoadda
H0271H.detail: He is a Benjamite, a member of the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned in the genealogies of the First Book of Chronicles. Ahaz appears as the son of Micah (1 Chronicles 8:35) and counts among his brothers Pithon, Melech, and Thaeréa. He occupies his place in the genealogical tree that traces back to Jonathan, the son of King Saul. Ahaz is the father of Jehoadda (1 Chronicles 8:36, 9:42), who himself had several children: Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri. He belongs to the time of the united monarchy of Israel and appears in the genealogical records intended to establish the family lineages of the tribe of Benjamin.
H0271H.origine: The name Ahaz means "he has seized" or "he has taken," formed from the Hebrew verb חזק (hazaq), which expresses the action of seizing, taking, or holding firmly. This root evokes the idea of strength and firmness. The name carries the image of a grasp or appropriation, a common characteristic of several Hebrew names from this period that express an action or disposition.
H0271H.emploi: Ahaz is mentioned four times in Chronicles, exclusively in the genealogies of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 8:35-36 and 9:41-42). These passages reproduce the same family succession in two places in the text: Ahaz always appears as a link in a genealogical chain connecting the ancestors of Saul to his descendants. His role is purely genealogical — he serves to establish the links of filiation and to preserve the memory of the Benjamite families of the united monarchy. No event or particular action is associated with him in the Bible.

sens: Real estate, land or field owned by someone
Inheritance passed down from father to son, right to possess land permanently
Exclusive right to enjoy and dispose of something
Portion of territory assigned to a tribe or family
H0272.detail:
1. It is primarily a land, a field, a real estate that one possesses. Abram receives the land of Canaan as a perpetual possession (Genesis 17:8): God gives him ownership, not just temporary use.
2. This word emphasizes inheritance: a possession is passed down from generation to generation. The daughters of Zelophehad request a possession among their father's brothers (Numbers 27:4), meaning a plot of land that their family can keep forever.
3. It is also the right to have and control something. The Levites have the possession of their fields in perpetuity (Leviticus 25:34): no one can take it away from them.
4. In territorial terms, it is the portion assigned to someone. Each tribe of Israel receives its possession at the time of the division of Canaan (Joshua 22:4, 22:9); Ezekiel describes the possessions of the tribes in the restored Promised Land (Ezekiel 45:7, 45:8).
H0272.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of seizing, holding, appropriating. It is related to other terms for "taking" or "grabbing." Possession is not something borrowed, but something firmly held, dominated, and enjoyed as a master. The basic image is therefore that of taking, of mastery.
H0272.emploi: The word appears 58 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Pentateuch and the Prophets. The earliest uses recount God's promise to Abram: Canaan will be his eternal possession (Genesis 17:8, 48:4). Leviticus 25 uses it intensively to regulate rights over lands: one can sell their possession, but not forever, because it is ultimately God's possession (Leviticus 25:10, 25:24 to 25:28). In Numbers and Joshua, the word describes the division of Canaan among the tribes (Numbers 27:4, Joshua 21:41, 22:4). Ezekiel uses it for the Vision of the Future Land (Ezekiel 44:28, 45:5 to 45:8, 48:20 to 48:22). The meaning remains stable: it is always about a territorial, durable, permanent, transferable asset.
H0272.portee: This word reminds us that Israel's relationship to the Promised Land is based on possession — not a human right, but a gift from God. It is also an invitation to understand the Christian inheritance: what is given by God must be received, kept, and passed on. Possession according to the Bible is never absolute: it always implies responsibility before the One who granted it.

sens: A Levitical priest from Jerusalem at the time of the return from exile
H0273.detail: Achzaï is a priest from the tribe of Levi, mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:13, where he appears in the genealogy of Amasiah. He lived in Jerusalem after the return from Babylonian exile, making him a figure of the restored people. His name means "my protector" or "one who supports me," reflecting the trust in God characteristic of this time of spiritual rebuilding.
H0273.origine: The name Achzaï likely derives from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of holding, supporting, or protecting. It is borne by a man from the tribe of Levi, whose function was religious service and worship in the temple. This name also appears in the form "Meshullam" to designate a character from the same priestly circle.
H0273.emploi: Achzaï is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:13, within a list of priests who returned from captivity and were established in Jerusalem. He appears in the genealogy of Amasiah as one of his paternal ancestors, underscoring the importance of priestly lineages after the temple's reconstruction. His exclusive appearance in this genealogical record highlights his role as a representative of the religious structures of the post-exilic community.
H0273.portee: Achzaï reminds the reader of God's faithfulness to His people: even after exile, the Levitical families persist and regain their place in the restored worship. His name, meaning "protector," invites recognition of divine protection over the remnant that God has preserved.

sens: King of Israel, son of Ahab and Jezebel, who reigned for about two years
A character whose name means "the Lord possesses"
H0274G.detail: Achazia is a king of the Northern Kingdom (Israel) who succeeded his father Ahab around the 9th century B.C. His story is brief but significant: he reigns only two years in Samaria, starting from the seventeenth year of King Jehoshaphat of Judah (1 Kings 22:52). His reign is marked by a dramatic event: he falls through the lattice of his upper chamber in Samaria and becomes ill; instead of seeking help from the Lord, he sends to consult Baal-Zebub, the god of Ekron (2 Kings 1:2), revealing his religious unfaithfulness. He is also the son of the most infamous couple in Israel: Ahab and Jezebel, known for their apostasy and injustice. The context of his uses shows a minor king in history, whose impious actions are noted by the Bible.
H0274G.origine: The name "Achazia" comes from Hebrew and means "the Lord (Yahu) possesses or holds." It is a classic Israelite theophoric name, combining the divine name and the idea of divine possession. Despite the spiritual meaning of his name, the biblical text shows that Achazia did not live according to its significance: instead of recognizing divine possession, he turned to idols.
H0274G.emploi: Achazia appears seven times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the historical books: 1 Kings 22 and 2 Kings 1 (with a mention in 2 Chronicles 20). He is first presented as the direct successor of Ahab (1 Kings 22:40), then in interaction with Jehoshaphat (1 Kings 22:50). His accession to the throne and the duration of his reign are specified (1 Kings 22:52). The essence of his story focuses on 2 Kings 1, where his accident and his consultation of foreign gods are reported. The passages emphasize that his life and actions are documented in the royal archives (2 Kings 1:18), and a mention in 2 Chronicles 20:35-37 describes him as a temporary ally of Jehoshaphat in a maritime venture disapproved by God.
H0274G.portee: The story of Achazia illustrates how a pious name does not guarantee a faithful life: although his name proclaims that the Lord possesses him, his actions reveal a heart turned toward idols and false gods. It also shows that illness and misfortune can be calls to seek God, but one can also turn away from Him. His double misfortune — being born of impious parents and choosing idolatry himself — served as a warning to the people of Israel about the consequences of forsaking the Lord.

sens: King of Judah in the 9th century B.C.
Son of Joram and Athaliah
Father of Joash
H0274H.detail: Achazia is a king of the tribe of Judah who reigned during the time of the divided kingdoms of Israel and Judah. He is the son of King Joram and Queen Athaliah (2 Kings 8:24). He succeeds his father on the throne of Judah and reigns for a short time before dying in dramatic circumstances during a revolt.
H0274H.origine: The name Achazia means "the Lord holds" or "the Lord possesses," composed of the divine name Yahu (Jehovah) and a verb meaning "to hold" or "to seize." This name expressed the faith of the parents at the birth: the child was entrusted into God's hands.
H0274H.emploi: Achazia appears in the accounts of the Kings and Chronicles of the kingdom of Judah. He is best known for having reigned briefly and for the political alliances of his family: his mother Athaliah, from the royal house of Israel (daughter of King Ahab), exerted great influence. At his death, his grandmother Athaliah seized power and reigned over Judah (2 Chronicles 22:10-11), while his son Joash was hidden and saved by the priest Jehosheba.
H0274H.portee: The story of Achazia reminds us how political and family alliances can lead a king away from faithfulness to God, and how the consequences of sin affect subsequent generations. It also shows divine providence: despite political chaos, God preserved the royal lineage by protecting the child Joash.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H0275.detail: Achuzzam is a man from the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible. He was the son of Ashhur and Naara, and had brothers named Hepher, Themeni, and Achaschthari (1 Chronicles 4:6). His name literally means "the possessor" or "one who possesses," reflecting the importance of inheritance and property in the genealogy of Judah.
H0275.origine: The name Achuzzam comes from the Hebrew root that expresses the idea of possession or ownership. This root emphasizes the attachment to the promised land, a central theme in the history of Israel. The name belongs to the descendants of Caleb, a major figure in the conquest of Canaan, which reinforces the image of possession and territorial inheritance.
H0275.emploi: Achuzzam appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:6, in a genealogy of the tribe of Judah. He is presented as one of the four sons of Naara, the wife of Ashhur. This brief mention in a genealogical list shows that he was a known figure of his time (the period of the divided monarchy), but the details of his life and actions are not reported. His presence in this genealogical record confirms his importance for the continuity of the lineage of Judah and Caleb.

sens: Character from the patriarchal era, friend of King Abimelech
H0276.detail: Ahuzath is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when King Abimelech goes to Isaac with his entourage. He is presented as the friend of Abimelech, accompanying him on this diplomatic visit (Genesis 26:26). His role is discreet but significant: he represents the close circle of the king, someone in whom the sovereign has confidence for important meetings.
H0276.origine: The name Ahuzath means "possession" in Hebrew, derived from the root that denotes the act of possessing or appropriating something. This name reflects the patriarchal era and the culture of the ancient Near East, where names often carried significance related to important material or spiritual realities.
H0276.emploi: Ahuzath appears only once in the entire Bible, in Genesis 26:26. He comes with Abimelech, king of Gerar, to visit Isaac. Also present are Pichol, the chief of the royal army. This visit occurs after God has blessed Isaac and his wealth has provoked the jealousy of the Philistines. Ahuzath's presence among the dignitaries suggests that Abimelech wishes to present himself in person with his closest advisors to meet Isaac, likely to establish or restore peaceful relations.

sens: Head of a family in the tribe of Gad during the divided monarchy
H0277G.detail: Achi is a man from the tribe of Gad mentioned only once in the Bible. He is presented as the head of his father's households (1 Chronicles 5:15), meaning he led an important clan or family within his tribe. He is the son of Abdiel and the grandson of Guni.
H0277G.origine: The name Achi literally means "my brother" in Hebrew (from the root אָח, "brother"). This type of theophoric name expresses a relationship of closeness or brotherhood, likely with God, although the name is simple and direct.
H0277G.emploi: Achi appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 5:15. He is listed in a genealogy of the heads of families of Gad, an administrative and genealogical context that enumerates the leaders of the various households. This mention places him in the history of Israel at a time when the tribes had well-established power structures.

sens: Son of Shamer, of the tribe of Asher
H0277H.detail: Achi is a man belonging to the tribe of Asher during the divided monarchy in Israel. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the genealogical record of the First Book of Chronicles. He is the son of Shamer and the brother of Rohega, Hubba, and Aram (1 Chronicles 7:34).
H0277H.origine: The name Achi comes from Hebrew and literally means "my brother." It is a personal name that, like many Hebrew names, incorporates a relational or familial element, expressing the bond of brotherhood.
H0277H.emploi: Achi appears only once in the known biblical texts, in 1 Chronicles 7:34, in the genealogy of the families of the tribe of Asher. He is listed among the descendants of Shamer as the head of his family during the period of the divided monarchy in Israel and Judah. This unique mention places him among the important ancestors of the people of Asher, even though his life is not recounted in detail.

sens: Son of Benjamin in the people of Israel
H0278.detail: Éhi is the name of one of the ten sons of Benjamin listed during the descent into Egypt. He appears only once in the Bible, in the genealogical list of Genesis 46:21 where Moses mentions the children of Benjamin who accompanied Jacob into Egypt. Although little known and rarely mentioned in biblical history, Éhi represents one of the tribal families that would later form the tribe of Benjamin.
H0278.origine: The name Éhi means "my brother" in Hebrew, formed from the root אח (ach, brother) with the first-person possessive suffix י (i, my). It was common for Hebrew parents to give their children names expressing a family relationship or personal affection, and this name likely reflects the emotional bond of the father Benjamin towards this son.
H0278.emploi: Éhi is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Genesis 46:21, in the list of the sons of Benjamin. Around the same time, he is also called Aharah in 1 Chronicles 8:1, which shows that names could vary slightly from one genealogical tradition to another. He was one of the twelve sons of Benjamin who would constitute the core of the future tribe of Benjamin, one of the twelve tribes of Israel.

sens: Elite warrior in the service of King David
H0279.detail: Achiam is one of the "thirty" most renowned warriors of King David, a roll of honor of the bravest fighters during the united monarchy in Israel. He is the son of Scharar (or Sacar according to a variant), from Arar or Harar. His name means "brother of the mother" in Hebrew, although this origin is obscure in the Bible. Achiam appears in two passages that list these warrior heroes: 2 Samuel 23:33 and 1 Chronicles 11:35.
H0279.origine: The name Achiam comes from Hebrew and literally means "brother of my mother" (akh = brother, am = mother). The etymology may suggest a familial relationship, but the biblical context reveals nothing more about its personal significance. This man lived during the time of David, during the period of the united monarchy of Israel.
H0279.emploi: Achiam is mentioned twice in the Bible, both in lists of David's chosen "thirty" warriors. The first mention is found in 2 Samuel 23:33, where he is presented as the son of Scharar, from Arar. A second parallel mention appears in 1 Chronicles 11:35, with a slight variant of his father's name (Sacar instead of Scharar). These two passages offer exactly the same context: the enumeration of the most valiant military heroes of King David. Achiam is never highlighted by a particular personal act in the Bible; he is mentioned solely due to his status as an elite warrior.

sens: A word or question that is obscure and difficult to understand, intentionally enigmatic
A problem presented to be solved by guessing the answer
Figuratively: that which is mysterious or hidden, requiring wisdom to be understood
H0280.detail:
1. A riddle is a word formulated in an obscure and veiled manner, expressly to test the listener. In Babylon, King Belshazzar honors Daniel because he possesses "the ability to interpret dreams, explain riddles, and solve difficult questions" (Daniel 5:12) — these three gifts go together, as they require a wisdom capable of piercing what is hidden or confusing.
2. A riddle can be a question or a play on words for which one must find the answer: what seems absurd or incomprehensible at first glance reveals sense when one grasps the deeper meaning of the words.
3. Beyond the play, the riddle designates everything that is mysterious or veiled and requires spiritual intelligence to be deciphered: God's ways, His secret judgments, are sometimes presented as riddles that only divine wisdom can resolve.
H0280.origine: This Aramaic word (the language spoken in Babylon) comes from the Hebrew root חִידָה (chidah, "riddle"). The root itself evokes the idea of tying, twisting, making sinuous — like a word that twists and coils to hide its meaning. In Hebrew, the word notably appears for the riddles of Samson (Judges 14) and for the enigmatic sayings of wisdom. It is the same word that the Bible uses to designate difficult questions that only superhuman wisdom can resolve.
H0280.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 5:12, where it is used in Aramaic (the language of the Babylonian court). The context is that of the captivity of Judah: King Belshazzar praises Daniel because he possesses the spirit of God, which allows him not only to dream prophetic dreams but also to interpret riddles — that is, to see beyond the apparent, to understand what is hidden. This ability to solve riddles is presented as a mark of divine wisdom and the spiritual gift of the one who is capable of it.
H0280.portee: For the Christian reader, this mention of riddles invites consideration that God does not always express Himself in a direct and simple manner. Sometimes, His ways, His judgments, His revelations are veiled or enigmatic, and true wisdom — that which the Spirit gives — is needed to understand them. This also reminds us that faith is not merely a matter of logic: it requires a deeper spiritual perception, capable of piercing the mysteries of God.

sens: Statesman during the reign of Solomon, son of Shisha
H0281G.detail: Ahijah was one of the two secretaries of King Solomon, mentioned only once in the Bible. Along with his brother Elihoreph, he was responsible for the administrative affairs of the royal court, alongside Jehoshaphat who held the position of archivist. It was a position of trust that demonstrated Ahijah's importance in the government of the united kingdom of Israel.
H0281G.origine: The name "Ahijah" literally means "brother of Yah" (Yah being an ancient divine name for the Lord). It is a theophoric name, composed of two elements: "ach" (brother) and "Yah" (God). This type of name was common in Israel and manifested the faith of parents in the God of Israel.
H0281G.emploi: Ahijah appears only once in the provided biblical text, in 1 Kings 4:3, where he is presented as one of Solomon's chief officials. This mention appears in the list of the king's high dignitaries, highlighting the important role he played in the administration of the kingdom during the height of the united monarchy. His position as secretary indicates that he was literate and trustworthy.

sens: Prophet of Israel during the united monarchy, notably known for announcing the schism of the kingdom
H0281H.detail: Ahijah is an important prophet during the time of Solomon and Jeroboam. He first appears in 1 Kings 11:29, where he meets Jeroboam on the road, wearing a new cloak which he tears into twelve pieces to signify that ten tribes will separate from the kingdom of Judah. He is a prophet whom God charges with specific missions: he announces to Jeroboam that he will be king (1 Kings 14:2), he receives a visit from Jeroboam's wife who comes to consult him about her sick son (1 Kings 14:4-5), and he conveys the word of the Lord with recognized authority. Although aged and blind during his encounter with Jeroboam's wife, he retains the prophetic gift and discerns the true identity of the one who comes to deceive him.
H0281H.origine: The name Ahijah means "brother of Yah (the Eternal)" in Hebrew. It expresses a relationship of brotherhood or closeness with God, which is fitting for a prophet who speaks on behalf of the Lord and conveys His will. This name reflects the prophetic function: one who stands alongside God to fulfill His purpose.
H0281H.emploi: Ahijah is mentioned in 1 Kings 11 to 15 and in 2 Chronicles 9 and 10. The provided usages primarily present him as the prophet who announces the division of the kingdom: he meets Jeroboam on the way (1 Kings 11:29), tears the cloak into twelve pieces (1 Kings 11:30), and this event is recalled as the fulfillment of the prophetic word (1 Kings 12:15). Later, he appears as a man of God consulted by the people, notably by Jeroboam's worried wife regarding her son (1 Kings 14:2-5). The text emphasizes his authority: although blind with age, he remains a true prophet to whom the Lord continues to speak and reveal the secrets of hearts.
H0281H.portee: The account of Ahijah teaches the believer that God communicates His will through His prophets, even in the historical turning points of the people. His example also shows that physical aging does not weaken the prophetic ministry: it is the Lord who speaks, not human strength. For the reader, Ahijah embodies prophetic faithfulness and reminds us that the divisions that occur among God's people are often the result of His judgment in response to unfaithfulness.

sens: father of Baasha, king of northern Israel
man from the house of Issachar who conspired against King Nadab
H0281I.detail:
1. Ahijah is best known as the father of Baasha. Baasha, his son, conspired against King Nadab of Israel and killed him at Gibbethon (1 Kings 15:27), then reigned over the northern kingdom for twenty-four years (1 Kings 15:33). The name Ahijah consistently appears attached to that of his son to identify the dynasty founded by Baasha.
2. Ahijah himself was a man from the house of Issachar who took part in this political uprising. His conspiracy marks a major turning point in the history of divided Israel, as Baasha established a new royal lineage and his house became one of the most powerful in the North, although the prophet Elijah predicted its decline (1 Kings 21:22 and 2 Kings 9:9).
H0281I.origine: The name means "brother of Yah" (Yah is a short form of the divine name), expressing a relationship of closeness with God. It is a common theophoric name in ancient Israel.
H0281I.emploi: Ahijah appears in four biblical passages, all in Kings, always mentioned as the father of Baasha. These references frame the story of the conspiracy and reign of Baasha: first the assassination of King Nadab (1 Kings 15:27), then the establishment of Baasha's reign (1 Kings 15:33), followed by the prophetic oracles against his house (1 Kings 21:22 and 2 Kings 9:9). The context remains constant: the genealogical and dynastic identification of the leader of the revolt that destabilized the North.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the united monarchy
H0281J.detail: Achija is a man from the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible. He is named in 1 Chronicles 2:25 as the mother (or wife) of Jerachmeel, and she bore several sons: Ram, Buna, Oren, and Otsem. This character belongs to the genealogy of Judah and is part of the important family lines of the Old Testament.
H0281J.origine: The name Achija literally means "brother of Jehovah" or "my brother is Jehovah." It is formed from two elements: "ach" (brother) and "Yahu" (short form of the divine name Jehovah). This theophoric name expresses religious trust: the one who bears it is considered to be under the brotherly protection of God. Several characters bear this name in the Bible, each occupying a different place in the history of Israel.
H0281J.emploi: Achija appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 2:25, in the context of the genealogy of the tribe of Judah. At this point, Achija is presented as the mother (or wife) of Jerachmeel, the firstborn of Hetsron. This unique usage shows that Achija is part of the genealogical figures that the Bible remembers, even if few details are given about her life. The genealogical context indicates her importance in the transmission of the lineage of Judah at a crucial time in the history of Israel.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin, ancestor in the genealogy of Israel before the monarchy
H0281K.detail: Achija is a man from the tribe of Benjamin mentioned in the genealogy of the people of Israel. He is listed as a descendant of Ehud and is the brother of Naaman, Guéra, and Uzza. He appears only once in 1 Chronicles 8:7, in the genealogical list of the families of Benjamin, where he is named between Naaman and Guéra.
H0281K.origine: The name Achija means "brother of Jehovah" (Jahu being one of the names of God). It is formed from two Hebrew elements: "ach" which means "brother" and "Yahu" which is a form of the divine name. This name expresses a close relationship with God and was borne by several important figures in the history of Israel.
H0281K.emploi: Achija is a proper name attributed to a Benjamite, son of Ehud, cited only once in the biblical genealogies in 1 Chronicles 8:7. He is an ancestor of the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned in the context of the families of this tribe before the establishment of the monarchy in Israel.

sens: Elite warrior of King David
H0281L.detail: 1. Achija is one of the thirty renowned warriors who formed the king David's elite guard. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:36, among the list of valiant men who served the king and participated in his military campaigns.
H0281L.origine: The name Achija means "my brother is Yahweh" or "brother of Jehovah," combining the word "ach" (brother) and the divine name Yahweh. It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing a relationship of trust in God. The same name designates several other characters in the Old Testament (prophets, scribes, leaders) at different times.
H0281L.emploi: Achija appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 11:36, where he is cited as one of David's thirty warriors. He is presented alongside Hépher of Mekera, indicating that he was a recognized man of arms known for his valor. No additional details about his life or exploits are provided in the Bible.

sens: Israelite Levite during the time of David, responsible for the management of the temple treasures
H0281M.detail: 1. Achija is a Levite (member of the tribe dedicated to temple service) who lived during the time of King David. He was responsible for the guarding and administration of the sacred treasures of the house of God — gold, silver, precious offerings, and worship objects. This was an important and trusted function that required great faithfulness. In 1 Chronicles 26:20, he is named among the Levites that David had established to manage the temple's wealth.
H0281M.origine: The name Achija (in Hebrew אֲחִיָּה) means "brother of Yahu" or "brother of the Eternal": it is composed of the word achí (brother) and the abbreviated divine name Yahu. It was a common name among the Hebrews, borne by several people at different times in the Old Testament, including a famous prophet from the Northern Kingdom.
H0281M.emploi: Achija appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 26:20. He is mentioned as one of the Levites that David had designated for the management of the sacred treasures — that is, the oversight and organization of the wealth intended for the temple and worship. This role shows the administrative organization of worship during David's time: the treasures of the temple were not kept by just anyone, but entrusted to Levites recognized for their seriousness and dedication to divine service.
H0281M.portee: Achija's role reminds us that in the people of God, material services — the management of resources, the stewardship of goods — are an integral part of worship and deserve the same faithfulness as more visible tasks. It is a discreet yet significant example of what it means to serve God in everyday life.

sens: Man who sealed the covenant with the Lord during the time of Nehemiah
H0281N.detail: 1. Achija is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, during the return from exile to Jerusalem. He is among those who solemnly sealed the covenant with the Lord, alongside Nehemiah and the other leaders of the people (Nehemiah 10:26). This is an act of commitment by the people to obey God's Law after the restoration of the Temple.
H0281N.origine: The name Achija means "my brother is Yahu" (Yahu being a shortened form of the divine name). It is a theophoric name, very common in Israel, which expresses a brotherly relationship with God. Several men bear this name in the history of Israel: the prophet who announced the revolt of the northern tribes under Jeroboam, the scribe of King Solomon, and others. This one is only known to us by his seal on the covenant document.
H0281N.emploi: Achija appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:26. He is among the signatories of the solemn pact that the leaders of Israel made with the Lord after the return from exile and the reconstruction of the Temple. His name appears in a list of witnesses who committed to respecting the Law and rejecting mixed marriages. Although we know nothing more about his life or specific role, his presence shows that the renewal of the covenant concerned all levels of the restored community.

sens: Priest, son of Ahitub during the reign of King Saul
Bearer of the ephod and responsible for the ark of the covenant
H0281O.detail:
1. Achija is an Israelite priest who serves in Shiloh during the reign of Saul. He is the son of Ahitub and the brother of I-Kabod; he descends from a prestigious priestly lineage, being the grandson of Phinehas and the great-grandson of the high priest Eli (1 Samuel 14:3).
2. He wears the ephod, the liturgical garment of the priest, and has charge of the ark of the covenant, the symbol of God's presence among Israel. Saul consults him when he needs God's advice (1 Samuel 14:18), showing that Achija played a mediating role between the king and the Lord.
H0281O.origine: The name "Achija" means "brother of Yahu (God)" in Hebrew. He belongs to a large family of priests who served at Shiloh, all bearing compound names mentioning the Lord: his father Ahitub ("brother of goodness"), his brother I-Kabod ("without glory"), his grandson Abiathar who will become high priest under King David.
H0281O.emploi: Achija appears only twice in the Bible, both in chapter 14 of 1 Samuel, in the account of Jonathan's victory over the Philistines. He is first presented as the priest of Shiloh wearing the ephod (1 Samuel 14:3), then Saul calls him to order him to bring the ark of God closer in order to consult the Lord before the battle (1 Samuel 14:18). His role is that of an officiating priest who consults the divine will through ritual means — probably the ephod — at the decisive moment of the war against the Philistines.
H0281O.portee: Achija illustrates the role of priests in ancient Israel: serving as mediators between God and His people, and placing the consultation of divine will at the heart of important decisions. For today's believer, his story reminds us of the importance of seeking God's direction in critical moments, rather than relying on our own strength.

sens: Prince of the tribe of Asher at the time of the conquest of Canaan
H0282.detail: Ahihud is a tribal leader whose name is mentioned only once in the Bible, during the designation of the princes responsible for distributing the promised land among the twelve tribes. He represents the tribe of Asher and belongs to the generation that crossed the desert after the exodus from Egypt. His name means "brother of majesty," reflecting the importance of his role: he is responsible for assigning the portions of territory to his tribe according to the instructions of the Lord given through Moses.
H0282.origine: His name, composed of two Hebrew elements, literally means "brother" (achi) and "majesty" or "glory" (hud). This composition reminds us that the princes of the tribes were not only military or administrative leaders but also men close to the power and authority of God. He is the son of Schelomi, of whom nothing else is known in the Scriptures.
H0282.emploi: Ahihud appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 34:27. This passage lists the twelve princes of the tribes of Israel, designated to oversee the distribution of the territory of Canaan after its conquest. Each prince represents his tribe and is given the authority to ensure fairness and justice in the allocation of the lands. Ahihud thus embodies the order and structure that God established for His people at the threshold of settling in the promised land.
H0282.portee: The fact that God appointed princes responsible for the distribution of the promised land shows that He cares not only about giving but also about distributing His blessings fairly. Ahihud represents just authority in service to the people of God, a model of the charge received to lead others toward the fulfillment of the divine promise.

sens: son of Abinadab, brother of Uzza
assistant during the transport of the ark of God
H0283G.detail: 1. Achjo is a figure from the time of the united monarchy in Israel, son of Abinadab who lived on the hill. His name means "brotherhood" or "one who is fraternal," which is fitting as he is presented as the brother of Uzza and Eleazar. 2. Achjo and his brother Uzza played a role during the solemn transport of the ark of God from their father's house to Jerusalem: they led or accompanied the new cart on which the ark had been placed (2 Samuel 6:3-4; 1 Chronicles 13:7). This was an important moment, but it ended dramatically when Uzza touched the ark and died.
H0283G.origine: The name Achjo comes from a Hebrew root meaning "brother" or "brotherhood." It is a meaningful name, common in Israelite families to express kinship or familial virtue. The Bible mentions him as the brother of Uzza and Eleazar, all three sons of Abinadab.
H0283G.emploi: Achjo appears three times in the Bible, always in connection with the transport of the ark of God during the time of King David. Two occurrences are found in 2 Samuel 6:3-4, where he is named alongside his brother Uzza: one mentions that they both drove the new cart, while the other specifies that Uzza walked beside the ark while Achjo went ahead. The third occurrence is in 1 Chronicles 13:7, a parallel account describing the same event. Achjo remains a secondary figure but a witness to a decisive moment in the history of God's people.

sens: Son of Bériah, man of the tribe of Benjamin
H0283H.detail: Achjo is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, in chapter 8 of the first book of Chronicles. His name means "fraternal" or "of brotherhood." He is presented as the son of Bériah and the brother of Arad, Shashak, Jeremoth, Zebadiah, Eder, Michael, Ishpah, and Joha. These genealogies of the people of Benjamin show us how God preserved the families of Israel, even after the exile.
H0283H.origine: The name Achjo comes from the Hebrew root that means "brother," and expresses the idea of brotherhood or family bond. This name, carrying the notion of fraternal relationship, reflects the importance of family in the structure of the people of Israel.
H0283H.emploi: Achjo is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:14, within a genealogical list of the descendants of Benjamin. This genealogy, which enumerates the families and heads of households of the tribe, served to establish the legitimate lineages of Israel after the return from exile. His unique appearance in this genealogical context shows that although his life is not recounted in detail, his name and existence were deemed worthy of preservation in the record of God's people.

sens: A man of the tribe of Benjamin during the time of the united monarchy
A name meaning "brotherhood" or "belonging to a brother"
H0283I.detail:
1. Achjo is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned in the genealogies of the united monarchy, son of Abiel and Maacah. He appears in the list of the descendants of Benjamin in 1 Chronicles 8:31.
2. The name Achjo carries a deep meaning: it evokes brotherhood and familial ties, which were central to the organization of Israelite families. This name reminds us that each person was first a member of a clan and a brotherhood before being an isolated individual.
H0283I.origine: The name Achjo comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of brother and family bond. Its literal meaning "brotherhood" or "of my brother" reflects the importance that Hebrew culture placed on kinship ties and the collective identity of the family. In genealogies, names were never arbitrary: they carried meaning and recalled the history or values of the household.
H0283I.emploi: Achjo appears twice in the Scriptures, both in the genealogies of Chronicles. He is listed among the descendants of Benjamin in 1 Chronicles 8:31 and again in 1 Chronicles 9:37. These two mentions seem to designate the same man, included in the genealogical records that traced the lines of descent of the tribe during the period of the united monarchy. The repetition in two different chapters shows the importance that the writers placed on preserving this genealogy.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Ehud
H0284.detail: Achichud is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:7. He is presented as the son of Ehud and the brother of Naaman, Ahijah, Gera, and Uzza. This genealogical passage lists the descendants of Benjamin and their family lines, placing Achichud in the history of the blessed families before the establishment of the monarchy in Israel.
H0284.origine: The name Achichud literally means "brother of mystery" or "brother of the secret," composed of the Hebrew "achi" (brother) and "chod" (which can mean mystery or enigma). Like many ancient Hebrew names, it encodes a reality or spiritual aspiration in the name given to the child.
H0284.emploi: Achichud appears only once in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 8, which lists the sons and descendants of Ehud, an important figure from the tribe of Benjamin. This genealogical passage places Achichud among the ancestors of the blessed families, without further detail about his life or deeds. His appearance is limited to his identification as the son of Ehud and a member of this tribal genealogy.

sens: Character from the time of the united monarchy in Israel
Father of the priest Ahimelech
Great-grandson of the high priest Eli
H0285G.detail: Achithub is a man who lived during the reign of King Saul, around the time when David emerged from his battles against the Philistines. He is known as the father of the priest Ahimelech, who serves at Nob and wears the ephod (the priestly garment). When Saul, furious with David, orders the massacre of the priests of Nob, Ahimelech and his entire household are put to death on the king's orders (1 Samuel 22:11-12). Only Abiathar, the son of Ahimelech, escapes the massacre and seeks refuge with David (1 Samuel 22:20). Achithub embodies a priestly lineage that traces back to the high priest Eli, of whom he is the grandson through Phinehas.
H0285G.origine: The name means in Hebrew "my brother is good" or "my brother is goodness," composed of "my brother" and "good." It designates a man from the priestly family of Eli, one of the great Levitical families of Israelite worship at Shiloh.
H0285G.emploi: Achithub appears five times in the account of 1 Samuel, always mentioned as lineage ("son of Achithub," "father of") rather than for his own deeds. He illustrates the continuity of the priestly function during Saul's time and shows how an entire family of priests was involved in the drama of David on the run. His son Ahimelech helps David without knowing the consequences; later, his descendants, including the priest Zadok, will play a major role at David's court.
H0285G.portee: Achithub reminds us that the priestly ministry in Israel was rooted in family lineages and that the decisions of kings could innocently strike entire families. His story also shows that God preserves a remnant (Abiathar) even amid persecution, and that lineages can be restored under a new benevolent reign.

sens: Grandson of the high priest Eli
Father of the priest Zadok
Man of the tribe of Levi during the united monarchy
H0285H.detail: Achithub is a character from the Old Testament belonging to the priestly lineage of the Levites. He is known as the grandson of the high priest Eli and as the father of the priest Zadok, who will become a central figure in worship during the time of David and Solomon. His name means "my brother is good" or "my brother is goodness," reflecting a blessing. He primarily appears in the genealogies of the priests (1 Chronicles 6:7-8) and in the lists of high officials of David's kingdom (2 Samuel 8:17 and 1 Chronicles 18:16), where he is presented as the father of Zadok, priest alongside other priests.
H0285H.origine: The name Achithub is composed of the Hebrew "ach" (brother) and "tub" (good, goodness). It designates an important member of the priestly family descended from Levi, establishing a direct genealogical link with the high priest Eli on one hand, and with Zadok, the priest of David, on the other. This name fits within the biblical tradition of naming children according to a quality or spiritual blessing.
H0285H.emploi: Achithub appears five times in the Bible, always in a genealogical or official context. He is mentioned in the lists of priests during David's time (2 Samuel 8:17 and 1 Chronicles 18:16), where his son Zadok performs the functions of priest. The other three references (1 Chronicles 6:7, 6:8, 6:52) place him in the complete genealogy of the Levites, showing his place in the continuity of the priestly lineage that traces back to Amaria and culminates in Zadok. His apparent role is mainly genealogical: he represents an important link in the transmission of the priesthood in Israel.
H0285H.portee: Achithub embodies the continuity of divine service across generations: he receives the sacred responsibility from his ancestors and passes it on to his son Zadok. For the Christian reader, this character reminds us that God preserves a faithful lineage for worship, even through troubled times, and that the priestly function requires a conscious and just transmission. The name itself, "my brother is goodness," suggests that true greatness lies not in personal power, but in the recognition of divine and fraternal goodness.

sens: Man of the tribe of Levi
Father of the high priest Zadok
Ancestor of the post-exilic priests
H0285I.detail:
1. Achithub is a man of the tribe of Levi, meaning he is a descendant of Levi. His name means "my brother is good" or "my brother is goodness." He belongs to the period of the Divided Monarchy (1 Chronicles 6:11), the time when the kingdom of Israel was split in two.
2. He is primarily known as the father of the high priest Zadok (1 Chronicles 6:12). Zadok became one of the most important priests under King David and later under Solomon. Achithub thus passed on the priestly responsibility to his son.
3. Through Zadok, Achithub is the ancestor of the line of priests that continued after the Babylonian exile. The genealogy in the book of Ezra (7:2) mentions him as one of the ancestors of the priests who returned from captivity, showing that his descendants exercised the priesthood for centuries.
H0285I.origine: The name Achithub is composed of the Hebrew "achi" (my brother) and "tov" (good). It was a common name among the Levites, reflecting the importance of brotherhood and goodness in the faith of the people of Israel. The Bible mentions several Achithub, but this one is identified as the father of Zadok.
H0285I.emploi: Achithub appears three times in the Bible, always in priestly genealogies. In 1 Chronicles 6:11-12, he is placed in the lineage of the descendants of Levi who served as priests, situated between Amaria (his father according to 1 Chronicles 6:11) and Zadok (his son). In Ezra 7:2, he appears in the genealogy of the priest Ezra, showing the continuity of the priestly lineage from the time of King David to after the return from exile. His significance lies less in his own actions than in his position as a link in the chain of the high priests of Israel.
H0285I.portee: Achithub reminds the reader that the priestly ministry does not belong to a single generation, but is part of a faithful transmission of a lineage. His story shows how God preserved worship and the priesthood of the Temple through the vicissitudes of history, even up to the return from exile. It invites the Christian to see in the generations of God's servants a continuity of divine grace.

sens: Levitical ancestor, father of Meraioth and grandfather of the priest Zadok
H0285J.detail: Achithub is a family name in the genealogy of the Levitical priests. He appears in the genealogical lists of 1 Chronicles 9:11 and Nehemiah 11:11, where he is mentioned as the ancestor of Seriah and Azariah, leaders of the house of God.
