His name means "my brother is good" in Hebrew, reflecting a family blessing. It is within this priestly lineage that the high priests of the time of the return from exile to Jerusalem are situated.
H0285J.origine: The name Achithub (אֲחִיטוּב) is composed of two Hebrew elements: "achi" (אָחִי, my brother) and "tov" (טוֹב, good or goodness). This nominal formation reflects a common practice in Israel of giving children names that express a blessing or favor from God. The name belongs to the Levitical family, and various individuals bore this name at different periods in Israel's history.
H0285J.emploi: Achithub is mentioned twice in the Bible, always in genealogical lists of the priests after the Babylonian exile. In 1 Chronicles 9:11 and Nehemiah 11:11, he figures as an ancestor in the priestly lineage of Seriah (or Azariah), both described as "princes of the house of God." These two parallel passages highlight the importance of his position in the Levitical hierarchy of the Second Temple. His name regularly appears in genealogies that establish the authority and legitimacy of the priests returned from exile.

sens: Father of Jehoshaphat, royal archivist of King David
Father of Baana, officer of King Solomon
H0286.detail:
1. Achilud is a high-ranking figure during the time of the united kingdom of Israel. He is best known as the father of Jehoshaphat, who was the royal archivist (official secretary) at the court of King David. Jehoshaphat appears several times in the lists of high officials (2 Samuel 8:16; 1 Kings 4:3), confirming that his father Achilud was a person of influence and responsibility.
2. Achilud is also the father of Baana, who served as a governor or officer under King Solomon. Baana was responsible for Taanach, Megiddo, and the surrounding regions (1 Kings 4:12), which shows that Achilud's family maintained an important position throughout the reigns of David and Solomon.
H0286.origine: The name literally means "brother of the child" or "brother child." It is a typical compound name of ancient Hebrew. Achilud belongs to the generation of David's great servants, several of whose names are known to us from royal administrative lists.
H0286.emploi: Achilud is mentioned 5 times in the Bible, always as the father of two important administrative figures of the united kingdom. His son Jehoshaphat is named four times as the archivist (or secretary) of David and Solomon (2 Samuel 8:16; 2 Samuel 20:24; 1 Kings 4:3; 1 Chronicles 18:15). Baana, his other son, is cited once as the governor of major districts under Solomon (1 Kings 4:12). Achilud himself never intervenes directly: he is always mentioned by the patronymic of his sons, illustrating how ancient Hebrew identified people by their lineage.

sens: Levite of the divided kingdom, son of Amasaï
H0287.detail: Achimoth is a man from the tribe of Levi mentioned only once in the Old Testament, during the time of the division of the Israelite monarchy (the period of the two kingdoms). He appears in the genealogy of the Levites as the son of Amasaï and the father of Elkanah (1 Chronicles 6:25). He is an ancestor of the Levitical lineage, whose role was likely related to the temple's cultic service.
H0287.origine: The Hebrew name אֲחִימוֹת (Achimoth) literally means "my brother is death" or "brother of death." It consists of two elements: אָח (ach, "brother") and מוֹת (moth, "death"). It is a theophoric name (containing a divine reference) typical of the time, although its meaning remains unusual. It is distinct from Mahath (מַחַת, H4287), although some Levitical genealogies mention the latter name.
H0287.emploi: Achimoth is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 6:25, in a genealogy of the descendants of Levi established at the time of the writing of the book of Chronicles (after the exile). He appears in the long list of ancestors who were responsible for singing and service in the temple of Israel. His appearance is purely genealogical; no particular event or act is attributed to him.

sens: Priest of Israel during the united kingdom
Man favorable to David fleeing from King Saul
Victim of King Saul's vengeance
H0288G.detail:
1. Achimelech is a priest serving at Nob, the city of priests, during the reign of King Saul. He is the son of Ahitub and the father of Abiathar, who will succeed him in the priestly function (1 Samuel 22:11).

2. David, while fleeing, comes to him at Nob, pretending to have a secret order from the king. Achimelech, unaware of the conflict between David and Saul, gives him consecrated bread and the sword of Goliath to aid him in his escape (1 Samuel 21:1-8). The priest acts loyally towards David, who is presented as a faithful servant of the king.

3. The informer Doeg reports this meeting to Saul, who orders the massacre of Achimelech and all the priests of Nob—an extreme act of violence against the servants of God. Achimelech dies for having helped David in good faith, without malice towards the king (1 Samuel 22:14-16).
H0288G.origine: The name literally means "my brother is king" or "brother of the king," composed of two words: "brother" and "king." It is a characteristic theophoric name of the time, expressing a close relationship with royalty or with God. In tradition, Achimelech is also called Ahijah, a variant of the same character.
H0288G.emploi: Achimelech appears eleven times in 1 Samuel and once in Psalm 52, always in direct relation to David in flight. In chapter 21, he receives David at Nob as a simple priest unaware of anything. In chapters 22-23, his name becomes a symbol of sacrificed innocence: Saul has him killed along with all the priests of his household, although Achimelech defends himself against having betrayed the king. Psalm 52 alludes to this event by mentioning Doeg, who caused this tragedy. Achimelech embodies the victim of royal passions.
H0288G.portee: The story of Achimelech shows how innocence does not immunize against suffering, and how faithfulness to God (his duty as a priest) can attract unjust condemnation from men. It teaches that serving the Lord and His chosen ones may require the sacrifice of everything. His son Abiathar, who escaped the massacre, will remain David's companion, revealing that there is no injustice that God does not ultimately redeem.

sens: Hittite warrior companion of David
H0288H.detail: Achimelech is a warrior of Hittite nationality (non-Israelite) who served in the army of King David. In 1 Samuel 26:6, he appears alongside Abishai, son of Zeruiah, when David considers descending into Saul's camp for a perilous mission. Achimelech remains a secondary figure in Scripture, mentioned only once, but he illustrates how David surrounded himself with warriors from neighboring peoples, drawn by his reputation and cause.
H0288H.origine: The name Achimelech literally means "my brother is king" in Hebrew, composed of two elements: the word for "brother" and the word for "king." It is a typical theophoric name of the Israelite royal period, expressing a relationship of trust or divine protection. Scripture also mentions another Achimelech, the high priest during Saul's days, but this is a different person.
H0288H.emploi: Achimelech appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 26:6. He is presented as a Hittite (a non-Israelite) among David's trusted warriors. In this scene, David solicits volunteers for a dangerous action against Saul, and it is Achimelech who offers to accompany him, thus demonstrating his loyalty and courage. His appearance, though brief, testifies to how David attracted men of value around him, regardless of their origin.

sens: Priest son of Abiathar, mentioned in David's records
Important figure in the organization of worship during King David's time
H0288I.detail: Achimelech is a name that appears in the historical texts recounting the reign of King David. He is a priest, son of Abiathar, who is recorded among the leaders of worship in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 8:17). He plays a particular role in organizing the groups of Levitical priests: David mentions him alongside Zadok when the paternal houses of the priests are drawn by lot to determine their order of service (1 Chronicles 24:3, 24:6). Achimelech thus represents an administrative and religious figure in the sacrificial system of the united kingdom of Israel.
H0288I.origine: The name literally means "my brother is king" or "brother of Melek" (from Hebrew *ach* = brother, and *melek* = king). It is a theophoric name where the divine king is invoked. In the provided biblical documents, this priest bears this name during the united kingdom, a period when religious institutions are structured around Davidic royalty.
H0288I.emploi: Achimelech is a minor but historically established character, mentioned four times in biblical texts, always in relation to the cultic administration during David's time. He first appears in 2 Samuel 8:17 among the sacrificial leaders. He then appears three times in chapter 24 of 1 Chronicles, where David proceeds with the formal organization of the priestly divisions: Achimelech is associated with Zadok to validate the lots drawn for the priestly houses, thus ensuring the legitimacy of this new cultic order (1 Chronicles 24:3, 24:6, 24:31).

sens: Son of Anak, one of the three Canaanite giants of Hebron during the time of the Exodus and conquest
Canaanite warrior defeated by the Israelites during the capture of Hebron
H0289G.detail:
1. Ahiman is one of the three sons of the giant Anak, who lived in Hebron at the time when the Hebrews explored the promised land. His two brothers are named Sheshai and Talmai. They are the enemies that the Israelites must defeat to take possession of Hebron (Numbers 13:22; Joshua 15:14).
2. He is a Canaanite warrior whom Caleb and the men of Judah defeated and drove out of Hebron during the conquest of the land (Judges 1:10). He represents the gigantic opposition — both literally and figuratively — that the Israelites had to overcome to enter the land that God had promised them.
H0289G.origine: His name means "my brother is a gift" in Hebrew. He is a son of Anak, the giant whose name means "neck" or "long neck." The family of Anak is famous in the Bible as the archetypal example of the giants who populated Canaan before the Israelite conquest.
H0289G.emploi: Ahiman appears three times in the Bible, always as one of the three sons of Anak who lived in Hebron. First mentioned during the exploration of the promised land (Numbers 13:22), he reappears when Caleb drives him out of Hebron (Joshua 15:14), and then during Judah's campaign against the city (Judges 1:10). These three passages recount the same Israelite victory seen from three different angles: the moment of recognizing the danger, followed by its resolution.
H0289G.portee: The mention of Ahiman and his brothers three times shows how significant this exploit was for the people of Israel. That terrifying giants could be defeated and driven out of Hebron taught future generations that God's promise was stronger than any obstacle, even the most imposing enemies. It is a concrete sign of God's faithfulness to His covenant.

sens: Levite doorkeeper of the temple at the time of the return from exile
H0289H.detail: Achiman is a member of the tribe of Levi who served as a doorkeeper at the temple after the return from exile. He is mentioned alongside Shallum, Akkub, and Talmon, all responsible for guarding the doors of the sanctuary (1 Chronicles 9:17). His role was to control access to the temple and ensure the proper order of worship, an important function entrusted to the Levites.
H0289H.origine: The name Achiman literally means "my brother is a gift" in Hebrew, formed from "ach" (brother) and "man" (gift). This name expresses a blessing or divine recognition. It is noteworthy that the same name was borne by a son of Anak in an earlier time (Numbers 13:22), but the character mentioned in 1 Chronicles 9:17 is a Levite from the time of the return.
H0289H.emploi: Achiman appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 9:17, in a list of doorkeepers and guardians of the temple after the return from exile in Babylon. This passage enumerates those responsible for liturgical order and access to the sanctuary. Although little known, he represents those faithful Levites who contributed to the reconstruction and restoration of temple worship upon the return from exile.
H0289H.portee: Achiman reminds us of the importance of the humble and discreet service of the Levites in Israelite worship. Though almost forgotten in history, this temple doorkeeper participated in the crucial work of restoration for the people of God after exile. His existence invites us to recognize that any service rendered to the Lord, even if unnoticed by men, holds value before God.

sens: Man from the time of the united monarchy in Israel
Father of Achinoam, wife of King Saul
H0290G.detail: 1. Achimaats is a character from the Old Testament living during the time of King Saul, when the kingdom of Israel was still unified under one king. He appears only once in the preserved biblical text, making him a minor figure in the history of Israel. 2. He is known as the father of Achinoam, who became the wife of King Saul (1 Samuel 14:50). This alliance connected him to the royal family.
H0290G.origine: The name Achimaats means "my brother is anger" or "my brother is fury" in Hebrew. It combines the elements "achi" (my brother) and "maats" (anger, fury). This type of theophoric name, where a familial relationship or emotion is associated with God, was common in ancient Hebrew onomastics.
H0290G.emploi: Achimaats appears only once in the biblical texts that have come down to us: in 1 Samuel 14:50, where he is identified as the father of Achinoam, the wife of Saul, the first king of Israel. The narrative mentions him in passing, listing the king's relatives and officers of his court. Despite this unique presence in the biblical text, later Jewish tradition distinguishes him from several other Achimaats mentioned in other rabbinic texts or in extended genealogies.

sens: Son of the high priest Zadok
Brave messenger in the service of King David
Trusted man during Absalom's rebellion
H0290H.detail: Achimaats is a character from the Old Testament living during the time of the united monarchy. He is the son of the high priest Zadok. During Absalom's rebellion against King David, Achimaats plays a crucial role: he serves as a messenger to communicate secretly with David. Along with Jonathan, son of the priest Abiathar, he hides near En-Roguel and receives information that a servant transmits to him to carry to the king (2 Samuel 17:17). His greatest action occurs after the battle: he asks Joab for permission to run and announce to David the victory and the death of Absalom. Although Joab initially sends Cushite, Achimaats insists and is allowed to go as well (2 Samuel 18:23). He arrives first to the king to shout the good news: "All is well!" (2 Samuel 18:28).
H0290H.origine: The name Achimaats means "my brother is anger (or wrath)" in Hebrew. He belongs to a family of great importance among the priests: he is the son of Zadok, who would become one of the greatest priests of Israel under David and Solomon. His descendants hold a major place in the priesthood for generations to come (see 1 Chronicles 6:8-9).
H0290H.emploi: Achimaats is mentioned thirteen times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the account of Absalom's rebellion (2 Samuel 15-18). He is portrayed as a loyal, swift, and bold young man. During David's flight, King Zadok entrusts Achimaats and Jonathan with the mission of espionage: they must stay near the city, receive information through a servant, and carry it to David in exile (2 Samuel 17:17). After the military victory, Achimaats shows his zeal by asking to run and announce the good news to the king (2 Samuel 18:19). Although Joab initially chooses another messenger, Achimaats confidently insists: "Whatever happens, I want to run" (2 Samuel 18:23). He even surpasses his competitor and arrives first to deliver the message. He is later found in the priestly genealogies (1 Chronicles 6:8-9 and 6:53), indicating that he founded a respectable lineage of priests.
H0290H.portee: Achimaats embodies faithfulness and courage in the service of the king and God. His willingness to put himself in danger for David, even in the face of uncertainty, illustrates the dedication of a loyal heart. His eagerness to announce the good news of a victory from the Lord also reminds us of the importance of carrying the message of salvation with eagerness and confidence.

sens: Officer in charge of provisions for King Solomon
H0290I.detail: Achimaats is an officer responsible for supplying the court of King Solomon, specifically for the region of Naphtali (1 Kings 4:15). He holds an administrative position in the territorial organization of the united kingdom.
H0290I.origine: The name Achimaats literally means "my brother is anger" or "my brother is irritation" (from Hebrew "achî" = my brother, and "mâats" = anger or disdain). It is a common theophoric name in Israel that places a fraternal relationship under the sign of emotion, perhaps to express a difficult context at birth.
H0290I.emploi: Achimaats appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 4:15, where he is listed among the twelve officers that Solomon had placed throughout Israel to collect taxes in kind and provide for the needs of the court. This role shows that he was a trusted man of the king, important enough to administer an entire region. He was married to Basemath, daughter of King Solomon, which strengthened his status and ties to the royal family.

sens: man of the tribe of Manasseh
son of Shemida
H0291.detail: Achjan is a man belonging to the tribe of Manasseh, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Shemida and the brother of Shechem, Likchi, and Aniam (1 Chronicles 7:19). His name means "brotherly" or "having a brotherly character," which is fitting as he is always mentioned alongside his brothers in the genealogy.
H0291.origine: The name Achjan comes from a Hebrew root that evokes brotherhood and family ties. Its meaning "brotherly" connects it to the importance of family lineage in the genealogy of Israel.
H0291.emploi: Achjan appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:19, in the list of descendants of Manasseh. He is a genealogist whose role is simply to record the continuity of the tribes and families of Israel. Although little known, he is part of the genealogical history of God's people.

sens: Son of Iddo, supply officer for King Solomon
H0292.detail: Achinadab is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 4:14. He is a son of Iddo who served as the officer responsible for the food supply of King Solomon. He was particularly in charge of providing provisions for the royal court in the district of Mahanaim, east of the Jordan. This role shows that Solomon organized his kingdom into administrative districts, each with a leader.
H0292.origine: The Hebrew name Achinadab is composed of two elements: "achi" meaning "my brother" and "nadab" meaning "to be willing, generous, noble." The name thus means "my brother is generous" or "my brother is noble." It was a name borne by high-ranking individuals, often linked to royal administration.
H0292.emploi: Achinadab appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 4:14, where he is presented as one of the twelve officers that Solomon established to provide for the needs of his court and administration. He was the son of Iddo and was responsible for supplying the royal palace from the district of Mahanaim. This mention is part of an administrative list that illustrates the organization of Solomon's empire at its height.

sens: wife of Saul, mother of Jonathan, Abinadab, Malchi-shua, Merab, and Michal
H0293G.detail: Achinoam is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 14:50, as the wife of King Saul and the daughter of Ahitub. She is the mother of five children: Jonathan (who became famous for his friendship with David), Abinadab, Malchi-shua, Merab, and Michal. She is a figure from the time of the united monarchy, linked to the first royal dynasty of Israel.
H0293G.origine: The name Achinoam means "my brother is joy" or "my brother is delight" ("achi" = my brother, "noam" = delight, sweetness). It is a typical compound name of ancient Hebrew, formed from a familial bond and a positive quality, like many proper names in Israel. There is also another Achinoam in the Old Testament, the wife of King David and mother of Amnon, but she belongs to a different time period.
H0293G.emploi: Achinoam appears only once by name in the preserved biblical text: in 1 Samuel 14:50, during the presentation of Saul as king of Israel. She is introduced as part of the genealogical context of the royal dynasty, alongside Abner, the commander of the army. Her importance is subtle but real: she is the mother of Jonathan, the second king de facto despite the rivalry with David, and of Michal, who will become David's wife. She embodies the royal wife at the time of the establishment of the Israelite monarchy.

sens: Wife of David during the United Kingdom
Mother of Amnon, David's firstborn son
From Jezreel
H0293H.detail: 1. Achinoam is a woman whom David took as a wife during his flight from Saul, while he was still in distress and wandering: she is mentioned alongside Abigail as one of his two main wives (1 Samuel 25:43). 2. She is the mother of Amnon, the first son that David had in Israel: this son was born in Hebron, David's capital at the beginning of his reign (2 Samuel 3:2). 3. She came from Jezreel, a city in the north (1 Samuel 25:43), which shows that David had connections with different regions of the country.
H0293H.origine: The name means in Hebrew "my brother is delight" or "my brother is joy" — a composition of the word "brother" (akh) and a term evoking sweetness or richness. This type of compound name was common in royal and noble families during the time of the United Kingdom.
H0293H.emploi: Achinoam appears six times in the Scriptures, always in the books of Samuel and Chronicles, which recount the story of David. She is first presented among the women that David marries during his life of wandering before becoming king (1 Samuel 25:43 and 27:3), then mentioned after the destruction of Ziklag where she is captured (1 Samuel 30:5), and then reappears in Hebron at the beginning of David's reign (2 Samuel 2:2). She is especially known as the mother of Amnon (2 Samuel 3:2; 1 Chronicles 3:1), which gives her an important place in the royal genealogy of David.
H0293H.portee: Achinoam illustrates the place of women in the history of God's people: although she has few actions of her own, she is the mother of an heir to David's throne and remains faithfully with him during his years of flight and precariousness. Her name, which means "my brother is delight," invites reflection on joy and brotherly bonds — an inner beauty that must have attracted David despite the perils of the time.

sens: Man of the tribe of Dan, father of Aholiab
Father of a skilled artisan for the construction of the tabernacle
H0294.detail:
1. Ahisamac is a man of the tribe of Dan mentioned three times in the book of Exodus. His name means "my brother is a support" or "my brother has supported," expressing trust in God. He is the father of Aholiab, a highly skilled worker.
2. Aholiab, son of Ahisamac, played an important role in the construction of the tabernacle under the direction of Moses. Although we see Ahisamac himself only in the background, he is presented as the father of a man to whom God has given wisdom, artistic talent, and teaching ability for the delicate works of the sanctuary (engraving, embroidery, weaving of dyed fabrics).
H0294.origine: The name Ahisamac combines two Hebrew elements: "ach" (brother) and "samach" (to support, to strengthen). The name reflects a spiritual trust: the brother is a support, an assurance. It is a typically Hebrew name, carrying a dimension of faith.
H0294.emploi: Ahisamac is mentioned only in Exodus (three occurrences: 31:6, 35:34, 38:23), always as the father of Aholiab. The Bible tells us nothing about him personally, except that he fathered a son gifted by God. His name appears in the context of the tabernacle project: God equips Aholiab with specialized talents, and the mention of his father emphasizes that this gift comes from the Lord who spans generations.
H0294.portee: Ahisamac reminds us that God honors talents and that excellence in service to God is passed down and recognized even among those who remain discreet. His son Aholiab shines with his skills; the father, though overshadowed, is part of the history of God's people.

sens: Leader of the tribe of Dan during the desert period
Son of Ammishaddai
H0295G.detail: 1. Ahiézer is a leader of the tribe of Dan designated to assist Moses during the counting and organization of the people in the desert. His name means "my brother is a help" — thus, he embodies the idea of aid and support. He appears several times in the organizational texts of the Book of Numbers, notably to lead the camp of Dan (Numbers 2:25) and to present the offering of his tribe during the dedication of the altar (Numbers 7:66). 2. Ahiézer is the son of Ammishaddai, which places him in a lineage that legitimizes his role as a leader. This lineage is consistently mentioned in every occurrence, showing the importance of genealogy in the structure of the organized people.
H0295G.origine: The name Ahiézer is composed of two Hebrew elements: "ahi" (brother) and "ezer" (help, aid). This construction expresses a relationship of protection and fraternal assistance. The word "ezer" appears in other biblical contexts to designate divine help or assistance provided by an ally, emphasizing that help comes from a relationship of intimacy and trust.
H0295G.emploi: Ahiézer appears five times in the Book of Numbers, always in an organizational or ceremonial context. He is first named among the leaders of the tribes during the first census (Numbers 1:12), then tasked with leading the camp of Dan during the journey in the desert (Numbers 2:25 and 10:25), where the tribe of Dan formed the rear guard of the entire assembly — an important and honorable position. Finally, he is mentioned during the altar dedication ceremonies (Numbers 7:66 and 7:71), when each tribal leader presented his offering. His role remains consistent: that of a responsible and faithful leader in his service.

sens: Danite military chief in the service of David
H0295H.detail: Achiézer is a chief of the tribe of Dan who joined David at Ziklag, at the time when he was fleeing from King Saul. He appears in the list of mighty warriors who sided with David (1 Chronicles 12:3), alongside his brother Joash, both sons of Schemaah of Gibeah. He is a man of military value, counted among the valiant who supported David even before he became king.
H0295H.origine: The name Achiézer literally means "my brother is help" or "my brother is a support." It is composed of two Hebrew elements: "ach" (brother) and "ezer" (help, support). This type of theophoric name, which evokes divine help or fraternal assistance, was common in ancient Israel to express trust in divine or familial protection.
H0295H.emploi: Achiézer appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:3. He is mentioned as one of the military leaders of Dan who came to Ziklag to reinforce David's ranks during his flight from Saul. His appearance in this list of valiant warriors indicates his importance in the military support that the tribes of Israel provided to David, who was to become king. He is identified as the son of Schemaah and the brother of Joash.
H0295H.portee: The account of Achiézer shows us how, even before David's establishment as king, men of value and courage from different tribes united to support him. It is a reminder that the Davidic kingship did not impose itself alone, but was built on the faithfulness and commitment of courageous warriors. For the reader, this illustrates the importance of fraternal support and solidarity in God's great projects.

sens: Son of Shaphan, officer of King Josiah
Protector of the prophet Jeremiah
Father of Gedaliah, governor of Judah after the exile
H0296.detail: Achikam is a key figure in the history of Judah at the end of the Southern Kingdom. He is first known as the son of Shaphan, an influential royal secretary during the reign of King Josiah (2 Kings 22:12). He plays a crucial role in protecting the prophet Jeremiah: when the leaders of Jerusalem wanted to put him to death, Achikam intervenes on his behalf (Jeremiah 26:24). After the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C., Achikam is no longer directly mentioned, but his son Gedaliah becomes governor of the cities of Judah under the authority of the king of Babylon (Jeremiah 40:5-9). Gedaliah continues his father's work by offering security and stability to the remaining people, until his assassination.
H0296.origine: The name Achikam means "my brother has risen" or "my brother has stood up" in Hebrew. It is composed of "achi" (my brother) and "qam" (has risen). This patronymic evokes the idea of fraternal help or providential intervention. Achikam belongs to a family of scribes and high officials influential in royal administration.
H0296.emploi: Achikam appears 20 times in the Bible, mainly in Kings, Chronicles, and especially in Jeremiah. He is first mentioned as an officer in the service of King Josiah, tasked with consulting the prophetess Huldah (2 Kings 22:12). His role becomes clearer in Jeremiah: he defends the prophet threatened with death (Jeremiah 26:24), then releases him after the capture of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 39:14). Most of his mentions in Jeremiah 40-43 concern him indirectly, through his son Gedaliah, who governs Judah and carries on his legacy of kindness towards the survivors and towards Jeremiah.
H0296.portee: Achikam illustrates the role of faithful believers placed in positions of authority: he uses his influence to protect the word of God embodied by Jeremiah, at the risk of opposing other leaders. His example shows that high influence can serve to preserve the prophetic testimony. His son Gedaliah extends this faithfulness by governing with justice and mercy after the catastrophe, offering refuge to the survivors. The family of Achikam reminds us that God always preserves a remnant and places in the hearts of some a compassion for their own.

sens: Son of Benjamin and chief of a tribal family
H0297.detail: 1. Achiram is a son of Benjamin, mentioned only once in the Bible during the census of the tribes in the desert. He represents a lineage of the tribe of Benjamin: from him descends the family of the Achiramites, which bears his name (Numbers 26:38). He lived during the time of Egypt and the desert, among the ancestors of Israel.
H0297.origine: The name Achiram means "my brother is exalted" or "brother of the lofty" — it expresses the idea that the brother (probably the elder brother, Benjamin) occupies a prominent or exalted place. It is a common Hebrew name of the patronymic type, formed with the possessive suffix "my."
H0297.emploi: Achiram appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:38, in the context of the second census of the Israelites in the desert, before entering the Promised Land. He is listed among the sons of Benjamin, alongside Bela, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, Ard, and Jediael. This passage shows how the tribes of Israel organized themselves around their eponymous ancestors, each family bearing the name of its founder.

sens: member of the clan of Ahiram, one of the sons of Benjamin
H0298.detail: 1. The Achiramites are the descendants of Ahiram, one of the sons of Benjamin. They form a family or clan within the tribe of Benjamin, listed with the other Benjamite families in the census of the people of Israel in the desert (Numbers 26:38).
H0298.origine: The word comes from the name "Ahiram," whose root means "brother of the mother." Achiramite is the gentilitial name, that is, the name given to members of the same family or clan: this is how the Bible designates family groups descended from a founding ancestor, like the Balites for the descendants of Bela or the Ashbelites for those of Ashbel.
H0298.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:38, during the second census of the Israelites in the desert, after the rebellion of Korah. The heads of families and warriors of each tribe are counted, and the text systematically lists the clans descended from each son of Benjamin. The Achiramites are included as one of these officially recognized clans.

sens: Leader of the tribe of Naphtali at the time of the departure from Egypt
H0299.detail: 1. Ahira is the prince designated to represent the tribe of Naphtali during the census of the Israelites in the wilderness. He first appears in Numbers 1:15 as the son of Enan, chosen for this responsibility. His role as a tribal leader places him among the twelve princes who lead the twelve tribes of Israel during the Exodus.
H0299.origine: The name Ahira literally means "my brother is evil" or "my brother is wicked" in Hebrew. It is composed of two elements: "ahi" (my brother) and "ra" (evil, wickedness). Although the meaning of the name is enigmatic, it may reflect an invocation or acceptance of a difficult reality, or it was borne without a direct connection to its literal meaning, as is often the case with biblical names.
H0299.emploi: Ahira is mentioned five times in the book of Numbers, all passages related to the departure from Egypt and the organization of the people in the wilderness. He appears in Numbers 1:15 during the census, in Numbers 2:29 when the marching order is established, and in Numbers 7:78-83 when he presents the offering of the princes to the Lord. Finally, he is cited in Numbers 10:27 at the head of the army of Naphtali during the departure from the wilderness of Sinai. Ahira thus represents tribal authority confirmed in all key moments of the organization of God's people.
